His music accompanied the happiest days of Laura’s childhood.
pages.brief: Four-year-old Laura rides in a covered wagon and watches the prairie slide away behind her. Back in Wisconsin she throws snowballs with her cousins among tall, dark trees, and on a long winter evening Pa plays his fiddle while the family gathers close.

pages.text: Hard Times “Everything from the little house was in the wagon, except the beds and tables and chairs. Pa could always make new ones.” —Laura Ingalls Wilder Pa Ingalls was a restless man, and he longed to return to the open space of the prairies. He made plans to relocate his young family to Minnesota. They faced difficulties even before they left. Laura caught scarlet fever, so the family bundled her in every blanket they owned before nestling her in the back of the covered wagon. Seven-year- old Laura watched her silent, snow-covered home disappear behind her. In Minnesota, Laura and Pa were happy to be back on the wide-open prairie. First, they moved into a sod house constructed from dense mats of grass roots, which appeared from a distance to be nothing more than a gentle hill rising from the banks of a creek. Later, Pa constructed a wood house and planted wheat near the town of Walnut Grove. Laura and Mary went to school, where Laura loved reading, writing, and reciting. Ma was expecting another baby.
pages.brief: Seven-year-old Laura, sick with scarlet fever, is bundled in blankets in the back of a covered wagon as her silent, snow-covered home disappears behind her. Later the family lives in a low sod house by a creek, then a wood house with wheat near Walnut Grove.

pages.text: After a few months of happiness, hardship struck. Grasshoppers, descending in swarms as big as thunderclouds, devoured the family’s wheat. Having lost their crop, the family moved into Walnut Grove and took odd jobs. Even little Laura cleaned and waited tables in a hotel. Then they lost their new baby brother, Freddie, to a fever. Their spirits lifted a little when another baby, Grace, arrived in 1877, but times remained tough. Mary fell ill, and either the illness or a stroke damaged the nerves of her eyes. No one knows for sure what caused the damage, but Mary would be blind for the rest of her life. Pa decided it was time to head west in search of a new start. Laura, right, stands beside her sisters Carrie, left, and Mary around 1880.
pages.brief: Grasshoppers come down in swarms as big as thunderclouds, darkening the sky and stripping the family's wheat field bare. Laura stands in the ruined field, and later she cleans and waits tables in a Walnut Grove hotel, with her sisters Carrie and Mary beside her around 1880.

pages.text: Settling in Dakota Territory The family boarded a train in Walnut Grove and rode west to join Pa, who had gone ahead to Dakota Territory to work. Eleven-year-old Laura described the hulking, smoking train, the ornately decorated cars, and the golden blur of wheat fields speeding by as Mary hung on every word. When they got off the train, there was no settlement— just a railroad stop. The Ingalls family and a few other white families were the first citizens of what would later become the town of De Smet, South Dakota. Pa built some of the first buildings, including the first store. As more settlers arrived, the Ingalls family acquired a homestead a few miles outside of town, and Pa built a cabin, a stable, and a garden. When winter came, the family resided above their store in town, where the girls would be closer to school. Did You Know? The U.S. government encouraged white settler-colonists to move west and offered homesteads, or nearly free living space, on land stolen from Native people. At that time, the U.S. government did not consider Native people citizens. Like many white settler-colonists, Laura had racist views of the Native people on whose land she lived. Her books often erase or present Native peoples in a negative way, while glorifying the white settler-colonists.
pages.brief: The family boards a train, and eleven-year-old Laura describes the hulking, smoking engine, the ornately decorated cars, and the golden blur of wheat fields while Mary listens. They step off at a lone railroad stop on open Dakota prairie, where Pa builds some of the first buildings.

pages.text: It was a lucky decision because one blizzard after another hammered the new town. The snow was so blinding that the girls couldn’t find their way to school. Trains couldn’t deliver food, and some families nearly starved. Laura and her sisters spent hours grinding raw wheat into flour by hand. A young man named Almanzo Wilder trudged through the snow to the only established farm in the area. He returned bearing all the wheat the farmer could spare, saving the settlers’ lives. It was not the last time Laura would hear about this good man.
pages.brief: Blizzard after blizzard hammers the new town, snow so blinding the girls cannot find the school. Laura and her sisters sit indoors grinding raw wheat into flour by hand, while young Almanzo Wilder trudges through deep snow to bring back wheat that saves the settlers.

pages.text: Young Lady Laura “Suffering passes, while love is eternal.” —Laura Ingalls Wilder At last the long winter broke, and the family returned to their homestead on the blooming Dakota prairie. Their farm, and the new town, soon thrived. Mary had heard about a college for blind students in Iowa, and she wanted more than anything to attend. Laura was now old enough to teach school, and she knew the income would help Mary pay for college. She accepted a teaching job in a settlement twelve miles from De Smet. Sixteen-year-old Laura bravely said goodbye to her family, but she dreaded being away from home for an entire semester. When the first week of school ended, she got a wonderful surprise. Almanzo Wilder, the young man who had helped save De Smet, pulled up to the schoolhouse in a beautiful horse-drawn sleigh, offering to bring Laura home on weekends. During their long drives across the prairie, their friendship blossomed into love. One night, Almanzo asked Laura to marry him. She said yes.
pages.brief: Sixteen-year-old Laura says goodbye to her family and takes a teaching job twelve miles from De Smet. When the first week ends, Almanzo Wilder pulls up to the schoolhouse in a beautiful horse-drawn sleigh, and during long drives across the prairie their friendship turns to love.

pages.text: Laura and Manly, as she nicknamed him, moved to his homestead outside De Smet, and soon they welcomed a daughter, Rose. Unfortunately, the young family was then hit with a string of bad luck. A hailstorm destroyed their wheat crop, and then Laura and Manly contracted a dangerous infection. Laura recovered fully, but Manly would walk with a limp for the rest of his life. Laura gave birth to a baby boy, but he only survived for two weeks. Then their house burned to the ground. Still a settler, Laura searched for a new place where they could get a fresh start, and it wasn’t long before she found her home. Laura stands next to Almanzo Wilder in 1885, shortly after their marriage. Sickness in Settler Days Before the twentieth century, people had few vaccines and very few effective medicines, so diseases were common and serious. Many members of Laura’s family were touched by illness, which was not unusual for the times.
pages.brief: Laura stands beside Almanzo Wilder in 1885, soon after their marriage, with their baby daughter Rose. A hailstorm flattens their wheat, Manly walks with a limp after a dangerous infection, and their house burns to the ground.

pages.text: Happiness at Rocky Ridge “It is the sweet, simple things of life which are the real ones after all.” —Laura Ingalls Wilder One day, a visitor presented Laura with a gleaming red apple from the Ozark Mountains. Twenty-seven-year-old Laura set out once more in a covered wagon, but this time, she headed east, toward the land of that beautiful apple. Laura and Manly bought an unassuming farm near Mansfield, Missouri, in the foothills of the Ozarks. It was rough, wooded, and rocky, but Laura instantly knew it was home. It took years of chopping trees, hauling rocks, plowing, building, and planting, but Rocky Ridge grew into a beautiful, prosperous farm. After a lifetime of wandering, Laura was content in her home. Rose, Laura’s daughter, inherited Pa’s restless spirit. Intelligent and ambitious, she moved away to San Francisco, where she became a respected journalist. One summer, Laura visited her adult daughter in California. She wrote to Manly, describing the towering redwoods, the glittering city, and the thundering Pacific Ocean. Rose was making a living at something Laura had always loved—writing. Now that life on her farm was comfortable, could Laura do the same?
pages.brief: Laura holds a gleaming red apple from the Ozark Mountains, then travels east by covered wagon with Manly to a rough, wooded, rocky farm near Mansfield, Missouri. She chops trees, hauls rocks, plows and plants until Rocky Ridge becomes a prosperous farm.

pages.text: The Little House Books Once home, Laura began to pour her memories onto the page, sometimes staying up all night writing at a little desk that Manly built for her. Soon she had written an entire book about her early years under the towering trees of Wisconsin, which she titled Little House in the Big Woods. Rose sent it to a publisher. Sixty-four-year-old Laura didn’t think much would come of it. After all, it was the 1930s. People had cars, electricity, radio—who wanted to hear about doing backbreaking chores in a dark forest? The book was an immediate sensation. Laura brought to life the howling winter wind, the crackling fire, and the joyful skip of Pa’s fiddle. She captured the thrill of meeting animals in the wilderness, and she evoked the joy that a simple rag doll could bring to a settler girl who lived in a rough log cabin. The mailbox at Rocky Ridge overflowed with letters from young readers begging for more. Laura recounted her time on the Kansas prairie in Little House on the Prairie and near Walnut Grove in On the Banks of Plum Creek. The frightful winter in De Smet became The Long Winter, and the town’s recovery became Little Town on the Prairie.
pages.brief: Laura stays up all night writing at a little desk Manly built, memories of Wisconsin, Kansas and De Smet pouring onto the page. The mailbox at Rocky Ridge overflows with letters from young readers begging for more books.

pages.text: Laura Ingalls Wilder smiles as she signs copies of her books sometime around 1940. Laura loved answering letters from her fans and traveling to readings and book signings, but she was always happy to return home to Manly and Rocky Ridge Farm. The couple both lived into their nineties. After Laura’s death in 1957, her books lived on, even becoming a TV series in 1974. Laura Ingalls Wilder’s stories of settler life still captivate young readers today. Her life has become part of American history.
pages.brief: Laura Ingalls Wilder smiles as she signs copies of her books around 1940, readers crowding around her table. Later she is at home again at Rocky Ridge with Manly, and her stories of settler life live on with young readers today.

books.title: Animal Discoveries
books.art_why: The book is about real animals and real scientific work that exist today, not a named famous person.

pages.text: Animal Discoveries.
pages.brief: A title-page scene for a book about animal discoveries, with many different animals from forests, oceans, and mountains visible near and far in a wide natural landscape, as if waiting to be found by curious young readers.

pages.text: The Bonaire banded box jellyfish’s scientific name is Tamoya ohboya. The name was chosen in a contest. The winner said most people would say “Oh boy!” when seeing the jellyfish. Introduction Question: If you wanted to discover a new animal species, where would you look? Answer: In places nobody has looked before. Many newly discovered species are found on expeditions to remote corners of Earth, while others may be discovered under a microscope. A species’ DNA can differentiate it from other species that may look similar. Some new life forms, though, are found in places people frequent and pass by every day. Scientists discover more than 15,000 animal species each year, which is about 1 percent of the more than 1.5 million species we know about already. At the same time, extinction is wiping out species at record rates around the globe. So each new species is an exciting and important discovery.
pages.brief: A Bonaire banded box jellyfish floats in dark blue seawater. Nearby, a scientist on a remote expedition studies a microscope and samples, while other researchers search in everyday places for new life forms and compare DNA from similar-looking animals.

pages.text: Monkey Mania In 2007, a new species of monkey was identified in the remote forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The lesula has large, expressive eyes and is described as shy and quiet. The first one found by scientists was being kept as a girl’s pet. The lesula was the first new species of monkey found in twenty-eight years. Yet in 2010, scientists found another new monkey by listening to its complex calls. The Caquetá titi monkey lives in the Amazon jungle of Colombia, along with about twenty other species of titi monkey. What distinguishes it from other titi monkeys is its bushy red beard and the absence of a white bar on its forehead. Another unique feature of this species: Its babies purr like cats. A healthy population of these monkeys should be in the thousands. However, fewer than 250 Caquetá titi monkeys are thought to exist today, so the newly discovered titi monkey is already considered endangered. lesula monkey Caquetá titi monkey.
pages.brief: A lesula monkey with large, expressive eyes sits quietly in the remote forest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. A Caquetá titi monkey with a bushy red beard climbs in the Amazon jungle of Colombia, and a tiny titi baby purrs like a cat nearby.

pages.text: Freaky, Fabulous Frogs No bigger than a pea, the Matang narrow- mouthed frog is one of the smallest known frogs in the world. It was discovered on Borneo, an island in Southeast Asia, in 2010. Although examples of these frogs are found in century-old museum collections, scientists simply thought they were juveniles of a different species. They learned otherwise when they heard the frogs calling at dusk from pitcher plants. Since only adult frogs make calls, scientists concluded that these tiny frogs must be full-grown. Matang narrow-mouthed frog Narrow-mouthed frog tadpoles in a pitcher plant Do You Know? Pitcher plants are important to the Matang narrow- mouthed frog because female frogs deposit their eggs on the sides of the pitcher and tadpoles grow in the liquid that gathers inside the plant.
pages.brief: A Matang narrow-mouthed frog, no bigger than a pea, sits on a pitcher plant in Borneo. Tadpoles grow in the liquid inside the pitcher, while adult frogs call at dusk from the plants, showing scientists that these tiny frogs are full-grown.

pages.text: The long-nosed tree frog is also known as the spike-nosed tree frog. A herpetologist discovered another frog species, the long-nosed tree frog, during an expedition to the Foja Mountains of New Guinea in 2010. The area is so remote, and so recently explored, that it has been nicknamed the “Lost World.” This tree frog is notable not for its size but rather for its long, unique nose. When the male frog calls, its nose points upward like a spike, and when the frog is done calling, its nose falls. No one knows why it does this. The frog was nicknamed the Pinocchio frog due to its long nose. The herpetologist spotted it sitting on a bag of rice in his campsite.
pages.brief: A long-nosed tree frog sits on a bag of rice in a campsite in the remote Foja Mountains of New Guinea. The male frog points its long nose upward like a spike as it calls in the recently explored Lost World area.

pages.text: When the blossom bat feeds on nectar, it also helps pollinate the flower, which can then make seeds to grow new plants. Furry Finds Another discovery from the same 2010 Foja Mountains expedition was the blossom bat. Although bats are mammals, this one has been called the “hummingbird of the bat world” because it uses its long tongue to drink nectar from the flowers of rainforest trees. A 2005 expedition to another island—Madagascar—uncovered Goodman’s mouse lemurs. Not much bigger than mice, these tiny lemurs jump around in the trees at night. In the daytime, they sometimes sleep in vacant birds’ nests. Do You Know? Lemurs are only found in Madagascar. Goodman’s mouse lemurs.
pages.brief: A blossom bat uses its long tongue to drink nectar from a rainforest flower, helping pollinate the plant. On Madagascar, Goodman’s mouse lemurs, tiny and mouse-sized, jump through trees at night; by day they sometimes sleep in empty birds’ nests.

pages.text: Sazima’s tarantulas are only found in the tabletop mountains of Brazil, which have a different climate than the surrounding area. Interesting Invertebrates Scientists estimate that vertebrates—animals with backbones—represent only 3 percent of all species. They include those species that are the most familiar (and similar) to us: amphibians, reptiles, birds, fish, and mammals. The remaining 97 percent of animal species known to science are invertebrates—animals without backbones. Tarantulas can be one of the more frightening invertebrates. They’re big and hairy, come in about nine hundred species, and are predators. The largest species can kill small mammals, lizards, and birds. Sazima’s tarantula, however, has a special beauty. Its dark blue body almost glows. This fantastic arachnid has an extremely limited habitat, only living high in the mountains of Brazil.
pages.brief: Sazima’s tarantula, dark blue and almost glowing, stands high in the tabletop mountains of Brazil. Around it, other big hairy tarantulas show the variety of invertebrate predators, while scientists note that invertebrates make up most animal species.

pages.text: Like most insects, planthoppers go through stages of development. This young planthopper is just beginning to develop wings. The “troll-haired” planthopper, discovered in 2013 in the rainforest of South America, may not be good-looking, but at least it has good hair. The wild hair isn’t hair at all, but instead waxy secretions from the insect’s belly. The theory is that when a predator attacks it, the “hair” breaks off and the planthopper can jump to safety, but scientists have yet to confirm this theory.
pages.brief: A young troll-haired planthopper rests on a rainforest plant in South America, its wild-looking waxy secretions sticking up from its belly. The insect is beginning to develop wings, and the strange hair-like tufts are thought to break off if a predator attacks.

pages.text: The Gorgon’s head starfish is named for the Gorgons from Greek mythology, which had hundreds of snakes on their heads instead of hair. Underwater Wonders Scientists discovered the Gorgon’s head starfish in 2010, about half a mile (800 m) beneath the surface of the North Atlantic Ocean. The Gorgon’s head, a species of basket star, has five curly, branching arm-like appendages that split off from its body. The five appendages include as many as five thousand tips. The tips help this basket star feed on plankton and shrimp floating by in the water. It also uses its appendages to walk along the seabed. They even protect the animal when it’s disturbed by curling around it to form a tight ball. Since Earth’s oceans are vast, large portions have yet to be explored. However, that’s not the reason it took until 2013 to discover the walking bamboo shark.
pages.brief: The Gorgon’s head starfish, a basket star with five curly branching arms, floats deep in the North Atlantic Ocean. Its many tips catch plankton and shrimp, and its arms curl around it into a tight ball when the animal is disturbed.

pages.text: The walking bamboo shark has different patterns of spots and bands than other bamboo sharks. Like most sharks, the walking bamboo shark is no threat to humans. It lives off the coast of Indonesia. Scientists discovered it because its coloration differs from that of other bamboo sharks. This new species is thought to reach about 30 inches (80 cm) in length. It uses its fins to push itself along the ocean floor in search of food. The wiggling movement makes it look as though the shark is walking. Because these sharks are so rare, the government of Indonesia is taking steps to protect them.
pages.brief: A walking bamboo shark pushes itself along the ocean floor off the coast of Indonesia, using its fins in a wiggling movement that looks like walking. Its spotted and banded pattern differs from other bamboo sharks, and the rare shark is protected by the Indonesian government.

pages.text: Hiding in Plain View The olinguito (oh-lin-GEE-toh) managed to escape notice for so long by being mistaken for something else. In 2013, researchers discovered that for more than a hundred years, the olinguito had been wrongly identified. This mammal, which looks a lot like a teddy bear, leaps through trees at night. The smallest member of the raccoon family, the olinguito can be found in Ecuador and Colombia. It is the first species of this type to be discovered in the Americas in thirty-five years. Mistaken Identity Humans may encounter an unidentified species for years while mistaking it for a familiar species. This often happens because the two species look similar, at least on the outside. These are called cryptic species. They are only found to be distinct when scientists study their genetic code. As DNA technology is used more and more, reports of distinct new species are on the rise.
pages.brief: An olinguito, a small mammal that looks like a teddy bear, leaps through trees at night in Ecuador or Colombia. Researchers study its genetic code to separate it from similar-looking cryptic species, because it had been mistaken for something else for more than a hundred years.

pages.text: Finding new species of birds is almost as rare as finding new mammals. Finding one in a major city is rarer still. Yet in 2009, researchers discovered the Cambodian tailorbird in and around Phnom Penh—including in the middle of a road construction site. A detailed set of tests revealed that this tailorbird was a separate, new species. Besides studying its genes and feathers, scientists studied its pretty song. While all tailorbirds warble, no two species sound quite the same. Sure enough, the song of the Cambodian tailorbird sets it apart from all the rest.
pages.brief: A Cambodian tailorbird sings in and around Phnom Penh, including near a road construction site. Researchers study its genes, feathers, and pretty song, finding that its warbling song sets it apart from all other tailorbirds.

pages.text: Number of Species Discovered by Type 2000–2009 1 Insects: 88,598 2 Plants: 23,604 3 Arachnids: 12,751 4 Fungi: 11,984 5 Crustaceans: 7,070 6 Mollusks: 5,949 7 Bacteria: 4,417 8 Fish: 3,587 9 All other: 18,351 What’s Next? Scientists continue to amaze us by finding new species. Estimates of just how many animal species fill our planet vary widely. However, experts agree that most have yet to be discovered. Those animals we have discovered highlight some challenges. For instance, many species have tiny populations. Human activity causes many species to face small and shrinking habitats.
pages.brief: Scientists and experts stand in a wide natural landscape filled with many kinds of animals, continuing to find new species while most remain undiscovered. Nearby, small groups of animals live in tiny populations as human activity shrinks their habitats.

books.title: Should Anyone Own the North Pole?
books.art_why: The Arctic, wildlife, ships, and people can be shown in real photographs.

pages.text: Introduction When you hear the words North Pole, do you think of a cold, empty place out in the middle of nowhere? Yes, it’s cold and remote, but it’s far from empty. Actually, the North Pole and the area around it—the Arctic region—are filled with natural wonders. Who should those treasures belong to— separate countries, all people, or the planet itself? Several countries are competing to own parts of the Arctic region beyond their own borders. These grabs for Arctic resources will affect not only the North Pole but all of Planet Earth. Sea ice surrounding the North Pole is visible from outer space.
pages.brief: A view from outer space shows Earth's northern cap, with the North Pole surrounded by broad fields of sea ice. The remote Arctic region appears cold and vast, while the ice stretches across the top of the planet and reveals the area's natural wonders.

pages.text: Geography The North Pole is in the Arctic Ocean, at the northernmost place on Earth. It’s surrounded by sea ice, which forms the Arctic ice cap. The size of the Arctic ice cap changes during different seasons as temperatures rise and fall. Overall, the Arctic ice cap has been shrinking at a rate of 3.2 percent every ten years since 1981. Scientists have evidence that the cause is climate change — permanent, lasting changes in Earth’s weather patterns. Five countries surround the North Pole: Norway, Russia, Canada, the United States, and Greenland. Each one owns an area that measures 200 nautical miles (230 mi., or 370 km) out from its coastline. Within those 200 nautical miles, each country or region controls the rights to resources. Those resources include water and wind for energy production as well as minerals and fish. Beyond that boundary are international waters. The International Seabed Authority (ISA) sets rules about taking mineral resources from the seafloor of the high seas. The ISA is part of an agreement between countries. The agreement states that international waters are supposed to benefit all people, not separate countries.
pages.brief: An aerial view shows the Arctic Ocean at the northernmost place on Earth, with the North Pole surrounded by sea ice that forms the Arctic ice cap. Coastlines of Norway, Russia, Canada, the United States, and Greenland lie around the icy ocean.

pages.text: Climate Change Earth’s climate patterns have been shifting over the past one hundred years. The past twenty years have seen many of the warmest years ever recorded. Not all parts of Earth are warming at the same rate. Even so, global air temperatures have increased about two degrees over the past century. Almost all scientists agree that an important cause of higher temperatures is carbon dioxide in Earth’s atmosphere. This gas is produced by human activities like burning coal to power factories and using petroleum products for cars. Carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere trap the Sun’s heat energy, preventing it from escaping into space. Scientists know this warming is linked to human activity because, currently, the climate is heating up about ten times faster than it heated up in other, naturally occurring warming periods. There are many different effects of climate change. Some places will experience droughts and extremely high temperatures, while other places will get more rainfall and hurricanes. In the ocean, coral reefs will die because coral can’t survive in high temperatures. And in the Arctic, climate change is causing glaciers and polar ice caps to melt and sea levels to rise.
pages.brief: A wide Arctic landscape shows glaciers and polar ice caps melting into the sea, with open water where ice once held. Above the scene, the atmosphere suggests trapped heat from the Sun, illustrating the warming climate described on the page.

pages.text: As of early 2014, 165 countries plus the European Union had ratified, or approved, this agreement. After approval, a country has ten years to file a request if it believes it deserves any areas beyond its exclusive economic zone (EEZ). If a country’s request is approved, all resources in the larger area belong to that country. Why might a country want to expand its territory? Carving Up the Arctic Circle The area measuring 200 nautical miles out from each country’s coastline is called an exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Exclusive: not shared by others Economic: related to buying and selling Zone: an area with a special purpose or set of rules Beyond those EEZs, some areas in the Arctic Circle belong to no one—at least for now.
pages.brief: An Arctic coastline meets open sea, with sea ice extending outward from shore. Beyond the coastal zone, the water stretches toward the horizon, suggesting the wide areas countries may claim and the international waters beyond their exclusive economic zones.

pages.text: Why the North Pole Is Valuable The Arctic region is the area north of the Arctic Circle. It has a wealth of natural resources. One of the ones people are most dependent on is petroleum, which includes both oil and natural gas. Although located under the Earth’s surface, petroleum is easier to reach now than in the past. That’s because the Arctic ice cap is melting. Right now, the Arctic region provides about 10 percent of the world’s oil and 25 percent of its natural gas. Experts estimate that an even larger supply of each may be discovered near the North Pole in the future. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, using petroleum-based energy causes a lot of pollution and is the main cause of climate change. Many climate scientists think that in order to reduce this pollution, countries will have to stop using petroleum-based energy immediately. However, petroleum products are the main energy sources around the world. We depend on them for more than half our energy. They’re nonrenewable, meaning they will run out someday—possibly as soon as forty to fifty years from now. As a result, many countries are scrambling for new supplies of petroleum. We could decrease our dependence on petroleum by using other energy sources, such as wind, solar, and electric power.
pages.brief: A broad Arctic scene shows a thinning ice cap over dark water, with an offshore oil and gas platform in the distance. The page explains that petroleum lies beneath the Earth's surface and becomes easier to reach as the ice cap melts.

pages.text: Beyond natural resources, the Arctic offers the promise of new shipping routes. Right now, most of those routes can be used only during warmer months, when much of the sea ice melts. However, with continued melting, routes may be open during much more of the year. For example, a ship recently traveled from northern Russia to China during February for the first time ever. Dangerous Business Obtaining natural resources in the Arctic region is riskier and more expensive than in most other parts of the globe. Here’s why: • Regular equipment can’t always handle the climate. Special equipment must be used (or, in some cases, developed) that can work in the extreme cold, wet conditions. • Transporting materials and people to and from such a remote location is expensive. • Higher wages need to be paid to people to work in such a remote place. • If accidents happen, the distance from search-and- rescue facilities might mean additional loss of life or increased damage to equipment or the environment. • Regular clean-up equipment can’t handle Arctic oil spills. Cleaning up oil spills in sea ice is much harder than in liquid water.
pages.brief: A cargo ship moves through broken sea ice in Arctic waters, following a route that may stay open longer as melting continues. Cold, remote conditions surround the vessel, showing the difficult environment for shipping and for transporting equipment and people.

pages.text: Scientists and environmental groups argue that the Arctic region is valuable not only to humans. It’s also valuable because of the natural environment and the wide variety of life forms it supports. These include tundra vegetation, caribou, polar bears, whales, and seals. Using more Arctic resources could upset the natural environment in many ways. Polar bears are already in danger of extinction, because of polar ice melt. Many scientists think that most polar bears will die out between 2050 and 2100. Scientists are also concerned that drilling for petroleum could negatively impact caribou and bird populations. Roads, trucks, power lines, and drilling cause noise and other disruptions for wildlife, which might impact migratory and mating patterns. A caribou and calf graze on the autumn tundra in Arctic Canada.
pages.brief: A caribou and its calf graze on the autumn tundra in Arctic Canada. Around them, the wide open landscape shows the natural environment that supports tundra vegetation and wildlife such as polar bears, whales, and seals.

pages.text: Indigenous Peoples of the Arctic Indigenous peoples make up about 10 percent of people living in the Arctic. The Arctic is home to forty distinct Indigenous ethnic groups, including the Saami (SAH-mee) and the Inuit. While all Arctic Indigenous tribes, nations, and groups are different, they are similar in that their cultures and survival are built on Indigenous knowledge. Indigenous knowledge has been developed over thousands of years, through observation of the Arctic’s unique environment and traditions that reflect the surroundings. Inuit people, both in the past and today, rely on wildlife such as caribou, seals, walruses, and whales. They use every part of these animals, such as bones, teeth, fat, and skins. These resources provide them with food, clothing, boats, and tools. Because the lifestyle of Arctic Indigenous peoples relies so much on the environment, they are uniquely hurt by climate change. When ice melts, it is more difficult for members of these groups to hunt the animals that are important to their way of life. Some Indigenous peoples are at risk of hunger because hunting provides much of their food. Changes in the environment also make water less safe to drink.
pages.brief: An Inuit person works with animal skins, bones, and tools in an Arctic camp, using every part of caribou, seals, walruses, and whales for food, clothing, boats, and tools. The cold tundra surroundings reflect the environment that Arctic Indigenous peoples rely on.

pages.text: Who Wants the North Pole? Four countries—Norway, Russia, Canada, and Greenland—have filed requests for larger territories than they now own. In other words, those four countries want more of the Arctic region than just their EEZ. In some cases, they want territory all the way to the North Pole. Russia’s Arctic coastline is about 4,300 miles (7,000 km) long. It has the longest coastline of any country bordering the Arctic Ocean. In 2007, Russia sent a small research ship to the seafloor at the North Pole. The ship gathered samples of soil and water from an underwater land feature called the Lomonosov Ridge. Scientists hoped to prove that the ridge is part of Russia and should belong to Russia. Ownership would give Russia the right to any natural resources found there. In 2021, Russia claimed even more of the seabed, adding 705,000 square kilometers to its claims. However, across the Arctic Ocean, the Lomonosov Ridge connects to Canada, which has the second-longest Arctic coastline. Canada also claims this underwater mountain ridge as part of its seabed. Denmark, too, seeks ownership of the ridge because it has a historic relationship with Greenland.
pages.brief: A small research ship sits at the North Pole, lowering equipment toward the seafloor. Below the icy water, the long Lomonosov Ridge rises from the seabed, the underwater feature Russia, Canada, and Denmark seek to claim.

pages.text: The North Pole Neighborhood Canada and the United States disagree about ownership of the Beaufort Sea. This body of water is north of both western Canada and Alaska. All these disputes have to do with mineral rights as well as control of shipping routes.
pages.brief: An aerial view shows the Beaufort Sea north of western Canada and Alaska, with sea ice and open water stretching between the two coastlines. The quiet polar seascape is the body of water Canada and the United States disagree over for mineral rights and shipping routes.

pages.text: Russia, Norway, and possibly other nations are also interested in expanding their territories for military purposes. They are worried that they might someday need to defend their Arctic resources. They also want good locations for military bases in case of a war between Eastern and Western Hemisphere countries. Arctic routes would shorten travel distances for military planes and ships to reach their targets. No decisions have been made yet about countries’ requests to own more of the Arctic region. Each country believes it has good reasons to expand its territory. The disputes continue to set the countries at odds with each other. Could there be a different plan for the changing Arctic region? What About the South Pole? The South Pole is at the other end of Earth’s axis. It is also a place of extreme cold. An international agreement prevents any country from owning Antarctica or using its resources. The continent is set aside for scientific research and peaceful purposes only. No military activity is permitted there. Should those same guidelines be applied to the Arctic region?
pages.brief: Arctic waters and icy coastline lie beneath a military plane flying overhead, while a naval ship moves through the sea. The scene reflects nations' interest in Arctic territory for military bases, defense of resources, and shorter travel routes for planes and ships.

pages.text: Conclusion Fifty or one hundred years from now, should any country own the Arctic region, including the North Pole? Some people believe that Indigenous groups, and their Indigenous knowledge, should be given greater consideration in these debates. Six Arctic Indigenous groups are considered permanent participants in the Arctic Council. This group encourages nations and groups that share Arctic concerns to work together to solve problems. Through the Arctic Council, these Indigenous groups have a voice in policies and laws that affect the Arctic. The countries that want to expand their areas of control in the Arctic region face important decisions. Which path will win: peaceful cooperation or competition for control? Should the threat of climate change, and the importance of the Arctic’s wildlife, impact these decisions? Which direction do you think the Arctic countries should choose? This woman of the Inuit people is cooking on the tundra. Indigenous peoples of the Arctic rely on the environment for their cultural traditions.
pages.brief: An Inuit woman cooks on the tundra, tending food over a fire in the open Arctic landscape. Her presence reflects how Indigenous peoples rely on the environment for cultural traditions, as Arctic nations and groups debate the North Pole's future.

books.title: Elephants: Giant Mammals
books.art_why: Elephants exist today, so a real photograph is possible.

pages.text: Elephants: Giant Mammals.
pages.brief: A single elephant stands prominently in a wild setting as the subject of this book about giant mammals. Its huge body, strong legs, and long trunk fill the scene, introducing the animal that the book will explore.

pages.text: How Big Can They Get? African elephant shoulder height: 13 feet (4 m) weight: 14,000 pounds (6,350 kg) Human height: 6 feet (1.8 m) weight: 175 pounds (79.4 kg) Asian elephant shoulder height: 10 feet (3 m) weight: 11,000 pounds (5,000 kg) Big and Brainy Without a doubt, elephants are the most gigantic land animals living on Earth today. To find a more immense walking creature, you would have to go back to the age of dinosaurs! Elephants aren’t just huge. They’re also highly intelligent, have many ways to communicate with one another, and are clever enough to work together to get things done.
pages.brief: A tall African elephant and a smaller Asian elephant stand beside a human, making their huge size clear. The African elephant is the largest, the Asian elephant is shorter, and the human is much smaller. The scene suggests elephants are big and brainy land animals.

pages.text: The tip of an elephant’s trunk is very sensitive. Elephants use their super-sized trunks for several significant purposes. They breathe through them, use them to pick up food and water, and blast air through them to make a deafening trumpeting sound. Elephants also touch other elephants with their trunks in different ways to communicate. Two elephants will often twist their trunks together to show affection. A mother elephant might use her trunk to gently stroke her calf and calm it down—or to scold it for misbehaving. Exploring the Elephant No other animal quite compares to the stately elephant, with its giant body, thick gray or brown skin, and round, sturdy legs. Most unusual of all is its long, snakelike trunk—an appendage that is the elephant’s all-in-one nose and upper lip.
pages.brief: An elephant curls the sensitive tip of its trunk around food while another blasts air to make a trumpeting sound. Two elephants twist their trunks together in affection, and a mother strokes her calf. The elephant's thick gray skin, round sturdy legs, and long snakelike trunk are visible.

pages.text: Interesting Elephant Facts An African elephant’s ears are twice as big as an Asian elephant’s. Young elephants drink milk from their mothers for up to three years. An elephant uses its trunk to breathe, drink, pick up food, and more. An elephant’s big, round feet have soft pads on the bottom. Elephants are mammals. All mammals: • have a backbone • have hair on their bodies at some time in their lives • are warm-blooded • produce milk to feed their babies.
pages.brief: An African elephant displays its large ears beside an Asian elephant with smaller ears. A young elephant nurses from its mother, and a close view shows a big round foot with a soft pad. The scene also suggests elephants are mammals with hair and backbones.

pages.text: African and Asian Elephants The two main species of elephants are African and Asian. It is simple to tell them apart if you know what continent you are in, but there are other clues as well. African elephants are greater in size than their Asian relatives, with males measuring 13 feet (4 m) tall and weighing up to 14,000 pounds (6,350 kg). Females are shorter and lighter, at around 9 feet (2.7 m) tall and up to 10,000 pounds (4,540 kg). Male Asian elephants are around 3 feet (0.9144 m) shorter and about 3,000 pounds (1,360 kg) lighter than African males. Females are even smaller and, unlike African females, often have no tusks at all. An African elephant’s appearance differs from its Asian counterpart in other ways, too. Its floppy ears are often twice as large as those of an Asian elephant. The back of an African elephant also dips down in the middle, unlike an Asian elephant’s. If you inspected the animal even more thoroughly, you would see two “fingers” at the end of its jumbo trunk. These handy flaps grab food and small objects.
pages.brief: A male African elephant stands taller and heavier than a male Asian elephant, while a female Asian elephant without tusks stands nearby. The African elephant has huge floppy ears and a dipped back; the Asian elephant has smaller ears. Close up, the African trunk tip shows two finger-like flaps.

pages.text: Elephants use their tusks to dig, fight, or move things around. African elephants also use their tusks to dig for water. In addition to having smaller ears, Asian elephants have large, round bumps on the tops of their huge heads. Spotting these bumps is a clear way to identify the species. The bumps are often the tallest point on an Asian elephant. Their backs are flat or arched, and we can’t forget their trunks, which have just one “finger” at the end instead of two. African elephant Asian elephant.
pages.brief: An Asian elephant shows large round bumps on top of its huge head and a flat or arched back. Its trunk tip has one finger-like flap. Beside it, an African elephant uses its tusks to dig for water. Both elephants have thick skin and sturdy legs.

pages.text: Elephant Hangouts Elephants are adaptable enough to live in many different types of habitats, as long as they can find enough food and water. In Africa, elephants live in hot, dry grasslands, rainforests, and even deserts. They can live at sea level or high in the mountains. Asian elephants live in wet rainforests and swamps as well as in other more arid forests with long dry seasons. Because of their hulking size, even ferocious lions and tigers rarely threaten elephants. Humans, however, often illegally hunt elephants for their ivory tusks and shoot them for harming crops. As human population increases, elephants’ natural habitats are disappearing. Humans build more roads, plant more crops, and cut down more trees all the time. Less and less land is available for wild animals—especially ones that need large amounts of food and space. Elephants once roamed almost all of Africa and South Asia, but today their habitats have shrunk a great deal.
pages.brief: Elephants stand in a hot, dry African grassland and a wet Asian rainforest. A lion and tiger watch from a distance but do not threaten the huge animals. Nearby, roads, crops, and cut trees show human pressure on elephant habitats, while an elephant with tusks stands in shrinking wild land.

pages.text: Where Elephants Live ASIA Asian elephant range EUROPE AFRICA African elephant range.
pages.brief: A world map shows the continents of Asia, Europe, and Africa. Shaded areas mark where Asian elephants live in Asia and where African elephants live in Africa. The two elephant ranges are separated by oceans and land, making their different homes clear.

pages.text: No Meat, Thanks Elephants are herbivores and therefore eat only plants. Other than that, they aren’t picky. They’ll chow down on grass, leaves, branches, tree bark, seeds, and fruits. The most important thing is that there is a lot of food to eat. An adult elephant can eat more than 300 pounds (136 kg) of food every day and slurp about 20 to 60 gallons (75.7–227.1 L) of water, using its handy trunk like an enormous straw. Then, the elephant sprays the water from the end of its trunk into its mouth. Only about 44 percent of the food elephants eat is digested.
pages.brief: An adult elephant stands among abundant grass, leaves, branches, tree bark, seeds, and fruit, all plant food. It curls its trunk to lift food and sprays water from the trunk tip into its mouth. The scene emphasizes the enormous amount it eats and drinks.

pages.text: Wowser! • Elephant pregnancies last eighteen to twenty-two months—longer than those of any other animal. • One of the elephant’s closest living relatives is the hyrax—a small, cute, furry animal. You might never think they’re related! hyrax • Elephants are closely related to woolly mammoths, which have been extinct for more than ten thousand years. woolly mammoth.
pages.brief: A pregnant elephant stands with her large belly. Nearby, a small furry hyrax sits on a rock, shown as a surprising close relative. A woolly mammoth with long curved tusks appears as an extinct relative. The scene connects the elephant to these unlikely family members.

pages.text: This Asian elephant mother uses her trunk to spray water. On sunny days, she might roll in sand or dirt to not get sunburnt. The Elephant Family Elephants, especially female elephants, are social animals. Adult females live together in family groups, most often led by the oldest among them. The herd might be made up of a grandmother elephant, her grown-up daughters, and the daughters’ calves. They take care of each other and eat, bathe, and play together. From the moment an elephant is born, the whole herd helps the mother care for her 250-pound (110 kg) calf. Adult elephants work together to drive away predators. Other adults will even nurse the calf if it’s hungry.
pages.brief: An Asian elephant mother sprays water over herself on a sunny day. She may roll in sand or dirt to avoid sunburn. Around her, a family herd of adult females, a grandmother, grown daughters, and calves eat, bathe, and play together. The adults stay close to a newborn calf, helping and protecting it.

pages.text: Young elephants have an extra-long childhood. They nurse from their mothers for up to three years. During this time, and for several years later, elephants learn vital survival skills, including where to find food and water, and how to use their trunks. They aren’t mature adults until they’re ten to fifteen years old. Then, males and females go their separate ways, with males leaving the herd to live alone or with other male elephants. Females stay with the herd and eventually raise their own calves. If an adult elephant doesn’t encounter serious trouble, it can live for sixty to seventy years. Sometimes an elephant lives so long that it runs out of teeth! It only grows six sets in its lifetime, and once they’re gone, the elephant can’t chew its food well anymore. Older elephants often stay in marshes. They find softer plants to chew there.
pages.brief: A young elephant nurses from its mother and stays close as older elephants show it where to find food and water. A grown male walks apart from the female herd, while females remain together. In a marsh, an older elephant chews softer plants, its worn teeth suggested by its slow feeding.

pages.text: Giant Friends It’s hard not to feel a connection to nature’s king-sized elephants. We know they’re brainy and caring, and they like to have fun. Their awesome size and distinctive personalities make them impossible to ignore. If we all work to protect elephants, these giants of nature will roam the Earth for a long time to come. African elephants on the Samburu National Reserve in Kenya, Africa.
pages.brief: A group of African elephants roams the Samburu National Reserve in Kenya, Africa. The huge animals stand together in the wild, showing their distinctive personalities and playful, caring nature. The scene invites people to feel a connection to nature and to protect these brainy, king-sized giants.

books.title: Condors: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Real condors, habitats, people, and conservation scenes exist today.

pages.text: Meet the Condor Weighing over 30 pounds (13.5 kg), an enormous bird lifts off high in the majestic Andes Mountains of South America. Its powerful wings, measuring an amazing 10.5 feet (3.2 m) across, propel the bird to a dizzying height of 15,000 feet (4,600 m). This is the largest flying bird in the world—the giant Andean condor. As it glides along, it uses its impressive wingspan and extra-keen eyesight to search for food far below. How Big Is It?
pages.brief: A giant Andean condor lifts off high in the Andes Mountains of South America, its powerful wings spread wide. The enormous bird glides at a dizzying height, using its 10.5-foot wingspan and keen eyesight to search for food far below.

pages.text: Where Condors Live Life on Wind and Rock Andean condors live in the western parts of South America, and California condors live in the American Southwest. All condors need a wide-open habitat so that when they spot food, they have enough space to fly down with their huge wings and land. Condors also need sufficient wind currents to enable them to climb high and fly long distances. These birds can fly as far as 150 miles (240 km) in one day to find food and may reach speeds of up to 50 miles per hour (80 kmph).
pages.brief: In western South America, an Andean condor flies over wide-open habitat; in the American Southwest, a California condor soars. Both need open space to fly down and land, and wind currents to climb high and travel long distances in search of food.

pages.text: Some condors live near the sea, and perch high up on cliffs, which provide an excellent view of the shoreline. Most condors, however, live in dry places where they can soar above rocky canyons, deserts, and mountains. Condors prefer to nest on elevated landforms. Lofty nests help keep condor eggs safe from potential predators on the ground. Condors don’t use twigs and feathers to make an inviting, cozy nest. Instead, they nest directly on rocky cave floors or jagged outer ledges. Some California condors nest in large holes near the top of the world’s tallest trees—the towering California redwoods.
pages.brief: Some condors perch high on sea cliffs with a view of the shoreline. Others soar above rocky canyons, deserts, and mountains, or nest on elevated ledges and cave floors. A California condor nests in a large hole near the top of a towering redwood tree.

pages.text: A condor can devour up to 4 pounds (1.8 kg) of food in one day and then go for days without eating. Condors have a special diet that you wouldn’t find very tasty. They only eat carrion —dead and decaying animals. California condors eat small mammals such as rabbits and gophers. However, they prefer to eat larger mammals such as deer and cattle. Condors feeding near the ocean clean the beaches of all kinds of seafood, from small fish to huge whales that have washed ashore. Decomposing animals can be filled with harmful bacteria that can cause disease. Condors, though, have special digestive systems and are not in danger from bacteria. Condors play an important role in nature. They do an expert job of gobbling up rotting flesh and helping to keep ecosystems a little more germ-free.
pages.brief: A condor eats carrion, feeding on a dead deer or cattle. Near the ocean, condors clean the beach by eating seafood, from small fish to a huge whale washed ashore. The bird's special digestive system protects it from harmful bacteria in decaying animals.

pages.text: Condors do not have a good sense of smell, but their excellent eyesight is an important tool when hunting for food. They can see their food from very high in the sky. Condors sometimes see other carrion-eating birds circling nearb y—a sure sign that they’ve found food. This sight often leads to a condor’s next meal. The condor will simply swoop in and eat the food that other birds have found.
pages.brief: High in the sky, a condor uses its excellent eyesight to spot food far below. It sees other carrion-eating birds circling nearby, a sign that they have found food. The condor swoops in to eat the food the other birds found.

pages.text: What Makes a Condor a Bird? All birds • have a backbone • have feathers • have wings.
pages.brief: A condor stands in an open natural setting, its feathers and wings clearly visible. Its strong body suggests the backbone of a bird, and the image focuses on these three features: backbone, feathers, and wings.

pages.text: Check Out the Condor There are definite similarities between adult male and female California condors—both have black feathers and fluffy black “collars” or necks. Andean males and females both have black feathers and white necks. Andean males, however, have large, fleshy lumps on their heads called combs. California condors don’t have combs, so when deciding which species of bird you’re looking at, check for a comb. If it’s present, it’s a male Andean condor.
pages.brief: An adult male Andean condor stands beside an adult female, both with black feathers and white necks. The male has large, fleshy lumps called combs on his head. Nearby, a pair of California condors shows black feathers and fluffy black collars, with no combs.

pages.text: Storks are one of the closest relatives of condors. They look nothing alike, though! Condors are very clean birds. After eating, they clean their heads on rocks and tree branches. They also bathe in water and then spend hours smoothing their feathers. All condors have a bald head—a very useful adaptation. Being feather-free from the neck up makes grooming simpler for condors, especially after they stick their heads in decaying animals to feed. Condors have hardly any feathers for the messy stuff to stick to.
pages.brief: A condor cleans its bald head on rocks and tree branches after eating. Later, it bathes in water and spends hours smoothing its feathers. The feather-free neck and head make grooming simpler, especially after the bird sticks its head into a decaying animal to feed.

pages.text: A One-Egg Nest A female condor produces just one egg every two years, so it’s crucial that the egg be protected. The female and male each sit on the egg, which hatches in about fifty-six days. As the chick matures, its feathers gradually turn from gray to black. The young bird starts to fly when it is around six months old. If they’re lucky, wild condors usually live about sixty years, and condors in zoos or refuges can live for more than seventy-five years. Most animals, including condors, live longer in captivity. In these protected environments, condors are pretty pampered! In the wild, though, condors face many hazards. Sadly, one of the most damaging influences on condors has been human beings.
pages.brief: A female condor sits on a single egg in a rocky nest, while the male takes his turn. The egg hatches after about fifty-six days, and the chick's gray feathers gradually turn black. The young bird starts to fly at around six months old.

pages.text: Condors in Trouble Andean condors and California condors are endangered. Their numbers are much lower today than they were two hundred years ago. The trouble began when people started moving into areas where condors lived. Many people in North and South America didn’t like the big birds, so they shot them. People also didn’t like coyotes and wolves, so they left poison out to kill them. When the condors ate the dead animals, they died from the poison, too. Many condors died of lead poisoning, too. They would feast on animals people had shot and sometimes accidentally eat lead bullets. In more recent times, electrical power has also proved a danger to condors. As sharp as condors’ eyesight is, they can’t always see power lines, so they fly into the wires and die. In 1987, California condors were dangerously close to extinction—only about ten were alive in the wild. Scientists captured the wild birds and brought them to refuges. There, the scientists could protect them and help the birds raise their young.
pages.brief: A condor faces danger from people: it may be shot, or it may eat a poisoned dead animal left out for coyotes and wolves. Another condor feeds on an animal shot by people and accidentally eats a lead bullet. Power lines also prove dangerous.

pages.text: After five years of hard work and dedication, scientists began releasing California condors back into the wild. By May 2013, over 230 California condors were flying free again. Since 1973, similar efforts have been made in South America to save Andean condors. Organizations there have set aside land for condors. Today, their numbers are rising, and it’s estimated that a few thousand birds live in the wild.
pages.brief: Scientists release California condors back into the wild after five years of work. By May 2013, more than 230 California condors fly free again. In South America, organizations set aside land for Andean condors, and their numbers are rising, with a few thousand birds estimated in the wild.

pages.text: A Truly Giant Bird Can you imagine what it would be like to see such a gigantic bird fly overhead? It’s an amazing sight since a condor’s wingspan measures twice as wide as an eagle’s and five times as wide as a falcon’s! Many California condors live in protected reserves, which is one of the only places left where the huge birds fly. Serious dangers remain for condors. But if people continue to protect these giant, high-flying birds and their environments, they will keep us in awe for centuries to come.
pages.brief: A gigantic condor flies overhead, its wings stretched wide. Its wingspan is twice as wide as an eagle's and five times as wide as a falcon's. Many California condors live in protected reserves, one of the few places left where these huge birds still fly.

books.title: Genetics at Work
books.art_why: Modern genetics, labs, farms, zoos and DNA work exist today, so photos suit.

pages.text: Family members look alike because they share the same inherited traits. Introduction Do you sometimes wonder what you want to be when you grow up? Have you ever thought about being a doctor or a detective, or working with animals? All these jobs have one thing in common— genetics. What is genetics? Genetics is the field of science that studies how all living things pass traits from one generation to the next. Traits are features such as hair color, finger length, and nose shape. Understanding genetics is important in many jobs. Farming, breeding animals, curing diseases, preventing possible illnesses, and solving crimes are just a few examples.
pages.brief: A family group stands close together, clearly sharing hair color, finger length, and nose shape. Nearby, a doctor, a detective, and a person working with animals show genetics-related jobs. The scene also suggests farming, animal breeding, disease care, illness prevention, and crime solving as examples of work that uses genetics.

pages.text: Farming Genetics is a new science. Even so, there is evidence of people using genetic techniques to create better crops and animals as early as 5000 BC. Selective breeding is one of these techniques. Scientists select plants with traits they like, such as quick-growing or attractive fruit, to breed with other plants that have those same traits. By selectively breeding these plants, scientists ensure that the plants’ desirable traits are passed on. The result is crops that grow faster and produce better fruit. Think about the many types of tomatoes you can buy at the supermarket. They are the result of the selective breeding of tomato plants. Wheat, soybeans, and corn are other common crops that are grown using genetic techniques. With the help of genetics, farmers will be able to grow plants that have higher protein and lower oil. Many varieties of tomatoes have been bred from a single wild variety.
pages.brief: Scientists in a field select tomato plants with quick growth and attractive fruit, then breed them with other tomato plants that share those traits. Nearby grow wheat, soybeans, and corn. A small group of wild tomato plants is shown alongside many different tomato varieties, including tomatoes in a supermarket display.

pages.text: Scientists also use genetic techniques with animals. For example, they use genetic breeding techniques to create chickens that lay more eggs. They create cows that grow faster and produce more milk. Genetics sounds great for farming. Why wouldn’t we want crops that grow faster and taste better? Why not help cows produce more milk? Some say that genetically changing our crops and animals will damage their genetic diversity. By only breeding for a select group of traits, many other useful plant and animal traits may be lost forever. The lack of genetic diversity among crops and animals may also leave them vulnerable to a single virus that could wipe out an entire species. Selectively bred piglets grow up faster than their wild cousins. People in favor of using genetics in farming want to improve food production. Those against it are concerned about the unknown effects it might have on our environment and our health.
pages.brief: A farmer stands near chickens that lay many eggs and cows that grow fast and produce more milk. Beside them, selectively bred piglets stand next to wild cousins that look different. On one side, people in favor of genetic farming point to food production; on the other, people against it look worried about environment and health.

pages.text: Animal Breeding Animal breeders use some of the same genetic techniques as plant scientists. These include selective breeding and hybridization. Hybridization is also known as crossbreeding. It involves breeding different varieties or even species to combine the best characteristics of both. For example, female horses can be bred with male donkeys to produce mules. Mules are a hybrid of horses and donkeys. They are tough like donkeys, but agile like horses. They make very good work animals. A donkey (top) crossed with a horse (left) yields a mule (right).
pages.brief: An animal breeder stands beside a female horse and a male donkey, showing how they are crossed. The result, a mule, stands nearby, looking tough like the donkey and agile like the horse. The mule is shown as a strong work animal, with the horse and donkey positioned as its two parents.

pages.text: Many dog breeders raise dogs only for show. However, many dog breeds are bred for specific purposes, such as hunting, herding, or guarding. Some of the earliest hunting dogs were spaniels. Spaniels such as springer and cocker spaniels were first bred in Spain to hunt water birds like ducks or land birds like pheasants. Dog breeders determine the traits they want in a dog. Then they select parents that, when bred, will pass on those traits to their offspring. Border collies are excellent herders. Herding is another desirable trait that is bred into some dogs. Herding dogs are used to protect and round up cattle and other livestock. Border collies and Australian shepherds are popular herding dogs. They have been so well bred that they continue to herd animals even if they aren’t trained to. Many people who own border collies report that their dogs attempt to herd cars and even people! The border collie breed was developed hundreds of years ago. It was first used to herd cattle and sheep along the border between England and Scotland.
pages.brief: Dog breeders stand with spaniels that hunt ducks and pheasants, and with herding dogs beside cattle and other livestock. A border collie and an Australian shepherd round up animals, and one border collie also tries to herd cars and people. The scene suggests the border between England and Scotland, where the breed was first used.

pages.text: The Australian shepherd was developed from several herding breeds, including the border collie, which English settlers brought with them to Australia. These shepherds are still widely used in Australia. Cattle and other livestock there are raised in open fields. Some dogs are bred as guard dogs. The Doberman pinscher and the German shepherd are two common guard dogs. The Doberman was first bred by a German watchman named Louis Dobermann in the late 1890s. The breed has a reputation for being dangerous. However, recent breeders have worked hard to make the Doberman more calm and friendly. Many dogs are hybrids—crosses between two or more breeds. Some people believe that hybrids make the best pets because they combine the best traits of both parents. Mutts combine the best traits of many breeds.
pages.brief: An Australian shepherd works cattle and other livestock in open fields, with English settlers and a border collie nearby. A German watchman named Louis Dobermann stands with a Doberman pinscher and a German shepherd as guard dogs. A calm, friendly hybrid dog and a mutt stand beside them, showing combined traits from many breeds.

pages.text: Giant pandas have been helped by captive-breeding programs. Animals in Zoos Many zoos perform animal research and provide education and entertainment. Some zoos use genetics in their research. This research is conducted to ensure that animal species survive well into the future. Genetics play an important role in protecting many endangered and threatened animal species.
pages.brief: In a zoo, a giant panda is shown with a captive-breeding program. Zoo staff perform animal research and provide education and entertainment. The panda represents endangered and threatened species that genetics research helps protect so they can survive well into the future.

pages.text: One technique that zoo scientists use to increase the populations of endangered species is captive breeding. Captive breeding is the breeding of animals that are living in captivity (such as in zoos). The purpose is to maintain genetic diversity within a species. Some offspring bred in captivity are released into wild populations. They introduce different genes that give the wild animals a better chance at survival. This type of captive breeding is only successful if the animals can survive and reproduce on their own once they are released into the wild. Captive breeding is being used with certain endangered and threatened species. These include the red wolf, gorilla, giant panda, cheetah, and rhinoceros. Another type of captive breeding is often done with species that are nearly extinct and cannot survive in the wild. It gives the animals a chance to reproduce in a protected environment. Although captive breeding is important, it cannot replace animals living and breeding in the wild. Zoo employees also try to educate people about the importance of protecting the habitats of endangered and threatened species. If wild animals such as rhinoceroses and tigers are not protected, future generations of people will only be able to read about those animals in books.
pages.brief: Zoo scientists care for a red wolf, gorilla, giant panda, cheetah, and rhinoceros in captivity, helping them breed and maintain genetic diversity. Some offspring are released into wild populations. Zoo employees educate people about protecting habitats, while a rhinoceros and tiger show what could be lost if wild animals are not protected.

pages.text: Solving Crimes When crime solvers put on their detective hats these days, they have more to work with than a magnifying glass. Police, detectives, and lawyers now use genetics and DNA to help them solve crimes. All genes contain DNA. DNA carries the code that determines an organism’s genetic traits. Like fingerprints, every organism’s DNA is different. Today, detectives have more clues to work with than ever before. By fingerprinting criminals, police can keep a database of fingerprints. Fingerprints at a crime scene can then be matched with the fingerprints of known criminals in the database. Since DNA, like fingerprints, is unique, we use the term DNA fingerprinting for the use of DNA to solve crimes. The advantage of using DNA is that you do not need to find a fingerprint. To get a DNA fingerprint of a criminal, all you need is a small bit of skin, a single hair, or a drop of fluid such as blood or saliva. It is almost impossible for a criminal not to leave behind a trace of skin, hair, or fluid. Everywhere a person goes, he or she leaves microscopic traces of DNA.
pages.brief: A detective wearing a hat examines clues at a crime scene with a magnifying glass set aside. Police and lawyers study DNA, skin, a single hair, and drops of blood or saliva. Fingerprints and DNA fingerprints are matched in a police database, showing how tiny microscopic traces can link a criminal to a crime.

pages.text: For example, imagine that investigators find skin cells under a victim’s fingernails. They can determine the DNA of the skin cells. They then take a DNA sample from the suspect. If the two samples match, the investigators are closer to solving the crime. Law enforcement agencies are now building databases of DNA samples, much like collections of fingerprints. These databases contain the DNA fingerprints of convicted criminals. They also store other evidence found at crime scenes. DNA also has been used to free people who were wrongly convicted of crimes. DNA fingerprinting has helped solve many crimes since it was first used in 1985. However, some people are concerned about possible contamination affecting the accuracy of DNA testing as well as its possible misuse. Even so, DNA fingerprinting will continue to be used as long as it helps identify criminals and solve crimes.
pages.brief: Investigators find skin cells under a victim’s fingernails and compare their DNA with a sample from a suspect. A law enforcement database stores DNA fingerprints and other crime-scene evidence. The scene also shows a wrongly convicted person being freed, while people nearby worry about contamination, accuracy, and misuse of DNA testing.

pages.text: Health Genetics is also used by many medical and health-care scientists. Genetics is used to diagnose, treat, and prevent diseases as well as to develop new medicines. Medical scientists are now discovering many genes that cause specific diseases. Identifying genes that cause a specific disease helps scientists develop medicines and vaccines to cure or prevent the disease. Genetics counselors also use genetics. They help parents and future parents figure out the odds of passing on genetic disorders to their children. Parents use this information to help them decide whether to have children. They also consider how to cope with the possibility of caring for children with genetic disorders. Some common genetic disorders that may be passed on from parents to their children are cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s disease, and breast cancer. Do You Know? In 2000, scientists completed the Human Genome Project, a full map of the location of every human gene. Humans have about twenty-four thousand genes arranged in a specific order on our chromosomes. It took powerful computers ten years to count and locate them all. Many diseases are caused by genes that are missing or in the wrong place.
pages.brief: Medical scientists work with medicines and vaccines while identifying genes that cause specific diseases. A genetics counselor sits with parents and future parents, explaining the odds of passing on genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s disease, and breast cancer. Nearby, powerful computers show the full map of every human gene from the Human Genome Project.

pages.text: A scientist compares DNA fingerprints on a computer screen. Conclusion The field of genetics offers many job opportunities. Genetics is an exciting and relatively new branch of science. It brings new developments and new opportunities almost daily. Whether in plant and animal breeding, medicine, the study of crime, or some other field, many career opportunities are linked to genetics. Check the library or the Internet for more information about this exciting field of science.
pages.brief: A scientist compares DNA fingerprints on a computer screen. Around the scientist, examples of genetics careers appear in plant and animal breeding, medicine, and crime study. Nearby, a library shelf and a computer offer more information about this exciting, relatively new field of science and its many job opportunities.

books.title: Hoover Dam
books.art_why: The book focuses on 1930s construction and historical events shown as drawings.

pages.text: Hoover Dam.
pages.brief: A wide view of Hoover Dam, the massive concrete landmark, standing in its desert canyon setting under a bright sky. The dam is shown as a whole structure, with its curved wall and tall canyon walls around it.

pages.text: From the western side of Hoover Dam, visitors can look across the dam to Arizona (left). Kayaking is popular on Lake Mead (right). Water in the Desert Every summer in parts of the southwestern United States, temperatures often exceed 100°F (38°C). Much of the region receives less than 10 inches (25.4 cm) of rainfall each year. So why do millions of people visit the area every year? Why do they come to fish, boat, water-ski, and swim in an enormous refreshing lake? How is this possible in such a dry, sun-baked place? The U.S. Southwest was transformed when Hoover Dam was built in the 1930s. Construction of this iconic landmark brought water and power to parched desert lands. The dam allowed cities, agriculture, and recreation to grow.
pages.brief: Visitors stand on the western side of Hoover Dam and look across the dam toward Arizona. On Lake Mead, kayakers paddle across the water, enjoying a refreshing lake in the hot, dry southwestern desert. The dam made this recreation possible.

pages.text: Why Build a Dam? Hoover Dam is located on the Colorado River in the Mojave (moh-HAH-vee) Desert on the border between Arizona and Nevada. The location is about 30 miles (48 km) southeast of Las Vegas, Nevada. The government built Hoover Dam in Black Canyon. This tall, narrow canyon was chosen because its bedrock and walls were solid. They needed to be to support such an enormous structure. Because Hoover Dam was the first dam on the Colorado River, it had to be extremely large to control the river on its own. A very tall canyon was required. Colorado River Watershed Nevada Utah Colorado California New Mexico Colorado River Arizona PACIFIC OCEAN Black Canyon before Hoover Dam was built Colorado River Watershed.
pages.brief: Hoover Dam is located on the Colorado River in the Mojave Desert, on the Arizona-Nevada border. Before construction, Black Canyon is tall and narrow, with solid bedrock and walls strong enough to support an enormous dam.

pages.text: Colorado River floodwaters filled much of Imperial Valley in 1905 and created the Salton Sea. It took two years to get the water under control. The Colorado River winds through the southwestern United States, bringing life-giving water to an otherwise dry region. People have lived along the Colorado’s banks for centuries. They used its water to irrigate crops. However, the Colorado was a fluctuating source of water long ago. Each spring, the river grew with snowmelt, often to the point of flooding farmlands. Later in the year when it shrunk to a trickle, crops would die. Early settlers were discouraged by the changeable water supply, so some people sought a way to control the river. In 1901, a private company built the Alamo Canal just north of the Mexican border. The canal’s purpose was to divert the Colorado’s flow westward to provide irrigation to California’s Imperial Valley. As a result, farming did very well. However, severe flooding in 1905 destroyed the canal’s control gates and ruined much of Imperial Valley.
pages.brief: Colorado River floodwaters fill much of Imperial Valley in 1905 and create the Salton Sea. The river winds through the dry Southwest, bringing water to crops, but severe flooding destroys the Alamo Canal’s control gates and ruins farmland.

pages.text: Imperial Valley residents wanted a larger canal. Arthur Powell Davis was chief engineer of the government agency that manages water in the West. He thought that constructing a dam along the river would be a better solution. It would get more water to more people. After studying the Colorado, he reported his findings to Congress in 1918. Ten years later, Congress approved construction of Hoover Dam along with a canal to provide irrigation to Imperial Valley. In 1930, President Hoover authorized spending for the project. The Great Depression began only eight months before the Hoover Dam project was approved. It was a time of great economic hardship in the United States. Millions were out of work. In total, 21,000 people flocked to southern Nevada for the construction jobs. President Hoover wanted to put as many people to work as possible. He ordered construction to begin before housing, drinking water, a hospital, or other facilities were in place. At first, some workers and their families lived in camps that lacked electricity and running water. Homes were tents, and people bathed in the Colorado River.
pages.brief: President Hoover authorizes spending for Hoover Dam during the Great Depression, when millions are out of work. Workers and their families flock to southern Nevada and live in tent camps without electricity or running water, bathing in the Colorado River.
