pages.text: Hoover Dam is considered an arch- gravity dam. downstream gravity arch upstream A Massive Dam Hoover Dam was the tallest dam in the world when it was built. Constructing the dam was an amazing engineering feat that required the skills of six different companies working together. Hoover Dam combines the features of a gravity dam and an arch dam. A gravity dam relies on its own weight to resist the force of stored water. An arch dam, which curves upstream, causes most of the water to flow against the canyon walls. The flow of water squeezes the arch, which compresses and strengthens the dam. Hoover Dam’s power plant converts the energy of moving water into electricity. Lake Mead, the dam’s reservoir, is the largest human-made lake in the United States.
pages.brief: Hoover Dam stands as a massive arch-gravity dam in Black Canyon, its curved wall holding back Lake Mead, the largest human-made lake in the United States. At the dam’s base, the power plant converts moving water into electricity.

pages.text: Hoover Dam Diversion Map Arizona diversion tunnels rock barrier cofferdam cofferdam Nevada diversion tunnels Constructing the Dam In order to build Hoover Dam, the dam site first had to be dry. The enormous task of diverting the Colorado’s water began in May 1931. Workers used dynamite to blast two tunnels on each side of the canyon to carry the Colorado’s water around the site. Once the tunnels were completed, they were lined with concrete. Creating the diversion tunnels was extremely dangerous. Workers were exposed to falling rocks and fumes from the use of gasoline-powered vehicles in the tunnels. Above the ground, other workers built watertight barriers called cofferdams above and below the dam site. The higher cofferdam would divert water into the tunnels. The lower one, along with a rock barrier, would keep water from flowing back upstream and flooding the construction site.
pages.brief: Workers blast diversion tunnels with dynamite on both sides of Black Canyon and line them with concrete, sending the Colorado River around the dry dam site. Above and below the site, workers build watertight cofferdams and a rock barrier to control the water.

pages.text: At the same time, “high scalers” removed loose rock from canyon walls and cut grooves where the dam would attach. These workers often dangled high above the river on wooden swings in 120°F (49°C) heat while using jackhammers and dynamite. Other projects were taking place at the same time. Boulder City was being built so workers would have homes, a hospital, and other facilities. Railroad tracks were installed near the dam site so supplies could be delivered. A road was built between Boulder City and the dam site. In addition, workers installed a power line 222 miles (357 km) long from San Bernardino, California, to Black Canyon to provide power for the dam’s construction. High scalers had perhaps the hardest jobs at Hoover Dam. Dozens of workers lost their lives as a result of falling rocks and tools. Almost one hundred men in total died of industrial accidents during the dam’s construction.
pages.brief: High scalers dangle from wooden swings high above the river in extreme heat, using jackhammers and dynamite to remove loose rock and cut grooves in the canyon walls. Below, railroad tracks and a road bring supplies to the dam site.

pages.text: Once the diversion tunnels were finished, the site was pumped dry. The dam had to sit on solid bedrock, which was buried under 135 feet (41 m) of silt and stones. The last of that material was excavated on June 6, 1933—about two years after work had begun on the tunnels. Finally it was time to build the dam. Workers lowered huge buckets of wet concrete into block-shaped molds, called forms. Other workers smoothed the concrete and got rid of air bubbles before the concrete hardened and more layers of concrete were added. Narrow steel pipes carried cold water through the forms to cool the concrete quickly. Once the concrete had hardened, the wooden form was taken apart and put back together on top of the finished block. After that block was finished, another one was built on top of it. When the columns of blocks reached their final height, the spaces between them were filled with grout. The dam was built from concrete blocks that were stacked to form columns.
pages.brief: Workers lower huge buckets of wet concrete into block-shaped forms, smooth the concrete, and remove air bubbles. Cold water runs through steel pipes inside the forms. Finished concrete blocks are stacked into columns, and grout fills the spaces between them.

pages.text: After the dam was complete, workers built passages called spillways to carry high water around the dam. This would help if the Colorado River ever flooded. Then they built the power plant and the four intake towers that would control water flow to the power plant. By February 1, 1935, the work was finally completed. Workers plugged the diversion tunnels that had been allowing the Colorado’s waters to bypass the dam site. Water started rising behind the dam, overflowing the cofferdam, and forming Lake Mead. By the time the project was finished, more than 21,000 men had worked on it, with an average of 3,500 each day. The project cost $165 million, which is equal to $3 billion or more today. • Hoover Dam, along with its power plant and other structures, contains enough concrete to pave a highway from San Francisco to New York City. • The construction of Hoover Dam used over 5,000,000 barrels of cement. That amounts to between 7,500 and 10,800 barrels each day. President Roosevelt dedicated the dam on September 30, 1935. He called it “the greatest dam in the world.”
pages.brief: Workers finish the spillways, intake towers, and power plant, then plug the diversion tunnels. Water rises behind Hoover Dam and forms Lake Mead. After construction ends, President Roosevelt dedicates the completed dam on September 30, 1935.

pages.text: Visiting the Dam Hoover Dam has welcomed visitors since 1937. Millions of people visit the dam each year. Close to a million take tours of the dam and power plant. The visitor center has displays about the region’s natural history as well as the history and construction of the dam. If you go, be prepared to be impressed. Visitors describe their experience with words like spectacular, amazing, and incredible. Fishing, boating, picnicking, and hiking are available year-round at Lake Mead. The area has nine wilderness areas, five hundred types of animals, and nine hundred types of plants. From inside the visitor center, tourists get a bird’s-eye view of Hoover Dam. Guided tours give behind-the-scenes details of the dam.
pages.brief: Visitors explore the Hoover Dam visitor center and take guided tours, looking down on the dam and power plant. Outside, people fish, boat, picnic, and hike around Lake Mead, where wilderness areas, animals, and plants are protected.

pages.text: In 1930, Las Vegas was a railroad hub with only about 5,000 residents. After Hoover Dam was built, the city’s population swelled. As of 2013, Las Vegas had over 600,000 residents. Changing the Southwest The Colorado River is the main source of water in the southwestern United States. Hoover Dam controlled the Colorado for the first time in history. It supplied farmers in Arizona, Nevada, and California with a trustworthy source of irrigation. The dam also provided drinking water and affordable electricity, which allowed Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas, Phoenix, and other cities in the Southwest to grow. In addition, Hoover Dam provided jobs for thousands of men and became a symbol of hope during a very hard time. The difficult and dangerous task of building Hoover Dam took place over seventy-five years ago. The dam’s last known construction worker died in 2014. Yet the stories live on in every ton of concrete in one of America’s most remarkable landmarks.
pages.brief: Las Vegas grows from a small railroad hub into a large city after Hoover Dam is built. Farmers in Arizona, Nevada, and California irrigate crops, while cities such as Los Angeles, San Diego, and Phoenix grow with drinking water and affordable electricity.

pages.brief: A close view of an ancient Greek vase shows a single mythical creature in a bold, simple pose. The creature is surrounded by curved decorative bands, suggesting the opening imagery of a story about legendary beings.

pages.text: Heracles (HAIR-uh-kleez), a Greek hero, greets Cerberus, the two- or three-headed guardian dog of the underworld on this vase from the fifth century bce. Introduction People in many cultures have myths. Myths are stories that explain important ideas, such as good and evil, in ways people can understand. A myth can take many forms. It can be a lesson, an explanation of a historical event or natural phenomenon, or even a warning. In ancient Greece, myths were an important part of religion. They weren’t told as entertainment. Rather, stories about gods and goddesses had deep meanings that Greek people used as guidelines for their lives. While gods, goddesses, heroes, and villains are the stars of Greek myths, fantastic creatures often play a central role as well. On this vase, the goddess Athena helps Heracles attack the Hydra, a monster composed of many snakes.
pages.brief: On an ancient Greek vase, the hero Heracles greets Cerberus, the guardian dog of the underworld. In another vase scene, the goddess Athena helps Heracles attack the Hydra, a monster made of many snakes.

pages.text: Centaurs Centaurs had the head and chest of a human and the body of a horse. These violent creatures’ animal side dominated their human side. Centaurs used giant stones and wooden sticks found in nature as weapons against the Greeks’ metal shields, spears, and swords. To the Greeks, the untamed Centaurs represented the direct opposite of their own culture. Centaurs were animal-like and were driven by their emotions, while the Greeks considered themselves to be civilized and driven by reason. The story of the Centaurs began with a Greek king named Ixion. Zeus had allowed Ixion to live among the gods and goddesses on Mount Olympus. Zeus heard a rumor that Ixion had fallen in love with Hera, Zeus’s wife. As a test for Ixion, Zeus created a cloud that looked exactly like Hera.
pages.brief: A Centaur with a human head and chest and a horse’s body charges with a giant stone and wooden stick against Greek fighters holding metal shields, spears, and swords. Above, Zeus creates a cloud shaped exactly like Hera to test King Ixion.

pages.text: Ixion indeed fell in love with the cloud, thinking it was Hera. The cloud gave birth to the first Centaur, and angry Zeus punished Ixion by forcing him to rotate around and around on a blazing wheel forever. Pictures of battle scenes showing Greeks fighting Centaurs were commonplace in ancient Greece on everything from drinking cups to stone temples. The Greeks rarely showed current events in their art. Rather, they used pictures of myths to express how they felt about what was happening in the world around them. For example, the Greeks connected one of their greatest enemies, the Persians, with the wild nature of the Centaurs. They portrayed great battles with Greeks fighting the Centaurs to show their superiority over the Persians. Do You Know? Honoring the relationship between a guest and his or her host was an important part of ancient Greek culture. The myth about Ixion and the first Centaur shows the importance of this relationship through Ixion's disrespect of Zeus, his host. Zeus's punishment was a lesson about the consequences of breaking this accepted custom.
pages.brief: King Ixion embraces a cloud shaped like Hera; from the cloud comes the first Centaur. Zeus punishes Ixion by binding him to a blazing wheel that spins forever. Nearby, a painted battle shows Greek warriors fighting wild Centaurs.

pages.text: Sirens Like Centaurs, Sirens were hybrid creatures. Sirens were women with the wings, legs, and bodies of birds. They represented the importance of self-control. They lived on an island in the middle of the sea, where they sang beautiful songs to lure sailors. The sailors would lose control of their ships and crash onto the island’s rocky shores. According to myth, the Sirens had once been human maids to the goddess Persephone (pur-SE-fuh-nee). Hades, god of the underworld, abducted Persephone to make her his wife. Their wings helped the Sirens search for Persephone. Unsuccessful in their search, they settled on the island.
pages.brief: Bird-bodied Sirens with women’s heads and winged legs sing from a rocky island in the middle of the sea. Below, sailors lose control of their ships and crash onto the shore. The Sirens’ wings recall their search for Persephone after Hades took her to the underworld.

pages.text: The Sirens killed many unsuspecting sailors, but a few sailors passed by them alive. The famous Greek musician Orpheus (OR-fee-uhss) played music so loud that it drowned out the Sirens’ song. The Greek king Odysseus, on his journey home from fighting in the Trojan War, instructed his sailors to tie him up tightly to the mast of his boat. His sailors plugged their own ears so that they wouldn’t be tempted to stop rowing. The Greeks prided themselves on their restraint. Resisting the Sirens’ song represented the strength of will that ancient Greeks valued. Word Wise ord ord ise ise The mythological Sirens are connected to the word siren, which is a device that gives off a loud warning sound. They also inspired the meaning of a siren song. That’s something so appealing that it makes you want it, even if it is dangerous.
pages.brief: The musician Orpheus plays loudly, drowning out the Sirens’ song. Nearby, King Odysseus is tied tightly to his ship’s mast while his sailors plug their ears and keep rowing past the rocky island. The Sirens sing from the shore, trying to lure the ship toward danger.

pages.text: Medusa While the Sirens were known for their beauty, Medusa was famous for her frightening appearance. Greek artists usually showed the Gorgons—Medusa and her two sisters—with large, round heads and huge, staring eyes. Snakes instead of hair grew out of their skulls. Pointed tusks, flared nostrils, and tongues sticking out of their mouths completed their features. Although Medusa’s sisters were immortal, she was mortal. This made her vulnerable to humans. She had her own defense against attacks, though. She could turn people to stone once they looked directly into her eyes.
pages.brief: Medusa and her two Gorgon sisters stand with large round heads, huge staring eyes, snakes instead of hair, pointed tusks, flared nostrils, and tongues sticking out. Medusa faces a person who looks directly into her eyes and begins turning to stone.

pages.text: The myth about Medusa began with an evil king who was in love with the mother of a boy named Perseus. To get Perseus out of his way, the king tricked Perseus into promising that he would bring anything the king wished. The king sent Perseus to kill Medusa and return with her head. The king thought this deed would be impossible. With the help of gods and goddesses, Perseus cut off Medusa’s head. From her body, two creatures sprang forth. They were Chrysaor (kriss-AH-or), a giant whose name means “golden blade,” which could refer to grain, and Pegasus, a winged horse whose name refers to springs of water. Some people think the killing of Medusa symbolized the ending of a drought, and that Chrysaor and Pegasus represented the good things that came afterward— thriving crops and flowing water. Wowser! The ancient Greeks believed that the frightening faces of the Gorgons would protect them and ward off evil. They put pictures of Gorgons everywhere, including on their shields.
pages.brief: Perseus, helped by gods and goddesses, cuts off Medusa’s head. From her body spring Chrysaor, a giant, and Pegasus, a winged horse. A Gorgon’s frightening face is painted on a shield to ward off evil, while crops and flowing water suggest good things after a drought.

pages.text: The Minotaur The Minotaur was another hybrid creature. It had a bull’s head and a man’s body. Its name came from Minos, the king of Crete, where the Minotaur lived, and taurus, the Greek name for a bull. The monster was so destructive that it was kept in a twisted maze called the Labyrinth beneath the king’s palace. After Athenian boys killed the king’s son, Minos sought revenge by attacking the city of Athens. To stop the attacks, the people of Athens agreed to send seven boys and seven girls every year to the terrible Minotaur.
pages.brief: The Minotaur, with a bull’s head and a man’s body, stands inside the twisted Labyrinth beneath King Minos’s palace in Crete. Outside, seven Athenian boys and seven girls are sent from Athens as victims to the destructive monster.

pages.text: A brave Athenian boy named Theseus volunteered to be one of the victims. When Theseus arrived in Crete, he was put in a cage with the other victims. It was then that the princess of Crete, Ariadne (ah-ree-AHD-nee), saw Theseus and fell in love with him. Ariadne didn’t want the Minotaur to kill Theseus. She asked the man who built the Labyrinth how Theseus could escape. She was told that she should give Theseus a ball of yarn to unwind as he made his way through the Labyrinth. She also gave Theseus a sword so he could kill the Minotaur. After Theseus killed the Minotaur, he followed the trail of yarn back out of the maze. The Minotaur myth was popular after the Greeks took over Crete. Just as Centaurs often represented the Persians, bulls could stand for Crete. Bulls were considered sacred to an important goddess in Crete. Theseus defeating the Minotaur could have symbolized the Greek conquest of Crete.
pages.brief: Princess Ariadne gives Theseus a ball of yarn and a sword. Inside the Labyrinth, Theseus unwinds the yarn as he goes, then kills the bull-headed Minotaur and follows the thread back out. A bull stands for Crete, so the victory suggests Greek conquest.

pages.text: Typhon The fierce Minotaur was tiny compared to the giant Typhon (TY-fon), a winged monster with one hundred heads that represented the destructive forces of weather. Typhon had one human head and ninety-nine heads of other creatures, including lions, bulls, boars, snakes, and dragons. Below the knees, his legs were giant snakes. Instead of fingers, fifty serpent heads coiled forth from each hand. Fire flashed in his eyes, and flames whipped out of his mouth.
pages.brief: The giant winged Typhon rises with one hundred heads: one human and ninety-nine lion, bull, boar, snake, and dragon heads. Below his knees are giant snakes, and fifty serpent heads coil from each hand. Fire flashes in his eyes and flames whip from his mouth.

pages.text: Only Zeus, the king of the gods, could match Typhon in battle. When Typhon threatened to take over the world, Zeus used thunder and lightning to combat Typhon’s fire and wind. Their battle shook the whole world. Zeus set all one hundred of Typhon’s heads on fire. He then imprisoned the monster beneath Earth. The ancient Greeks blamed Typhon for stirring strong winds that spread across land and sea during great storms. They also blamed him for sending forth lava from volcanoes. People were comforted by the idea that Zeus could defeat the destructive natural forces that Typhon represented.
pages.brief: Zeus, king of the gods, hurls thunder and lightning at the giant Typhon, whose fire and wind threaten to take over the world. The battle shakes the whole world as Zeus sets all one hundred of Typhon’s heads on fire and imprisons him beneath Earth. Storms and lava show forces the Greeks blamed on him.

pages.text: Conclusion Mythical creatures did not simply entertain or terrify the ancient Greeks. These creatures and the myths about them had deep meanings that helped people understand the world around them at the time and cope with challenges they faced. Mythical creatures played significant roles in ancient Greek culture, and they’re still popular today. Children and adults remain fascinated by their amazing stories. Mythical creatures of ancient Greece inspired some famous logos for major businesses, including Medusa's head for the fashion label Versace (vur-SAH-chee), Pegasus for Mobil Gas, and a Siren for Starbucks Coffee Company.
pages.brief: Children and adults look at drawings of ancient Greek mythical creatures. Nearby, modern business symbols inspired by the myths appear: Medusa’s head for Versace, Pegasus for Mobil Gas, and a Siren for Starbucks Coffee Company.

books.title: Natural Wonders of the World
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing for this illustrated natural-wonders survey.

pages.text: Natural Wonders of the World.
pages.brief: A wide, dramatic view for a book about natural wonders shows a varied planet-like landscape under a broad sky, with a deep canyon, a smoking volcano, a tall waterfall, a snowcapped mountain, and a coral reef arranged together to invite readers into a journey across the world.

pages.text: Natural Wonders Natural Wonders of the World of the World.
pages.brief: A second title-page scene repeats the grand natural landscape, with the same wide sky and distant landforms suggesting a world of wonders. The view stays calm and inviting, giving young readers a moment to take in the scale of the journey ahead.

pages.text: Arizona’s Barringer Meteorite Crater shows how space rocks striking Earth create amazing landforms. Introduction What makes something a natural wonder? A wonder is a natural structure so amazing and beautiful that it makes you ponder how it was formed. Natural wonders are landforms that have been created by nature, not by humans. Some of these wonders are created in a few years. Others take millions of years to form. Our planet is home to many natural wonders. In this book, we will learn about five of them: • A young volcano that took over a village • An immense coral reef.
pages.brief: In the Arizona desert, a huge round meteorite crater lies in dry, rocky ground, showing where a space rock struck Earth. Beyond it, a young volcano and a vast coral reef appear as examples of natural wonders created by nature, not by humans, over very different spans of time.

pages.text: Grand Canyon Between five and six million years ago, the Colorado River wound through a large plateau (pla-TOE), or an area of raised ground. Over time, the river picked up small pieces of the plateau and carried them as it flowed to the sea. This process is called water erosion (e-RO-zhun). The speed and volume of the water are two factors that determine how much soil and rock is carried away. Different kinds of rocks also factor into water erosion. Some rocks, such as limestone and shale, are soft and break easily. Other rocks, such as granite and slate, are hard and break less easily. In the Grand Canyon, the Colorado River carried pieces of softer rock downstream, leaving behind the harder rocks. Over millions of years, this process carved deep canyons in the rocks. UNITED STATES Grand Canyon Arizona The Colorado River slowly carved the rock of the Grand Canyon into the wondrous structure we see today.
pages.brief: The Colorado River winds through a broad, raised plateau in Arizona, carrying small pieces of rock downstream. The river has cut a deep canyon through layered rock; softer rock has worn away while harder rock remains, leaving the Grand Canyon’s steep walls.

pages.text: Colorado River The layers of rocks that form the canyon walls show geologists what happened in the area over a period of two billion years. These rocks make up the layers in the canyon walls. The top of the canyon, where most visitors enjoy their first view, is the youngest layer of the canyon. The bottom layer, near the river, is the oldest. Scattered rocks located at the bottom of the canyon date back as long ago as two billion years. The Grand Canyon is a great place to study rocks and the Earth’s history because the rock layers are so easy to see and reach. Geologists often visit the site. One of the first geologists to visit was John Newberry, who traveled to the canyon in 1858. Newberry was the first scientist to record the canyon’s layers. He identified many of the geologic layers, although he wasn’t the first to see them.
pages.brief: A nineteenth-century geologist, John Newberry, stands beside the Colorado River at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, studying the stacked rock layers. The canyon walls rise in bands, with the youngest layer at the top and the oldest near the river; scattered ancient rocks rest at the bottom.

pages.text: Rattling Reptiles More than forty-seven different kinds of reptiles live in the Grand Canyon. While most of these reptiles are harmless, visitors should keep an eye out for snakes. Although they rarely bite humans, the Grand Canyon rattlesnake and the diamondback rattlesnake are venomous. In the winter, rattlesnakes hibernate in dens. Hundreds of rattlesnakes may live in one den. This is one of the only times rattlers live together. In the spring when the weather warms up, the snakes come out of their dens and go their separate ways. In late summer, females give birth to live babies. The babies only stay in the area where they were born for about seven to ten days. Then they shed their first baby skin, add their first rattle, and move on in search of food. As a rattlesnake grows, it sheds its skin at least once a year. It adds a new rattle to its tail with each shed. A mature diamondback may grow to be 2 meters (about 6.5 ft.) long and weigh up to 6.8 kilograms (15 lb.). Rattlers can live to be twenty-five years old.
pages.brief: A large diamondback rattlesnake lies coiled on rocky ground in the Grand Canyon, shaking its rattle. Nearby, a female with newborn babies stays close to a den entrance in late summer, while other rattlesnakes hibernate together deeper inside the den during winter.

pages.text: Native Americans lived in and around the Grand Canyon for more than four thousand years before European explorers arrived. These early groups of people hunted local animals and gathered edible plants. By 1150, most of the original tribes had moved away. Only the Havasupai people remained. Some of them still live and work in the Canyon. Every year, millions of people travel to Grand Canyon National Park to hike, raft, and see this majestic wonder of nature.
pages.brief: Havasupai people live and work in and around the Grand Canyon, with pathways and homes among the red rocks. In the foreground, early Native Americans hunt local animals and gather edible plants; in the distance, visitors hike and raft in the national park.

pages.text: Paricutín Many of nature’s creations are millions of years old. They began forming long before humans lived on Earth. Other creations have formed in modern times. The Paricutín (pah-ree-koo-TEEN) volcano in Mexico is one such formation. Paricutín began forming in 1943 in a field. That year, a farmer discovered a fissure (FISH-ur), or opening in the ground, in his cornfield. The crack was about 1.8 meters (6 ft.) long. Soon more fissures appeared. Black smoke came from the holes, and ash piled up on the ground, forming a cone. In about twelve hours, the cone had grown to 10 meters (33 ft.) high. After a day, it had grown to 50 meters (164 ft.). The volcano continued to grow, reaching a height of 100 meters (328 ft.) in just a week. The brand-new volcano grabbed the attention of news organizations all over the world. GULF OF MEXICO MEXICO Paricutín PACIFIC OCEAN Paricutín volcano erupts in 1943.
pages.brief: A farmer stands in a cornfield in Mexico, staring at a long crack in the ground. Black smoke rises from new fissures, and ash piles into a growing cone; within a week, the young Paricutín volcano towers over the field as news photographers watch.

pages.text: A church steeple is all that remains visible after ash and lava covered the town of Paricutín. The people of Paricutín hoped that their village would be safe, but after a few months, the cone had grown so large that the slow-moving lava started to reach their town. The villagers had to evacuate, leaving behind their homes and farms. Over a nine-year period, lava and ash eventually covered the entire village of Paricutín and most of the nearby town of San Juan. In the end, all that was left of Paricutín was the church steeple rising out of the black rock as a reminder of nature’s power.
pages.brief: A lone church steeple rises from a field of black volcanic rock where the village of Paricutín once stood. In the distance, villagers evacuate with belongings, leaving homes and farms as slow lava and ash spread across the town and nearby San Juan.

pages.text: Volcanoes such as Paricutín are called cinder cones. They are the simplest type of volcano because they appear suddenly, erupt, and then go dormant for decades or centuries. Cinder cones are formed when lava, which is under pressure inside Earth, shoots out from a central vent in the ground. As the lava explodes into the air, it cools and breaks into small pieces that harden and fall as rocks and ash, or cinders, around the central vent to form a cone. Most cinder cones have a bowl-shaped crater at the top. Because Paricutín volcano is young, scientists have been able to observe its growth since it first appeared. Today, the volcano stands about 424 meters (1,391 ft.) tall and covers 26 square kilometers (10 sq. mi.). Its development has allowed scientists to better understand the powerful forces that shape Earth. cinder cone crater rock fragments central vent.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a cinder cone volcano shows a central vent in the ground. Lava shoots upward, cools, and breaks into rock fragments and ash that fall around the vent to build a cone with a bowl-shaped crater at the top; scientists observe the young Paricutín volcano.

pages.text: AFRICA Zambia Victoria Falls Zimbabwe INDIAN OCEAN Victoria Falls, like the Grand Canyon, was formed by water. Victoria Falls Victoria Falls is the largest mass of falling water on the planet. The water falls 108 meters (354 ft.) into a deep pool. The people of Zambia call the Falls Mosi-oa-Tunya (MOH-see wah TOON-yah) (the smoke that thunders). It’s a perfect name. The thunder refers to the booming sound created by the water crashing over the Falls into the pool below. The smoke refers to the water vapor that comes up from the bottom of the Falls. The colorful mist can be seen from 20 kilometers (12 mi.) away.
pages.brief: A huge curtain of water pours over Victoria Falls into a deep pool below, sending up a tall cloud of mist. The Zambezi River crashes over the cliff with a booming roar, and colorful spray rises high enough to be seen far across the African landscape.

pages.text: Victoria Falls is located on the Zambezi River along the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe in Africa. The Falls began forming millions of years ago when a shallow crack in the rock appeared across the path of the river. The crack was caused when parts of the earth shifted about 150 million years ago. Over the years, the river flowed over the rock, eroding away the softer rock, and forming a cliff over which the river now falls. The pool into which the water falls is called a plunge pool. The Scottish explorer David Livingstone visited the Falls in 1855. He was probably the first person from outside of Africa to see the wondrous formations. He named the Falls after Queen Victoria of England. But many people think that Mosi-oa-Tunya is a more accurate name. The Falls is now part of two national parks, one in Zambia and one in Zimbabwe, that draw almost two million visitors each year. cliff hard rock soft rock plunge pool.
pages.brief: The Zambezi River flows across a wide cliff at Victoria Falls, dropping into a deep plunge pool. A Scottish explorer, David Livingstone, stands on the rocky edge in 1855, looking at the falls; soft rock has worn away while hard rock remains beneath the falling water.

pages.text: Victoria Falls Fun Facts • Victoria Falls is actually divided into six waterfalls: Devil’s Cataract, Armchair Falls, Horseshoe Falls, Main Falls, Rainbow Falls, and the Eastern Cataract. • A bridge at the Falls is a popular site for bungee jumping. • During a full moon, the park stays open late so people can enjoy the rainbow that is made when moonlight shines through the water vapor. • People go rafting and kayaking on the water below the Falls. They can even surf on the rapids below.
pages.brief: At Victoria Falls, a bridge spans the gorge where a bungee jumper leaps above the water. In the foreground, people raft and kayak on the rapids below; mist rises in the moonlight, forming a faint rainbow over the falls while visitors watch from the park.

pages.text: CHINA Mount Everest NEPAL PACIFIC OCEAN Mount Everest Mount Everest is named for Welsh surveyor and geologist Sir George Everest. It is the tallest mountain in the world and one of the most amazing sites on Earth. Called “Forehead in the Sky” by the Nepali people, this magnificent landform in the Himalaya mountain range reaches a height of 8,850 meters (29,035 ft.). It lies on the border between Nepal and Tibetan China. The snowcapped Himalayas might appear old, but they are actually quite young for mountains. The mountains formed millions of years ago when two parts of Earth’s crust crashed into each other. Over time, the pressure of the two parts rubbing against each other caused the ground to crumble and rise above the sea. Since Mount Everest is a young mountain, its peaks are still jagged and steep. They haven’t yet been eroded and smoothed down by endless years of wind, ice, and snow.
pages.brief: The jagged, snowcapped peak of Mount Everest rises high above the Himalaya mountain range on the border between Nepal and Tibetan China. Sharp ridges and steep faces show a young mountain, with two parts of Earth’s crust pressing together and lifting the land above the sea.

pages.text: Although Mount Everest is beautiful to look at, the conditions on the mountain are very harsh. The average temperature is about −36°C (−33°F) and can drop to −60°C (−76°F) in January. Even in July, the warmest month, the temperature only reaches −19°C (−2°F). It never gets above freezing, and as a result, the ice and snow at the top of the mountain never melt. Because of its elevation, storms can arrive unexpectedly and cause temperatures to drop quickly. Mount Everest’s summit Storms dump more snow on Mount Everest every year.
pages.brief: The icy summit of Mount Everest stands under a dark, stormy sky. Freezing wind blows snow across the jagged peak, and a sudden storm drops more snow onto the mountain; the temperature is far below freezing, so the ice and snow never melt.

pages.text: The extreme conditions on Mount Everest make it difficult for animals and plants to survive. One of the only animals that can live on the mountain is the wild yak. This large animal can weigh more than 454 kilograms (1,000 lb.) and grow up to 1.8 meters (6 ft.) tall. One of the reasons the yak is able to survive is because its blood can take in more oxygen than the blood of other animals. This adaptation is a lifesaver on Mount Everest, where the air contains little oxygen. The yak also has a dense undercoat of soft hair and a shaggy outer coat that help the animal stay warm. Wild yak grazing The people who originally settled in the Himalayas believed that the gods made their homes in the peaks. As a result, no one tried to climb Mount Everest until British and other European explorers arrived in the early 1900s. The earliest climbers quickly learned about the harsh conditions on the mountain—freezing temperatures, powerful winds, changing weather, and rough terrain.
pages.brief: A large wild yak grazes on a high, rocky slope of Mount Everest, its shaggy coat and dense undercoat protecting it from the cold. In the background, early climbers struggle against powerful winds and rough terrain, while Himalayan peaks rise like the homes of gods.

pages.text: Mountaineers Hillary and Norgay accept awards recognizing their achievement. The yeti (YEH-tee), or Abominable (a-BOM-in-a-bal) Snowman, is a legend of Mount Everest and the Himalayas. Sherpas tell stories about seeing large footprints and gnawed yak bones in the mountains. Hillary’s team took what was said to be a yeti scalp and skins to Europe and the United States, where scientists agreed that the scalp was from a goat and the skins were from a bear. To this day, no one has been able to prove the existence of the yeti. Despite all the obstacles, experienced and inexperienced mountaineers alike continued to come to Mount Everest, hoping to be the first to make it to the top. No one was successful until 1953, when Sir Edmund Hillary (a beekeeper from New Zealand) and Tenzing Norgay (a Sherpa from Nepal) became the first men to successfully climb the mountain. Since then, many climbers from all over the world have risked their lives to get to the top of the “Forehead in the Sky.”
pages.brief: Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay stand together receiving awards for reaching the summit of Mount Everest. Around them, Sherpa storytellers describe large footprints and gnawed yak bones linked to the yeti legend, while a scientist examines a scalp and skins said to be from the mysterious creature.

pages.text: AUSTRALIA Great Barrier Reef A diver explores coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef. Great Barrier Reef The Great Barrier Reef—really a collection of reefs—is more than 2,300 kilometers (1,429 mi.) long. It is located off the northeast coast of Australia and is full of enchanting sea creatures, from sea turtles, sea slugs, and urchins to dolphins, whales, and sharks. More than two hundred species of birds and reptiles inhabit the reef system. A reef is a chain, or range, of rocks that lies at or near the surface of the water. The Great Barrier Reef is the largest system of coral reefs in the world.
pages.brief: A diver explores colorful coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef off Australia’s northeast coast. Sea turtles, sea slugs, urchins, dolphins, whales, and sharks swim around the reef, while seabirds and reptiles inhabit the reef system; the long chain of coral lies near the surface.

pages.text: The life and death of coral polyps are responsible for the formation of coral reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef. Coral reefs are found in all tropical oceans of the world, but none is as large as the Great Barrier Reef. Most established coral reefs are between five and ten thousand years old. Many experts agree that the most recent growth of the Great Barrier Reef began between six and eight thousand years ago. At first glance, the Great Barrier Reef might look like a rock, but it’s not. It’s made from the outer skeletons of millions of animals called polyps (POL-ips), which are related to anemones and jellyfish. As the polyps die, new ones grow on top of the old skeletons. The many layers of skeletons form the limestone base of a coral reef. Other kinds of plants and animals also help make up the reef, such as algae, sponges, and shellfish. But the tiny polyp is responsible for most of this natural wonder’s structure.
pages.brief: A close view of tiny coral polyps living on the Great Barrier Reef shows their soft bodies and hard outer skeletons. New polyps grow on top of old skeletons, building layers of limestone; algae, sponges, and shellfish cluster around them in warm tropical ocean water.

pages.text: Reefs are made from animals, and they supply food and shelter for other animals. They are sensitive to temperature changes in the ocean. Thousands of species live on the reef. They include 1,625 kinds of fish, more than 30 kinds of marine mammals, 50 kinds of seaweed, and 6 kinds of marine turtles. The reef is also an important breeding area for animals, including birds, sea turtles, and several endangered species, such as the humpback whale and the sea cow. As one of the most interesting and beautiful places on Earth, the Great Barrier Reef is a popular destination for scientists, scuba divers, and tourists. In 1981, it was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO, a department of the United Nations. Today, environmentalists work with all of these groups to protect the reef so future generations can learn from it and enjoy its beauty. Look, But Don’t Touch! Reefs are alive and full of delicate creatures. Responsible snorkelers and scuba divers should always follow these important rules: • When snorkeling, float over the reef. Never stand on it. • Take pictures, not coral souvenirs. • Stock saltwater aquariums with fish that are raised in captivity, not those taken from a coral reef. • Always pack out your plastics and other trash.
pages.brief: Snorkelers and scuba divers float over a lively coral reef, watching fish, sea turtles, a humpback whale, and a sea cow. On a boat above, visitors take pictures and pack away their trash; no one stands on the coral or takes coral souvenirs, while scientists and tourists enjoy the protected World Heritage Site.

pages.text: Wonders Everywhere From Arizona to the coast of Australia, natural wonders are everywhere. Whether they formed millions of years ago or within the span of a lifetime, they are all unique. These amazing landforms are some of the largest, highest, and most breathtaking places on Earth. Travelers, scientists, and adventure seekers will continue to visit these special places for generations to come for both study and recreation. The Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and Great Barrier Reef are only five of the many wonders that surround us. Other well-known natural wonders include: • The Northern Lights, a light show that brightens up the skies in the Northern Hemisphere • The Barringer Meteorite Crater, a massive hole in the Arizona desert that is almost a mile wide and 174 meters (570 ft.) deep • Ayers Rock, the world’s largest solid rock, rising 862.5 meters (2,830 ft.) above sea level in Australia • Ha Long Bay, Gulf of Tonkin, Vietnam, a large bay that contains more than 1,600 limestone islands.
pages.brief: A sweeping world map-like landscape shows the Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and the Great Barrier Reef together. Beyond them, the Northern Lights glow above the Barringer Meteorite Crater, Ayers Rock rises in Australia, and limestone islands fill Ha Long Bay in Vietnam.

books.title: Route 66
books.art_why: The book spans historical Route 66 eras and roadside landmarks suited to illustration.

pages.text: Route 66 takes drivers across the entire American West. Introduction The year is 1957 and you’ve just taken the top down on your cherry-red convertible. Sun glints off the shiny metal fins of your car, rock ’n’ roll music blasts from the speakers, and ahead of you lies nothing but open road. Could this drive get any better? You think not—until you pass a three-story- tall ice cream cone covered in sprinkles. Your mouth waters. Should you stop? Wait, there’s a cheeseburger the size of a bus. Time for a quick lunch instead! When it’s time to retire for the night, you park next to your teepee-shaped hotel room— complete with a bed, bathroom, and shower. What a spectacular day it was on the road! Who knows what tomorrow will bring? If you thought this was a dream or an imaginary road trip, you’d be mistaken. You’ve just taken a real trip down America’s favorite highway, Route 66.
pages.brief: A driver in a cherry-red convertible with the top down rolls along an open road under bright sun, rock ’n’ roll blasting from the speakers. Ahead stands a three-story ice cream cone covered in sprinkles, then a bus-sized cheeseburger, and later a teepee-shaped hotel room with a bed, bathroom, and shower.

pages.text: America’s Main Street If you’ve ever seen a road map of the United States, it looks a lot like an intricate spiderweb. Huge highways zigzag from coast to coast, crisscrossing from Canada to Mexico, and connecting nearly every city in between. Getting around is easy: just jump in a car and hit the road! A hundred years ago, driving across the country wasn’t quite so easy. Most “roads” were just small dirt trails. Cars were modern inventions, and they often broke down, got stuck in mud, or popped tires on jagged rocks. If you ran out of gas, you were out of luck; there were just a few gas stations in the wilderness. If you needed to sleep, your only option was to pitch a tent by the side of a road. In the 1920s, the United States government created a new system of numbered highways to better connect cities and states. The first fully paved highway stretched 2,400 miles (3,862 km) from Chicago to Los Angeles. Its name was Route 66, but many would call it the “Main Street of America.”
pages.brief: A road map looks like an intricate spiderweb of highways crossing the United States. On old dirt trails, cars break down, get stuck in mud, or pop tires on jagged rocks; gas stations are scarce. A tent sits by the roadside. A newly paved Route 66 stretches from Chicago to Los Angeles.

pages.text: America’s Main Street was soon put to the test. In 1929, the stock market crashed, causing many people to lose their money, jobs, and homes. The dire period that followed was known as the Great Depression. Meanwhile, a series of droughts caused huge dust storms to destroy farms on the Great Plains, especially in Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico. This phenomenon was known as the Dust Bowl. Suddenly, many people were forced to leave their homes to seek a better life elsewhere. Many believed paradise lay out west—especially in California. Thousands packed up their belongings and made the long journey. How did they get there? On a new road named Route 66. Many believed Route 66 would take them away from their troubles and lead them toward opportunity and riches elsewhere. The Dust Bowl in Literature The Grapes of Wrath, by John Steinbeck, is a classic novel published in 1939. It is about a family fleeing Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl era and making the long journey down Route 66 to seek work in California. Steinbeck described Route 66 as “the mother road” and “the road of flight.”
pages.brief: During the Great Depression, people lose money, jobs, and homes after the stock market crashes. Dust storms from droughts destroy farms across the Great Plains. Thousands pack belongings and travel west to California on Route 66. A family fleeing Oklahoma is shown, recalling a classic novel about the Dust Bowl.

pages.text: In the 1930s, 1.2 million people moved to California. More than half a million of them went because of difficult conditions during the Dust Bowl era. On December 7, 1941, the Japanese military bombed United States naval ships in Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The United States entered World War II the following day. Thousands of soldiers, workers, and supplies needed to be quickly mobilized and transported from around the country to military bases in the West. How did they get there? On Route 66, of course. On the long journey, wartime workers needed food, gasoline, and shelter, so restaurants, gas stations, and hotels began to spring up along the route to accommodate them. Times were tough in America, but business on Route 66 was booming. When the war ended in 1945, Americans celebrated. Soldiers came home, started families, constructed houses, and purchased cars. Many wanted to drive their new cars west to see sights like the Grand Canyon and the Pacific Ocean— by way of Route 66!
pages.brief: Soldiers, workers, and supplies move west on Route 66 after the Pearl Harbor bombing brings the United States into World War II. Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels spring up for wartime travelers. After the war, returning soldiers start families, buy cars, and drive west toward the Grand Canyon and Pacific Ocean.

pages.text: Route 66 in Popular Culture The years after World War II were glory days for Route 66. Shiny blue roadsters, cherry- red convertibles, bubble gum–pink coupes, and yellow Checker cabs cruised up and down the route. Route 66 was no longer just a way to get somewhere else; it was the new place to be. In 1946, a song called “Route 66” became a top hit. Its most famous line urged listeners to “get your kicks on Route Sixty-Six,” which helped define the highway’s place in popular culture. In 1960, a new TV show called Route 66 followed two friends who drove across the country in a Corvette. They weren’t going anywhere in particular; instead, they were looking for adventure on the road. The original version of the song “Route 66” was performed by the Nat King Cole Trio in 1946. The popular television show Route 66 aired from 1960 to 1964.
pages.brief: Shiny blue roadsters, cherry-red convertibles, bubble gum–pink coupes, and yellow Checker cabs cruise along Route 66 in its glory days. A radio plays a hit song inviting listeners to get their kicks on Route 66. Two friends drive a Corvette across the country, looking for adventure on the road.

pages.text: By 1970, most of the original Route 66 was bypassed by a new highway. However, references to Route 66 continued to appear in American popular culture through the end of the century. Fast forward to the year 2000: John Lasseter, the director of Pixar Animation Studios, was driving along Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the imaginative buildings and colorful art installations he saw. He decided to turn his experiences into a Disney-Pixar movie called Cars, which was released in 2006. Lasseter sent a team down Route 66 to do research for the movie. Some of the roadside art they found inspired characters in Cars, and they used Route 66 landmarks in the movie, too. For example, the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, became the Cozy Cone Motel. Cars was so successful that many families who saw it took their own vacations along Route 66, which helped create a resurgence of the popular route. This rusty tow truck (top) in Galena, Kansas, became the inspiration for the Cars movie character Tow Mater (bottom).
pages.brief: John Lasseter and his family drive along Route 66, seeing imaginative buildings and colorful art installations. A research team later travels the route, finding roadside art and landmarks like the Wigwam Motel. A rusty tow truck in Galena, Kansas, stands as inspiration for a movie character, while families take Route 66 vacations after the film.

Route 66 is also full of unusual art, historic gas stations, and vibrant theaters. In addition, travelers can see live shows. For instance, you can experience a real Native American dance ceremony in Lookout Point, New Mexico, or the Will Rogers Memorial Rodeo in Vinita, Oklahoma. One thing’s for sure—you won’t be bored on Route 66!
pages.brief: Roadside attractions line Route 66 across the states: giant statues, museums, motels, historic gas stations, and theaters. Travelers see the Gemini Giant, Paul Bunyon, Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower, Red Rocker, Blue Whale, Cadillac Ranch, Wigwam Motel, Elmer’s Bottle Tree Ranch, Cabazon Dinosaurs, and Chicken Boy. A Native American dance ceremony and a rodeo offer live shows.

pages.text: Cadillac Ranch sits in a pasture where cows graze. Cadillac Ranch In 1974, a group of alternative artists from San Francisco buried ten Cadillacs nose down in a field, rear bumpers sticking up toward the sky. The cars have had many colorful paint jobs over the years, but one of the most visible was in 1990, when all the cars were painted pink. Now they appear in every color of the rainbow because visitors have covered them with graffiti. At the nearby VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.
pages.brief: Ten Cadillacs sit nose down in a pasture where cows graze, their rear bumpers sticking up toward the sky. The cars shine with many colorful paint jobs and graffiti; in 1990 they were all painted pink. Nearby at the VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.

pages.text: Elmer’s Bottle Tree Ranch When folk artist Elmer Long looks at garbage, he sees a forest. He built Bottle Tree Ranch out of recycled bottles, car parts, and objects of all kinds—including buffalo jawbones. As if feasting your eyes on this forest wasn’t enough, it’s also filled with music: the desert wind blows through all the open bottles, creating a medley of different tones. Growing up, Elmer Long collected bottles and other items people had thrown away. Blue Whale What do you give the woman who has everything? If you are Hugh Davis, you build your wife an 80-foot (24.4 m) blue whale for your anniversary. For many years, kids loved to slide and dive from the Blue Whale’s body into the swimming hole below. Now visitors can climb inside to get a view from tiny windows in the whale’s head. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma, has a boardwalk along its spine.
pages.brief: Elmer Long stands among bottle trees made from recycled bottles, car parts, and buffalo jawbones; desert wind blows through the open bottles. Nearby, an 80-foot blue whale with a boardwalk along its spine sits by a swimming hole, and visitors can climb inside to look through tiny windows in its head.

pages.text: Paul Bunyon, Atlanta, IL Chicken Boy, Los Angeles, CA Gemini Giant, Wilmington, IL A Land of Giants Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory called International Fiberglass built thousands of colossal fiberglass statues and sold them to businesses along Route 66 for advertising. The factory created unusual costumes to transform the giants into cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and even chickens. Many of the biggest statues on Route 66 are food statues. Humongous oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones make for a mouthwatering ride. Look out the window near Collinsville, Illinois, and you may even catch a glimpse of the largest catsup bottle in the world! Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower, Collinsville, IL.
pages.brief: Colossal fiberglass statues stand along Route 66, made by International Fiberglass and sold to businesses for advertising. Some giants wear costumes as cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and chickens; others are giant food statues like oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones. Near Collinsville, Illinois, the Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower rises.

pages.text: Dinny cost $300,000 to build and was made from roadside construction materials. Dinosaurs by the Dozen Dinosaurs may be extinct everywhere else on Planet Earth, but not on Route 66—where you can be greeted by towering prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. At 150 feet (45.7 m) long, Dinny is likely the largest concrete dinosaur in America. He lives at a dinosaur park in Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to lure visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn. The dinosaur park became famous and was even featured in the 1985 movie Pee-wee’s Big Adventure. Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, is a popular feature at Cabazon Dinosaurs.
pages.brief: Dinny, a 150-foot-long concrete dinosaur likely the largest in America, towers at a dinosaur park in Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to lure visitors to his nearby Wheel Inn restaurant. Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, stands as a popular feature at the park, which became famous and appeared in a 1985 movie.

pages.text: Saving Route 66 With Route 66’s popularity came traffic—lots of it. Heavy traffic congestion caused the highway to deteriorate. From 1956 through the 1980s, the United States government began building new interstates—high-speed highways with many lanes—around Route 66. As more and more travelers chose to take interstates, businesses on Route 66 suffered. Peeling paint, faded signs, and boarded-up windows became common sights. In 1999, the United States Congress passed a law to protect Route 66. The government started offering money to help businesses and towns pay the cost of preserving important landmarks. In 2008, the World Monuments Fund declared Route 66 “ endangered ” and put together plans to help attract tourists, such as a virtual reality map. Route 66 Red Rocker, Fanning, MO Now Route 66 is resurging in popularity as many return to seek its amusing artwork and creative spirit. The best way to catch the spirit of Route 66 is to drive it— and have your own classic American experience!
pages.brief: Traffic congestion wears down Route 66 as new interstate highways draw travelers away; businesses show peeling paint, faded signs, and boarded-up windows. Congress passes a law to protect Route 66, and money helps preserve landmarks. The World Monuments Fund declares the route endangered and plans a virtual reality map. The Red Rocker in Fanning, Missouri, stands along the resurging route.

books.title: Pyramids
books.art_why: Ancient Egyptian scenes and events from thousands of years ago cannot be photographed, so drawings are needed.

pages.text: Introduction The country of Egypt sits at the northeastern corner of the African continent. It was once home to the ancient Egyptian civilization. Ancient Egypt was one of the most fascinating cultures ever to exist. Thousands of years ago, the Egyptians studied and practiced agriculture, irrigation, architecture, engineering, and much more. They built great structures, including the pyramids. Learning about these pyramids can help us learn a great deal about this amazing civilization.
pages.brief: A broad view of Egypt at the northeastern corner of Africa shows the ancient Egyptian civilization with large pyramid structures rising from the desert. The scene suggests the Egyptians' work in agriculture, irrigation, architecture, and engineering, with the pyramids standing as their great creations.

pages.text: Ancient Egypt Egyptians began to settle along the banks of the Nile River about seven thousand years ago. At first they lived in villages, but over time the villages formed into larger groups and eventually became tribes. By about 3200 bce, these tribes were united under one king, who was called the pharaoh. The majority of pharaohs were men, but there were powerful women who ruled Egypt in later dynasties. The culture of ancient Egypt was dependent on the life-giving Nile River. It provided the Egyptians with fish and birds to eat, as well as water to irrigate their crops. It also served as a waterway for boats, both for travel and to ship goods. The Nile has been a busy waterway for thousands of years.
pages.brief: Along the banks of the Nile River, ancient Egyptian villages and tribes are shown near the water. Boats carry goods and people on the busy river, while people fish and tend irrigated crops. A pharaoh stands as the uniting ruler over the gathered communities.

pages.text: Paintings in a tomb show scenes of the next life. The ancient Egyptians believed in life after death. They believed that their next life would be similar to their present life and that they would need the same kinds of tools and objects in their next life. Therefore, many people were buried with a collection of some of the things they possessed in their current life. Of all the people living in ancient Egypt, no one was given a more lavish burial than a pharaoh. According to the beliefs of the ancient Egyptians, the pharaoh was the son of the Sun god, Re (or Ra). While the pharaoh was alive on Earth, they were known as Horus. After they died, they were united with Re. The new pharaoh, who replaced the dead pharaoh, became the new Horus.
pages.brief: Inside a tomb, painted scenes show the ancient Egyptian next life. A pharaoh is honored with a lavish burial, surrounded by tools and objects for the afterlife. The pharaoh is shown as Horus on Earth and united with the Sun god Re after death, while a new pharaoh becomes the new Horus.

pages.text: Do You Know? The shape of a pyramid represents the Sun’s rays shining on the Earth. Ancient Egyptians believed that a pharaoh who died ascended to heaven on the rays of the Sun.
pages.brief: A pyramid rises beneath the Sun, its sloping sides shown as rays of light reaching down to Earth. The dead pharaoh is pictured ascending to heaven along the Sun's rays, reflecting the ancient Egyptian belief about the pyramid's shape and the pharaoh's journey after death.

pages.text: Building a Pyramid.
pages.brief: A large ancient Egyptian pyramid is shown while it is being built, its stone sides rising in the desert. The image focuses on the building of a pyramid, with the structure itself as the main subject and no specific people or events identified.

pages.text: Many people were needed to pull each large stone on a sledge. In addition to these specialized tasks, other workers were required to move the heavy stones. They moved some stones from the quarry to the building site by boat. Other stones were put on sledges, or large wooden sleds, which were then dragged across the desert sands. Until recently, historians believed that much of this difficult work was forced on enslaved laborers. But in 1990, a tourist traveling in Egypt stumbled on the remains of an ancient city where workers who helped build the pyramids of Giza were once believed to have lived. Evidence from the city suggests that the people who built those pyramids were not enslaved people, but rather skilled craftspeople—about 15,000 of them. Written records suggest that the workers were treated well while they worked on the pyramids. It is believed that farmers also participated in the building of pyramids, especially during the flood season when they could not farm.
pages.brief: A group of workers pulls a huge stone on a wooden sledge across desert sand, while others move heavy stones from a quarry. Boats carry stones along the Nile. Nearby, an ancient workers' city suggests skilled craftspeople, about 15,000 of them, were treated well and that farmers joined the work during flood season.

pages.text: Farmers depended on floods to deposit fertile soil for crops. Because the pharaoh was believed to be the son of a god, farmers thought the pharaoh was able to guarantee good floods. They were glad to serve the pharaoh in exchange for the fertile soil brought by the floods. The location of a pyramid had to be determined very carefully. The site needed to be on rocky ground to support the immense weight of the finished pyramid. Do You Know? Each stone in the Great Pyramid weighed up to two tons or 2000 kilograms. This is as much as a car weighs!
pages.brief: Farmers stand beside fields fertilized by floodwaters, grateful to the pharaoh for good floods. In the background, builders choose rocky ground to support a massive pyramid. A single huge stone from the Great Pyramid is shown beside a car to compare their weight.

pages.text: The Egyptians sailed heavy stones down the Nile River. The pyramid also needed to be near the Nile River so that some of the stones could be taken by water from the quarry to the building site. The site had to be located on the west bank of the Nile because the west was where the Sun set each night and where the dead were believed to exist. The exact position of the pyramid also needed to be determined carefully, since the sides had to face exact north, south, east, and west. An astronomer-priest was summoned to observe the stars in order to determine true north. During the actual building of a pyramid, many ceremonies were performed to ensure the support of the gods in the endeavor.
pages.brief: Workers sail heavy stones down the Nile River toward a pyramid site on the west bank. An astronomer-priest observes the stars to find true north, while ceremonies are performed to seek the gods' support. The pyramid's sides are aligned to face north, south, east, and west.

pages.text: Several kinds of stone were used in the building of a pyramid. The core of the pyramid was made from local limestone. Other limestone of finer quality, brought from far away, was used to make the outer shell of the pyramid. Granite from even farther away was used for the pharaoh’s coffin, called a sarcophagus, as well as to decorate the burial chamber. After the location and position of the pyramid were decided on, the surface of the ground was leveled. After leveling the ground, the workers began the actual labor of building the pyramid. The tomb of King Tutankhamun (King Tut)
pages.brief: Workers level the ground at a pyramid site, using local limestone for the core, finer limestone for the outer shell, and granite for the pharaoh's sarcophagus and burial chamber decoration. Nearby, the tomb of King Tutankhamun is shown as a separate burial place.

pages.text: The internal structure of a pyramid was designed to outsmart thieves and keep them from the burial chamber and its treasures. If the burial chamber was at or below ground level, it was put in place first, and then the pyramid was built around it in horizontal layers. Ramps were built against the sides of the pyramid, and the huge stones were dragged up the ramps and put in position. A series of passageways and rooms included dead ends and empty chambers to confuse anyone trying to loot the tomb. Enormous slabs of stone blocked the entrance to the real tomb.
pages.brief: Inside a pyramid, a hidden burial chamber is surrounded by confusing passageways, dead ends, and empty rooms meant to outsmart thieves. Workers drag huge stones up ramps against the pyramid's sides, building it in horizontal layers. Enormous stone slabs block the entrance to the real tomb.

pages.text: Try This! Build a Pyramid Using sugar cubes or cubes fashioned out of clay, build a model pyramid. You can build a pyramid with steps, a flat- sided pyramid, or one of your own design.
pages.brief: A hands-on scene shows a model pyramid built from sugar cubes or clay cubes. Different designs are visible: a stepped pyramid, a flat-sided pyramid, and a pyramid of the builder's own design, arranged as a simple craft activity.

pages.text: Preparing the Body The ancient Egyptians had a special procedure for preparing the body of an important person for burial. This technique, called mummification, preserved the body for thousands of years. The body was taken to an embalmer, who removed the insides and preserved them in canopic jars. Each jar had a lid in the shape of a guardian god. The body then was left to dry for forty days. Then it was washed, rubbed with oil and spices, and packed with preservatives. Afterward, it was wrapped with many layers of linen soaked in resin to hold its shape. A decorative mask was placed on the head, and the entire body was placed in a sarcophagus. Each sarcophagus was ornately painted.
pages.brief: An embalmer prepares an important person's body for burial. The removed insides are placed in canopic jars with guardian-god lids. The body dries for forty days, then is washed, oiled, packed with preservatives, wrapped in resin-soaked linen, fitted with a decorative mask, and placed in an ornately painted sarcophagus.

pages.text: An elaborate ceremony marked the burial of a pharaoh. The decorated coffin, plus the canopic jars, were carried to the pyramid. A parade of mourners was led by priests and priestesses. Following the mourners were servants who carried all the items meant to travel with the pharaoh into the next life— food, clothes, furniture, and more. Before burying the dead pharaoh, the body’s mouth was opened by a priest. This practice was believed to allow the person to breathe, eat, and speak in the next life. Then the coffin was placed in the tomb and sealed inside the pyramid, in a chamber designed to keep it safe. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A solemn burial parade moves toward a pyramid. Priests and priestesses lead mourners, followed by servants carrying food, clothes, and furniture for the pharaoh's next life. A priest performs the opening-of-the-mouth ceremony before the decorated coffin and canopic jars are sealed inside the tomb chamber.

pages.text: Famous Egyptian Pyramids The first pyramid, built for King Zoser at Saqqâra, is called a step pyramid because it was shaped like giant stairways up the sides. Later pyramids had smaller steps. The design eventually changed into straight-sided pyramids, such as the Great Pyramid at Giza, which was built about 4,500 years ago for King Khufu. The Great Pyramid is 147 meters (482 ft.) tall and contains about 2,300,000 blocks of stone. The Great Pyramid at Giza is part of a complex of pyramids built by King Khufu, his son Khafre, and his grandson Menkaure. Their pyramids are surrounded by other structures. There are pyramids for Queen Meritites and Queen Hetepheres. There are also stone mastabas — tombs made of mud bricks—for the rest of the royal family and members of the court. The Sphinx, a limestone statue with the face of a king and the body of a lion, guards the entire site. The Sphinx represents the Sun god.
pages.brief: The Great Pyramid at Giza rises with straight sides beside the step pyramid of King Zoser at Saqqara. The Giza complex includes pyramids for Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure, queens' pyramids, and mud-brick mastabas. The Sphinx, a limestone statue with a king's face and lion's body, guards the site as a Sun god.

pages.text: All of the ancient Egyptian pyramids have had their treasures looted. Very few tombs have been left intact. The only intact burial of an Egyptian king ever found is that of King Tutankhamun. His tomb, in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, was built underground, rather than inside a pyramid. Because it was found intact, it has helped archaeologists to learn a great deal about the culture of ancient Egypt.
pages.brief: Inside the underground tomb of King Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings, the only intact burial of an Egyptian king is shown. Unlike the looted pyramids, this tomb still holds its treasures, helping archaeologists learn about ancient Egyptian culture.

pages.text: Pyramids in Other Lands Pyramids were also built in the Americas. They were first built in Central America and in northwestern South America, but soon the practice of building pyramids spread to North America as well. Several of the New World cultures that built pyramids are mentioned below. The Mayan people and other cultures in Central America built stepped pyramids. These pyramids had stairways decorated with sculptures and inscriptions that led to temples at the top. Sometimes, but not always, these pyramids contained the tombs of kings. One of the most famous Mayan pyramids is Chichén Itzá. Rebuilt over an earlier pyramid, the current one was built just before 1100 bce. Locations of pyramids in the New World.
pages.brief: A Mayan stepped pyramid in Central America rises with decorated stairways leading to a temple at the top. The structure is shown as one of the pyramids built in the Americas, with sculptures and inscriptions along the stairs and a king's tomb sometimes placed inside.

pages.text: Chichén Itzá, the most famous Mayan pyramid The earlier one, built 100 years before, contained a stone sculpture of a jaguar that was painted red and had eyes made of jade. The jaguar, a Mayan symbol of the Earth’s fertility, was worshipped as a god. The Aztecs, another Central American culture, built the Great Pyramid Temple, most likely in the 1300s, in their capital city of Tenochtitlán, on an island in Lake Texcoco in Mexico. The Aztecs believed that the Sun god needed blood from human hearts to stay strong. Without human blood, the Sun would die and the world would come to an end. Human sacrifices of prisoners taken in war were a regular part of Aztec life, and these sacrifices took place at the Great Pyramid Temple.
pages.brief: The famous Mayan pyramid of Chichén Itzá stands in Central America, while an earlier pyramid contains a red-painted stone jaguar with jade eyes. In Mexico, the Aztec Great Pyramid Temple rises on an island in Lake Texcoco, where human sacrifices of war prisoners are shown taking place for the Sun god.

pages.text: Cultures in northwestern South America also built flat-topped, stepped pyramids. The Moche people, who flourished between 100 bce and 800 ce, built the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. About 600 to 700 years later, the Inca people built pyramids. The Temple of the Sun was the most sacred shrine in the Incan empire. It was a pyramid that contained a huge gold disk that represented the Sun god. The Incas believed that their rulers were direct descendants of the Sun. Pyramid of the Moon in Teotihuacan, Mexico.
pages.brief: In northwestern South America, the Moche people build the flat-topped, stepped Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon. Later, the Inca build a pyramid Temple of the Sun containing a huge gold disk representing the Sun god. The Pyramid of the Moon in Teotihuacan, Mexico, is also shown.

pages.text: Meroë Pyramids, Sudan The pyramid shape has been used in building designs in other cultures around the world. The Meroë Pyramids in Sudan are an example of the cross-cultural exchange between ancient Egypt and the empire of Nubia, one of the earliest civilizations of Africa. Cross-cultural exchange is when two cultures help change, develop, or shape each other. Nubian-style pyramids were built between 700 bce and 300 bce. They used Egyptian cultural forms combined with other African influences. Pyramid designs can also be found in parts of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. The pyramid shape is used in modern architecture in many countries, including France, England, and the United States. A modern pyramid was built in Egypt to honor President Anwar Sadat, who was assassinated in 1981.
pages.brief: The Meroë pyramids in Sudan show Nubian-style pyramids built between 700 and 300 BCE, combining Egyptian forms with other African influences. Pyramid designs appear in Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, and modern pyramids are shown in France, England, and the United States, including one in Egypt honoring President Anwar Sadat.

pages.text: Conclusion Efforts are being made to preserve and protect the pyramids of ancient Egypt, as well as pyramids in other parts of the world. Pollution, urban expansion, tourism, and other problems threaten the pyramids at Giza. The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza is the only one of the famous “Seven Wonders of the Ancient World” that still stands. All of the pyramids and tombs are wonders worthy of preservation. By studying pyramids, we learn about complex and fascinating ancient cultures and the accomplishments of humans who lived during those times. We also learn how ancient cultures honored their leaders and worshipped their gods. Millions of tourists from across the world visit the pyramids at Giza each year.
pages.brief: The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza stands as the only surviving wonder of the ancient world, while pollution, urban expansion, and tourism threaten the site. Preservation efforts are shown around the pyramids, and millions of tourists visit Giza each year to learn about ancient cultures, their leaders, and their gods.

books.title: Mount Kilimanjaro
books.art_why: Mount Kilimanjaro is a real, modern place that can be photographed.

pages.text: Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, Africa The Roof of Africa As the highest peak on the continent of Africa, Mount Kilimanjaro has earned the nickname “the roof of Africa.” The mountain measures 5,895 meters (19,341 ft.) in altitude and rises 4,877 meters (16,000 ft.) above the surrounding land. It is also the world’s tallest freestanding mountain—one not part of a mountain range. Mount Kilimanjaro is located in the country of Tanzania (tan-zuh-NEE-uh), close to its border with Kenya. Kilimanjaro National Park, a World Heritage Site, was established in 1973 to protect the area of the mountain above the tree line. The park was expanded in 2005 to protect the forested areas lower down on its slopes. As a national park, the mountain’s habitats and life forms are under the protection of the Tanzanian government.
pages.brief: Mount Kilimanjaro rises high above the surrounding land in Tanzania, near Kenya. Its high peak and forested lower slopes are protected inside Kilimanjaro National Park. The mountain stands alone, not part of a range, under the sky of Africa.

pages.text: Three Peaks Mount Kilimanjaro began as a volcano. It started forming about 750,000 years ago as a result of eruptions in the Great Rift Valley, an enormous crack in Earth’s crust located in East Africa. Those eruptions created Shira, Kilimanjaro’s oldest volcano. Shira stopped erupting some 500,000 years ago. It left a huge caldera when it collapsed. Over the next forty thousand years, two other volcanoes, Mawenzi and Kibo, formed. Repeated eruptions over time caused Kibo’s summit to grow taller than the other two and created various features in all three peaks. The most recent strong eruption occurred about two hundred years ago. Kibo Mawenzi Shira Kilimanjaro is the tallest volcano outside of South America. Shira and Mawenzi are extinct—not expected to erupt again. Kibo is dormant, meaning it may erupt again in the future.
pages.brief: Three volcanic peaks—Shira, Mawenzi, and Kibo—form Mount Kilimanjaro. Kibo rises tallest, while Shira has a collapsed caldera. The peaks show features made by ancient eruptions in the Great Rift Valley. Shira and Mawenzi are extinct; Kibo is dormant.

pages.text: The contrast between Kilimanjaro’s black rock and white glaciers is part of its beauty. Glaciers have also helped shape Mount Kilimanjaro. Because of their great weight, they have carved the underlying rock into ridges and valleys as they have moved downhill. It may seem surprising that Kilimanjaro has glaciers at all since it is only about 322 kilometers (200 mi.) from the equator. Lower parts of the mountain have warm weather year-round. The whiteness of the glaciers reflects much of the sunlight that reaches them, allowing their ice to remain cool. Naming the Mountain Kilimanjaro is a name believed to have come from two words. Kilima means mountain in Swahili. Njaro is the Kichagga word for the whiteness of Mount Kilimanjaro’s snowy peaks.
pages.brief: Dark rock and white glaciers contrast on Mount Kilimanjaro. Heavy ice has carved ridges and valleys into the rock as it moved downhill. Although the mountain lies near the equator, its lower slopes stay warm year-round. The white ice reflects sunlight and helps keep itself cool.

pages.text: Even so, the mountain’s glaciers are slowly melting because of global warming as well as nearby forests being cut down. The loss of trees reduces the amount of moisture in the air around the mountain. This leads to fewer clouds and less rain in the area, which increases evaporation of moisture from the glaciers. Kilimanjaro’s glaciers have lost more than four-fifths of their mass since 1912, when they were first measured. Some researchers predict that they may disappear completely by 2060. The ice in glaciers holds important historical information about Earth’s atmosphere and climate. Kilimanjaro’s ice holds the only such information for all of Africa. If it melts, that information will be lost forever. So will much of Kilimanjaro’s beauty. Do You Know? Ice cores are cylinders of ice drilled out of an ice sheet or glacier. Bubbles in the ice hold samples of Earth’s atmosphere from thousands or even hundreds of thousands of years ago. Scientists study these air pockets to measure how the makeup of gases in the atmosphere has changed over long periods of time. Ice cores also hold clues about past temperatures and other aspects of the environment.
