pages.brief: Kilimanjaro’s glaciers are shrinking. Fewer trees mean less moisture, fewer clouds, and less rain, so the ice melts faster. The glaciers have lost much of their mass since 1912 and may vanish by 2060. Cylinders of ice hold ancient air bubbles and climate clues.

pages.text: The Chagga People People have lived on or near Mount Kilimanjaro for centuries. At the beginning of the eleventh century, many people from across Africa migrated to northern Tanzania. Many of these people were from various Bantu tribes. They settled the southern and eastern slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Meru, and the nearby town of Moshi. They established themselves as a new community, the Chagga people. Several different tribes were already living in the area when the Chagga arrived. In time, however, only the Chagga remained. The Chagga make up the third-largest ethnic group in Tanzania. While the Chagga have remained Bantu speakers, their language has several dialects that can sound like whole separate languages.
pages.brief: Chagga people live on and near Mount Kilimanjaro. Long ago, Bantu-speaking migrants settled the southern and eastern slopes, Mount Meru, and Moshi, forming the Chagga community. Today the Chagga are Tanzania’s third-largest ethnic group, and their Bantu language has several dialects.

pages.text: Before German colonists and missionaries arrived in the late 1800s, the many Chagga chiefdoms were often at war. But after German colonial rule imposed order, the Chagga banded together. They developed advanced methods to farm the mountain slopes and prospered. They continued to improve their farming methods after Tanzania gained independence in 1961. Today, the Chagga are the wealthiest and the most highly organized communities in Tanzania. Bananas are their main crop, but they also grow yams, beans, and maize in Kilimanjaro’s rich volcanic soil. Around the world, the Chagga are famous for a type of coffee that is now important to Tanzania’s national economy. Over time, their traditional ways of life have changed, but they still have a strong sense of pride in their cultural identity. Moshi Town in Tanzania has a beautiful view of Kilimanjaro.
pages.brief: Before German colonists arrived, many Chagga chiefdoms often fought; later they banded together. Chagga communities farm the rich volcanic slopes of Kilimanjaro. They grow bananas, yams, beans, and maize, and are famous for coffee. They became wealthy and highly organized. Moshi Town has a beautiful view of the mountain.

pages.text: Uhuru Peak is the highest point on the rim of Kibo’s crater. Visiting Kilimanjaro At least twenty-five thousand people from around the world climb Mount Kilimanjaro each year. As the tallest mountain in Africa, Kilimanjaro is one of the Seven Summits— the highest peaks on Earth’s seven continents. Climbing these seven peaks is a goal of many mountaineers. Kilimanjaro is one of the easiest of the Seven Summits to climb. Most of the routes to Kibo’s peak (the highest point of Mount Kilimanjaro) do not require training. Climbers don’t need ropes or mountaineering gear—just good hiking boots and camping equipment. Still, Kilimanjaro is not an easy climb. To avoid altitude sickness, climbers must be careful to adjust slowly to the thinner air as they move up the mountain. A round-trip climb typically takes between five and nine days. About two-thirds of the people who attempt it succeed.
pages.brief: Climbers from around the world travel to Mount Kilimanjaro each year. Many aim for Uhuru Peak, the highest point on Kibo’s crater rim. Most routes need good hiking boots and camping equipment but no ropes. Climbers adjust slowly to thin air; a round trip takes five to nine days.

pages.text: Reaching Kibo’s summit isn’t the only reason to travel to Kilimanjaro. Many nature hikes are available for less ambitious visitors. These include day trips to Lake Chala, a beautiful crater lake, and Shira Plateau, which formed when Kilimanjaro’s first volcano collapsed. Trout fishing is popular in Kilimanjaro’s rivers, and the entire area is great for photography. Tourism brings more than $20 million each year into the local economy. Mountain climbing and other activities create jobs for guides, porters, hotel staff, food producers, travel agents, construction workers, and others. The economy of the entire region benefits. Lake Chala looks blue, turquoise, or green, depending on the time of year.
pages.brief: Visitors hike to Lake Chala, a crater lake, and Shira Plateau, formed when Kilimanjaro’s first volcano collapsed. Trout fishing in rivers and photography draw tourists. Tourism brings more than $20 million yearly and creates jobs for guides, porters, hotel staff, food producers, travel agents, and construction workers.

pages.text: Plants and Animals One of the amazing parts of the experience of climbing Kilima njaro is the changing scenery. Climbers pass through several different ecosystems as they move up the mountain. • The cultivated zone is 800 to 1,800 meters (2,625–5,906 ft.) above sea level. It receives the most rainfall and has many rivers formed by melted ice from glaciers. Due to the plentiful water, this zone contains farmland and small villages. The cultivated zone is located around the base of the mountain. • The montane forest is 1,800 to 2,800 meters (5,906–9,186 ft.) above sea level. This is where the climb begins. The south and east sides have thicker vegetation because they get the most rainfall. Monkeys, elephants, leopards, giraffes, rhinos, and other animals are present but hard to spot. Elephant’s trunk flower grows in the forest on the cool upland slopes. It is Mount Kilimanjaro’s semiofficial symbol.
pages.brief: Climbers pass through changing ecosystems. The cultivated zone around the base has farmland, villages, rivers, and the most rainfall. Above it, the montane forest begins the climb; monkeys, elephants, leopards, giraffes, and rhinos are present but hard to spot. The elephant’s trunk flower grows there.

pages.text: • Above the tree line, the heather and moorland zone is 2,800 to 4,000 meters (9,186–13,123 ft.) above sea level. It’s sometimes listed as two separate zones. This zone is drier and windier than the forest below. Temperatures can reach 40° Celsius (104°F) during the day and drop below freezing at night. Climbers often see clouds at eye level. Wild grasses and giant heathers are the main vegetation. The most common animal is the four- striped grass mouse. Larger animals sometimes wander up the slopes but don’t stay long. Giant groundsels live in the moorland zone. These plants in the sunflower family can live at high altitudes. • The alpine desert is 4,000 to 5,000 meters (13,123–16,404 ft.) above sea level. It receives less than 20 centimeters (8 in.) of rain each year. The few plants that can survive at this altitude must be able to withstand strong sunlight as well as subzero temperatures. Animals include birds of prey and a high-altitude spider. • Kibo’s summit is 5,000 to 5,895 meters (16,404– 19,341 ft.) above sea level. Almost nothing lives here because of the lack of water. Lichens are the main life forms.
pages.brief: Above the tree line, the heather and moorland zone is drier and windier, with wild grasses and giant heathers. The four-striped grass mouse is common there. The alpine desert receives little rain, and near Kibo’s summit almost nothing lives because of the lack of water; lichens are the main life forms.

pages.text: A Symbol of Freedom Tanzania, where Mount Kilimanjaro is located, was called Tanganyika (tang-guh-NYEE- kuh) before it gained independence from Britain in 1961. Two years earlier, the country’s future president, Julius Nyerere (nih-RAIR-ee), said, “We, the people of Tanganyika, would like to light a candle and put it on the top of Mount Kilimanjaro.” He envisioned the candle shining beyond the country’s borders, offering love in place of hate and hope and respect where neither existed before. Because of Nyerere’s words, Kilimanjaro has become a symbol for independence for all of Africa. Kibo’s summit, called Uhuru Peak, gets its name from the Swahili word for “freedom.” Julius Nyerere served as president of Tanzania from 1964 to 1985.
pages.brief: Julius Nyerere, Tanzania’s future president, spoke of lighting a candle on Mount Kilimanjaro so it would shine beyond the country’s borders. His words made the mountain a symbol of independence for Africa. Kibo’s summit is called Uhuru Peak, from the Swahili word for freedom.

pages.text: Author Ernest Hemingway described Mount Kilimanjaro as “wide as all the world, great, high and unbelievably white in the sun.” The Jewel of Africa Mount Kilimanjaro is a rich natural area that is home to a wide variety of plants and animals, some found nowhere else on Earth. It is also a dramatic example of the creative force of volcanoes and a fascinating part of Earth’s geologic history. To travelers who come from every corner of the world, Kilimanjaro is a mountain to climb and a personal goal to reach. To local people, it is a source of prosperity and pride as well as a powerful symbol of freedom and self-government. And to people from all walks of life who are lucky enough to see it, Mount Kilimanjaro is a place of stunning beauty.
pages.brief: Mount Kilimanjaro is called the Jewel of Africa. Its rich natural area holds many plants and animals, some found nowhere else, and shows the creative force of volcanoes. Travelers see a mountain to climb; local people see prosperity, pride, freedom, and self-government. Its stunning beauty draws people from all walks of life.

books.title: Amazing Migrations
books.art_why: The book shows real animals and migrations that exist today.

pages.text: African elephants migrate through Kenya. During a very dry season, they may cover more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.). The Journey Begins It has been said that a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. It may also begin with a swish or a flutter. Traveling by land, sea, and air, many animals journey hundreds and even thousands of miles yearly to feed and breed. This seasonal or annual relocation is known as migration. Such long hauls are not only impressive because of their great distance and exact routes. They are also amazing because of the many challenges migrating animals face as they travel.
pages.brief: A herd of African elephants walks in single file across a dry Kenyan landscape during a very dry season, traveling more than 100 kilometers. Around them, the wide land stretches under a hot sky as the elephants begin their long seasonal journey to feed and breed.

pages.text: The Migration Mission In many parts of the world, the presence or absence of certain wild animals marks the seasons. Forests filled with birdsong in summer grow quiet in winter. The stillness of early spring is broken by the chirps of tiny frogs as temperatures start to rise. Some of the creatures that seem to come and go may simply be dormant during months when food is scarce and conditions are harsh. Frogs, for example, burrow underground in winter or when extreme dry spells occur. Many other animals, however, do not go dormant. Instead of reducing their need for food and water, these animals travel to habitats where they and their young will have plenty of both. In Australia, burrowing frogs come out of the ground after the first winter rains. Do You Know? In the Northern Hemisphere, many animals head south for the winter. In the Southern Hemisphere, it’s just the opposite —they head north. The reason? On the bottom half of the globe, the seasons are reversed.
pages.brief: In an Australian forest after the first winter rains, small burrowing frogs climb out of the wet ground and begin chirping as temperatures rise. Nearby trees stand quietly, and the scene suggests a seasonal change from a bird-filled summer forest to a still winter woodland.

pages.text: A road closing helps Christmas Island red crabs cross safely during their annual migration. Some migratory animals travel a relatively short distance. Australia’s Christmas Island red crabs, for example, make an annual 8-kilometer (5 mi.) journey. They travel from the island’s forests to breed on nearby beaches at the start of the rainy season. Compare their migration to that of North America’s monarch butterflies. These beautiful insects fly up to 4,800 kilometers (3,000 mi.) in the fall and again in the spring! Monarch butterflies pollinate many types of wildflowers. However, they need milkweed plants to reproduce and lay their eggs.
pages.brief: On Christmas Island at the start of the rainy season, a crowd of bright red crabs moves from forest toward the beach, crossing a road made safe for their annual 8-kilometer journey. Farther away, monarch butterflies flutter over wildflowers and milkweed plants.

pages.text: Timing Is Everything All animal migrations take place regularly at certain times of the year. How animals know just when to begin their migrations is a bit of a mystery, however. Getting started before food supplies run out is key, but what triggers migrators to get moving? Day length cues some birds to begin migrating. These migrators are called obligates —they are hardwired to go at a certain time, no matter what. One example of such a migrator is semipalmated sandpipers. These birds breed and nest on Arctic coasts in summer. There, they feast on coastal marine life to build up fatty reserves. Gaining weight is important to these long-distance migrators. As the days begin to shorten, the sandpipers set out on an amazing 4,000-kilometer (2,500 mi.) nonstop journey. They fly south to their winter homes in South America. Most of the route is over open waters with nowhere to stop for a snooze or a snack! semipalmated sandpiper.
pages.brief: A flock of semipalmated sandpipers stands on an Arctic coast in summer, feeding on coastal marine life along the shore to build fat reserves. As days shorten, the birds lift off and fly in a tight group over open ocean toward South America, with no land in sight.

pages.text: Half a million migrating sandhill cranes are common along Nebraska’s Platte River in early spring. Other bird species, such as sandhill cranes, seem to start their spring and fall migrations based on changes in temperature and weather. The cranes’ long migration between the Arctic Circle and Mexico may be delayed or advanced by days or even weeks. That’s because the cranes use tailwinds and rising columns of warm air called thermals to carry them up to 650 kilometers (400 mi.) in a single day. Waiting for optimal conditions reduces the birds’ effort as they journey over North America.
pages.brief: Huge flocks of sandhill cranes gather along Nebraska’s Platte River in early spring. Some stand in shallow water while others rise into the air on rising columns of warm air and tailwinds, traveling together over North America on their long route between the Arctic Circle and Mexico.

pages.text: Gray Whale Migration Gray whales mate and give birth in the warm waters off Mexico’s Baja Peninsula. Mothers wait until their calves get strong enough. Then the pairs make the long journey back toward the cold seas of the Arctic, where food is plentiful. It is the longest annual migration of any mammal on Earth. Optimal conditions may also trigger migration in other animal species. For instance, gray whales summer in the cold waters between Siberia and Alaska. There, they spend up to twenty hours a day eating. The whales begin to migrate south when ice cover over the sea increases in the fall. Gray whales seek warmer water where pregnant females can safely give birth to calves. The whales eat very little as they migrate between 16,000 and 23,000 kilometers (10,000–14,300 mi.). They live off the fatty blubber they have built up during the summer.
pages.brief: A gray whale mother swims beside her calf in warm water off Mexico’s Baja Peninsula, then the pair turn north toward cold Arctic seas where food is plentiful. The mother’s body is rounded with blubber, and ice-covered water waits far away in the north.

pages.text: Which Way Do We Go? Humans use memory, maps, and technology to help them find their way. Long-distance migrators use a mix of navigational tools as well. Airborne migrators like birds and insects have a built-in sense of direction that is based on something called celestial bearings. During daylight hours, they determine their position in relation to the Sun’s position in the sky. Migrating birds that travel at night, such as warblers and blackcaps, use the stars. One scientist projected images of night skies on a domed ceiling to study how some of these night travelers determine direction. He placed caged indigo buntings beneath a display of the night sky. They fluttered and turned themselves in the direction they would normally migrate. When he rotated the starry display, the birds turned as well. The experiment showed that birds use the position of the stars as a guide. indigo bunting.
pages.brief: In a laboratory, a scientist projects a night sky full of stars onto a domed ceiling above caged indigo buntings. The small birds flutter and turn in the direction they would normally migrate; when the starry display rotates, the birds turn with it.

pages.text: What do birds do when skies grow cloudy? Birds and some other animals use Earth’s magnetic field to navigate. Earth is sort of like a giant magnet surrounded by this field. Certain animals can sense the pull of the magnetic field at their location and use it to guide them. Researchers are still studying just how animals do this. One theory is that animals such as sockeye salmon have an internal compass that points them to their destination. When salmon are born, they can somehow sense exactly where they are within Earth’s magnetic field. This location becomes imprinted in their memory. After spending up to four years in the Gulf of Alaska, the salmon return to their freshwater birthplace. They travel thousands of kilometers to release eggs, or spawn, at this exact spot. The salmon are able to sense this point as they make their way back from the sea. Sockeye salmon return to their birthplace in British Columbia to spawn.
pages.brief: Sockeye salmon swim upstream in British Columbia toward the freshwater birthplace they remember, after up to four years in the Gulf of Alaska. Their bodies move against the current as they return to the exact spot where they will release their eggs, guided by a sense of Earth’s magnetic field.

pages.text: But what accounts for the multigenerational migration of monarch butterflies? The round-trip migration from Hudson Bay to Mexico takes longer than a monarch’s life span. The generation that is born in Mexico must find its way back to a place it has never been. Just as some animals have the instinct to begin migration on specific days, monarchs have the instinct to follow the same routes taken by previous generations. The idea of a magnetic “map” stored within their genes may explain this instinct. Genes are basic units of heredity that transfer a trait from one generation to the next. In the case of monarchs, their genes somehow code their destination in their memory. Thousands of monarch butterflies cover a single tree in the oyamel fir forest of central Mexico. They pack in tightly for warmth, wait out the winter, then fly north in spring.
pages.brief: Thousands of monarch butterflies crowd tightly onto a single oyamel fir tree in the mountain forests of central Mexico, covering its branches in orange and black. They rest together through winter for warmth, then many rise into the spring air to begin the long journey north.

pages.text: Wildebeest Migration Many migrating mammals depend on landmarks and a sharp sense of smell to guide them. Africa is home to two of the largest mammal migrations known. The great Serengeti wildebeest migration takes place yearly when 1.5 million wildebeest make their way between feeding grounds in Tanzania and Kenya. Their journey takes them 2,900 kilometers (1,800 mi.) across grassy plains and the rushing Mara River. As they follow the rain and greener pastures to the north, the wildebeest are often joined by zebras and gazelles.
pages.brief: A vast herd of wildebeest moves across grassy plains in the Serengeti, traveling between feeding grounds in Tanzania and Kenya. Some plunge through the rushing Mara River while zebras and gazelles join the 1.5 million animals following rain and greener pastures to the north.

pages.text: Just as impressive is the Kasanka bat migration. In fact, it is the biggest mammal migration on Earth. From almost every corner of sub-Saharan Africa, ten million straw-colored fruit bats gather on a patch of swamp forest in northern Zambia. For several weeks, they feast on the fruit that grows after the start of the rainy season. By day, they cover the trunks of the trees and fly out to forage at dusk. Math Minute The sooty shearwater is a dark seabird that migrates great distances over ocean waters. Its migration route can stretch 14,000 kilometers (8,700 mi.) between New Zealand and the North Pacific Ocean. If it takes a shearwater 29 days to make the trip, how far does the bird travel in an average day?
pages.brief: In a swamp forest in northern Zambia, ten million straw-colored fruit bats hang in dense clusters on tree trunks by day. At dusk they fly out to forage for fruit that grows after the rainy season, while a dark sooty shearwater wings over the open ocean far away.

pages.text: Overcoming Obstacles Knowing when and where to go are just two of the problems migratory animals face. An increasingly bigger problem is dealing with both natural and constructed hazards. jackal Many migrators are prey animals that must be wary of predators as they travel. The wildebeest of the Serengeti are a main food source for lions and jackals as well as crocodiles lurking in lagoons and rivers. Hawks and humans hunt African fruit bats, which grow plump from eating dates and figs. Hawks also hunt the migratory routes of songbirds that travel North America’s flyways. Bad weather presents other challenges to migrating species. Sudden storms can disrupt the flight plans of migrating birds and force large flocks to land in unusual locations. This type of event is known as a fallout. One songbird fallout occurred in South Texas in April 2013. Thousands of tired and hungry migrating songbirds landed on South Padre Island, off the coast of Texas. Island residents put out fruit and worms to help the birds gain enough strength to resume their migration north.
pages.brief: On South Padre Island off the Texas coast, thousands of tired, hungry songbirds rest on the ground after a storm. Island residents place fruit and worms nearby to help the small migrants regain strength before they continue their long flight north.

pages.text: Shifting weather patterns have sometimes interrupted land and water migrations as well. Warm spells can cause early snowmelt, leading to flooding that complicates the migration of animals such as elk. Flooded rivers can overrun their banks and send migrating salmon off course, leaving them high and dry when waters recede. Droughts can make food scarce and can also spark wildfires that put migrating herds in danger. Human-made barriers threaten long-distance migrators as well. Dams block waterways that migrating fish once used. Highways that cross migration routes put animals and people on a collision course. Fences block migrating range animals from following established trails that lead to important feeding grounds. A herd of migrating pronghorn encounter a barbed wire fence in Wyoming. A closer look at the bottom wire, however, reveals that it is not barbed. Pronghorn can slide under it without cutting themselves.
pages.brief: A herd of migrating pronghorn in Wyoming approaches a barbed wire fence that crosses their trail. The bottom wire is smooth, not barbed, and the animals lower themselves to slide underneath without cutting their bodies, continuing toward important feeding grounds despite the human-made barrier.

pages.text: Even useful and important structures harm migrators. The huge blades of giant wind turbines used to produce clean electricity are deadly to migrating birds and bats. Large-scale solar farms, such as the Ivanpah solar plant in California’s Mojave Desert, are responsible for killing thousands of birds that fly into the concentrated beams of sunlight and are instantly burned to death. To address these problems, researchers use tracking devices to monitor migratory animals. They include the information in studies showing the impact of construction on the environment. This information may be helpful in placing new construction away from migration routes. New awareness of these routes and the behavior of migrators has inspired people to find ways to help rather than hurt them. A young loggerhead sea turtle in Florida is tagged by a scientist before it sets out on a journey of 7,250 kilometers (4,500 mi.). Even more incredible, turtles make the trip in just seventy days.
pages.brief: In Florida, a scientist gently holds a young loggerhead sea turtle and attaches a small tracking tag before it begins a 7,250-kilometer journey across the sea. The turtle rests on the sand near the water, ready to set out on a trip that will take about seventy days.

pages.text: The Grand Champion of Migration If any one species deserved to be crowned the grand champion of migration, it would be the arctic tern. Tiny tracking technology enabled scientists to follow the flight of this bird on its long migration between the North and South Poles. What researchers learned was astounding: the tern’s journey was twice as long as once thought, an unbelievable 70,800 kilometers (44,000 mi.)! Instead of following a straight north-south line, many Arctic terns zigzag from Greenland to Antarctica and back again. They do this to take advantage of swirling wind currents that carry them on their way. The additional distance saves these birds the tremendous effort of having to fly directly into the wind.
pages.brief: An arctic tern wings over the ocean between Greenland and Antarctica, following a zigzag route across the globe. The small seabird uses swirling wind currents to help carry it along its enormous 70,800-kilometer migration between the North and South Poles, saving effort by not flying straight into the wind.

pages.text: Some regions now have wildlife overpasses and underpasses where roadways and land migration routes cross. These wildlife bridges and tunnels help keep migrators and drivers away from each other and safe. Engineers are working to improve clean-energy devices that unintentionally harm migrators. Vertical wind turbines in development may one day replace the giant horizontal propellers on wind farms. Specially constructed “fish ladders” have been placed next to dams on salmon migration routes. These ladders help the fish safely reach their spawning grounds. Information about how pollution affects migrators already stressed from their long journeys could lead to regulations designed to keep migrators safe. A salmon leaps up a fish ladder in Alaska. What’s most impressive about amazing migrators is how, despite these obstacles, they set out on their epic journeys year after year. These migrations across land, in the air, and through the sea are critical to the survival of these species. Understanding their importance can inspire us to take action to ensure that these important journeys continue for many years to come.
pages.brief: A salmon leaps up a fish ladder beside a dam in Alaska, climbing toward its spawning grounds. Nearby, a wildlife overpass crosses a roadway and a vertical wind turbine stands in development, showing ways people try to keep migrating animals and drivers safe on their journeys.

books.title: Dust Storms and Sandstorms
books.art_why: The book describes modern real-world dust storms, named events, and actual places that can be photographed.

pages.text: Dust in the Sky In September 2009, the people of eastern Australia watched their world change color. Strong winds had whipped up bone-dry dirt. The storm rolled eastward, building a moving cloud of dust measuring more than 500 kilometers (311 mi.) wide and 1,000 kilometers (621 mi.) long. Dust covered towns and cities. It painted the sky and landscape an eerie reddish-orange. Australians said the sky during a 2009 dust storm reminded them of scenes from a disaster movie. Meteorologists called it the worst dust storm the area had seen in almost seventy years. Poor visibility forced drivers to slow down and turn on their headlights. Airlines canceled flights due to hazardous conditions. Doctors warned people with asthma and other health issues to stay inside. By the time the dust settled, the storm had dumped about 2.5 million metric tonnes (2.75 million tn.) of dust into the ocean. Meteorologists categorize the dramatic dust storm that struck Australia as an SDS event (sandstorm/dust storm). These extreme weather systems pose a serious threat to human health and even the land itself.
pages.brief: People across eastern Australia watch an enormous reddish-orange dust cloud roll over towns and cities, while drivers slow down with headlights on. The storm hides the sky and landscape, cancels flights, and leaves doctors warning people with asthma to stay indoors as dust settles into the ocean.

pages.text: How Sandstorms and Dust Storms Form Thunderstorms and other powerful weather systems that disturb the atmosphere often produce high winds. Whenever strong gusts cross stretches of dry land, the wind blows particles of earth forward or lifts them into the air. Earth and wind—that’s the simple recipe for SDS events. SDS events are most common in Earth’s arid regions—deserts and other places that receive little rain. These lands cover about 40 percent of Earth’s total land area. Areas Around the World at Risk for SDS Events.
pages.brief: Powerful thunderstorms and other weather systems stir the atmosphere and create high winds. Strong gusts cross dry land, lifting particles of earth into the air. In deserts and other arid regions that receive little rain, these winds can raise dust and sand across nearly 40 percent of Earth’s land area.

pages.text: A sandstorm blows across the Middle Eastern country of Jordan. The different types of storms are sometimes lumped together. However, some meteorologists and other scientists distinguish between types of SDS events. What are the different types? As their name suggests, sandstorms occur in sandy regions, such as the Gobi Desert, in Asia, and the Arabian Desert, in the Middle East. A large gust of wind picks up the top layer of sand from the ground. Sandstorms stay close to the ground, rarely rising more than 15 meters (49 ft.) in the air. Since dust weighs less than sand, sandstorms usually include dust as well. On the other hand, dust storms can happen wherever the ground is dry, especially areas parched by drought. Without moisture, dirt doesn’t stick together and breaks down into smaller dust particles. These particles are smaller and lighter than sand grains. That means winds can carry dust farther and faster than sand. In fact, dust storms often carry dust 10 kilometers (6 mi.) or higher into the atmosphere!
pages.brief: A sandstorm blows across Jordan, lifting the top layer of sand and keeping it close to the ground. Nearby, smaller, lighter dust particles rise much higher into the air above dry land, showing how dust storms can carry material up to 10 kilometers above Earth.

pages.text: Haboobs are a specific type of SDS event. They are caused by severe weather. They can occur wherever conditions for SDS exist. Haboobs happen when a powerful weather front, such as a thunderstorm, produces very cold, high winds. Gusts traveling downward can pick up a large amount of sand and dust from the ground. The winds create giant walls of these materials measuring 457 to 1,524 meters (1,500–5,000 ft.) high. The walls may even block out the Sun, which makes visibility very low. Because they can make daytime seem like night, haboobs are also called “black blizzards.” The storms can cover very large areas—up to 160 kilometers (100 mi.) wide. They can also travel as far as 320 kilometers (200 mi.). Occasionally they travel even farther, such as across the Pacific Ocean. How Haboobs Form Haboobs happen during thunderstorms. Cold air moves from high in the sky to the ground. This forces sand and dust to rise to great heights. thunderstorm cold downdraft sand and dust Word Wise Haboob comes from the Arabic word for “wind” or “to blow”: habb. Haboob means “blowing furiously.”
pages.brief: A powerful thunderstorm sends cold air downward, forcing sand and dust upward into a giant wall. The wall can block out the Sun and make daytime seem like night, forming a black blizzard that stretches wide and travels far across the land.

pages.text: Each year, dust storms carry orange dust from the Sahara Desert across the Atlantic Ocean to North and South America. That’s a distance of about 2,600 kilometers (1,616 mi.). How frequent and how severe SDS events are depends on the location and conditions. Sandstorms and dust storms generally occur during the driest seasons. In much of China and other parts of Asia, that period may last from November to April. SDS events in North Africa’s Sahara Desert most often occur from June to September. In Arizona and other parts of the American Southwest, haboobs are common during the summer months, when heavy rains are frequent. A massive haboob moves across Phoenix, Arizona, in 2012.
pages.brief: In the driest seasons, strong winds lift orange dust from the Sahara Desert and carry it across the Atlantic Ocean toward North and South America. A massive haboob also sweeps across Phoenix, Arizona, during the summer, when heavy rains are frequent.

pages.text: Health Threats When sandstorms and dust storms strike, they can make life very unpleasant. Blowing dust forces people to stay indoors. High winds can knock out electrical power. Drivers may also face great risk. The blinding dust from a sudden storm can result in car accidents. To stay safe, officials ask vehicles to pull off the road until a dust storm clears. However, the worst effects of SDS events usually appear after storms pass. Around three million people die each year due to air pollution. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that some of those people become sick as a result of SDS events. However, it is difficult to tell the number of people who suffer as a direct result of sandstorms and dust storms. As a preventive measure, WHO recommends that people wear masks if they must walk or work outdoors during an SDS event. In particular, those with asthma or lung and heart problems are asked to stay indoors.
pages.brief: Blowing dust forces people indoors and knocks out electrical power, while drivers pull off the road because blinding dust makes car accidents likely. Outdoors, people wear masks for protection; those with asthma or lung and heart problems stay inside until the storm clears.

pages.text: Other major threats from SDS events are bacteria, viruses, and fungal spores that sand and dust particles can carry. Once lifted into the atmosphere, these particles become easier to inhale. Research indicates that SDS events can spread serious infections great distances. In North Africa, for example, these storms have been linked to thousands of cases of meningococcal meningitis (muh-nin-juh-KAH-kuhl meh-nin-JY-tiss). This serious bacterial infection of the brain and spinal cord can result in death. In the American Southwest and northern Mexico, dust storms sometimes carry fungal spores that cause an illness called valley fever. Symptoms include chest pain, coughing, rashes, and respiratory infections. In some cases, valley fever can also result in death. Africa in the Amazon Not all dust storms bring bad news. Each year, winds carry about 18 million metric tonnes (20 million tn.) of dust from Africa’s Sahara Desert across the Atlantic Ocean. Much of it settles in South America, including around the Amazon River. The African dust delivers important nutrients that the Amazon area lacks. Without that dust, the Amazon would not be a lush rainforest.
pages.brief: Tiny sand and dust particles carry bacteria, viruses, and fungal spores through the air, spreading infections in North Africa and the American Southwest. Far across the Atlantic, Saharan dust settles around the Amazon River, delivering nutrients the rainforest needs to stay lush and green.

pages.text: Losing Soil Sandstorms and dust storms pose a different kind of threat to farmland and food production. The most vulnerable areas affected have little plant life to prevent erosion —the process of soil being washed away by water or ice or blown away by wind. The roots of trees, bushes, and grasses usually hold soil in place. Without them, erosion can cause soil to disappear once a sandstorm or dust storm blows through. Dry conditions can turn topsoil into dust. Plants need this layer of earth to get the nutrients they need to grow. When winds strip away topsoil, the remaining land is bare and impossible to cultivate. In the United States, the Dust Bowl in the 1930s offers an extreme example of what dust storms can do to land. Farmers in the Plains states, located in the middle of the country, suffered a severe drought throughout the 1930s. Beginning in 1934, major dust storms made conditions even worse. The Dust Bowl was one of the major causes of the Great Depression. During that time, many Americans faced hunger and homelessness.
pages.brief: On dry farmland with few trees, bushes, or grasses, wind strips away nutrient-rich topsoil and leaves bare ground that cannot be cultivated. In the U.S. Plains states during the 1930s Dust Bowl, severe drought and major dust storms ruined fields as farmers faced hunger and homelessness.

pages.text: In the most affected areas, animals died because they couldn’t breathe. Houses were also half buried in dirt. By 1940, some 2.5 million people had left Dust Bowl areas to start fresh somewhere else. In response to this crisis, the U.S. government started programs to help rural areas. Efforts included education to teach farmers better ways to protect the soil and prevent erosion. Another major threat of SDS events is the spread of deserts, a process known as desertification. Every year, topsoil near the edges of deserts dries out and blows away. This causes desert areas to expand. Frequent and severe SDS events cause this process to intensify. China’s State Environmental Protection Administration has noted that the country is losing almost a million acres of farmland each year. In parts of Asia, Africa, and the Middle East, desertification is forcing farmers and villagers off their land. Without healthy soil, fields and gardens can no longer grow food. A farmer in Yemen, in the Middle East, herds his animals during a drought in 2014.
pages.brief: In Dust Bowl areas, houses sit half buried in dirt and animals have died, while families leave to start again; education programs teach farmers to protect soil. Near expanding deserts, a farmer in Yemen herds his animals during a 2014 drought as dry topsoil blows away.

pages.text: Ways to Settle the Dust The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) monitors sandstorms and dust storms around the world. It warns that the number and intensity of these storms are rising. It worries that the increase in storms is a troubling sign of climate change. Normal, gradual climate change is a natural process. Over a long period of time, the amount of energy produced by the Sun changes. However, Earth is currently warming at an alarming rate. Most scientists blame certain human activities for causing climate change. The mass destruction of forests and the burning of fossil fuels, such as oil and coal, are two major examples. As long as global temperatures continue to rise, the threat of stronger and more frequent SDS events remains constant. Wowser! Scientists are fascinated by dust storms on planets other than Earth, such as Mars. Some of these storms grow so large that they go around the entire planet. They can even be seen through telescopes on Earth. Martian dust can make space missions to the Red Planet difficult. It sticks to equipment and blocks solar panels that recharge electrical batteries. An artist made this image of what a dust storm on Mars might look like.
pages.brief: Scientists monitor Earth’s dust storms and warn that warming temperatures, forest destruction, and burning oil and coal are making stronger storms more frequent. On Mars, enormous dust storms can wrap around the whole planet, stick to equipment, and block solar panels; an artist imagines one such storm.

pages.text: WMO officials encourage communities and countries to do more to prepare for SDS events. One way to reduce the negative effects of future SDS events is to protect vulnerable land, mainly by reducing erosion. People and governments are fighting desertification by planting and reforesting at-risk areas. Well-placed rows of trees and shrubs serve as windbreaks capable of blocking strong winds. They also hold dirt and moisture in place. Farmers in West Africa have been planting and caring for trees that help preserve soil and crops, and help prevent the Sahara Desert from encroaching on more farmland. Efforts have restored millions of acres of trees to hold back the desert. Improved forecasting and monitoring of SDS events can also help limit the damage they cause. Like other types of weather reports, forecasts can alert people of storm conditions so they can take precautions. Monitoring sandstorms and dust storms also leads to the collection of valuable data about where and how they form, their behaviors, and their impacts. A woman plants a tree for the Great Green Wall project. This project combats desertification along the Sahara Desert.
pages.brief: People and governments plant rows of trees and shrubs as windbreaks to hold soil and moisture in place. In West Africa, farmers care for trees that protect crops and hold back the Sahara, and a woman plants a tree for the Great Green Wall project; improved forecasts help communities prepare for storms.

pages.text: A sandstorm from the Sahara Desert turned snow in Russia and eastern Europe orange. When the Dust Blows Climate scientists have noted a rise in sandstorm and dust storm activity in the last fifteen years. They have also reported an alarming growth of arid regions around the world. Warmer global temperatures are causing more frequent and more powerful thunderstorms and winds. With these strong winds come more frequent SDS events. The stage has been set for a sandier, dustier, and stormier future in the driest parts of the world. Changing the conditions that contribute to this surge in SDS events will require substantial global efforts, including new ideas and long-term planning.
pages.brief: Orange dust from a Sahara sandstorm colors snow in Russia and eastern Europe. Climate scientists note more frequent and powerful dust storms and growing arid regions as warmer temperatures drive stronger winds, setting the stage for a sandier, dustier, stormier future in the driest parts of the world.

books.title: Mount Fuji
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing; the book mixes deep geological history with modern views.

pages.text: Important religious shrines and cherry blossoms dot the landscape around Mount Fuji. Peaceful Mountain Earth’s tallest mountains are known for their high winds, cold temperatures, and steep cliffs of rock and ice. They often look like harsh, unwelcoming places. The opposite is true of Japan’s highest mountain. Although scientists consider it an active volcano, Mount Fuji conveys a sense of peace and calm. Snowcapped for most of the year, it is considered one of the most beautiful mountains in the world. For many Japanese people, Mount Fuji is not just a mountain, however. It’s also a symbol of their country and a place of worship. Throughout history, Mount Fuji has been a source of inspiration. It continues to inspire people today.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji rises snowcapped over a peaceful Japanese landscape, with religious shrines and cherry blossoms dotting the area around it. The volcano looks calm despite being active, conveying beauty and serenity as a symbol of Japan and a place of worship. Throughout history it has inspired people.

pages.text: A Japanese Treasure Mount Fuji towers over the surrounding land at 3,776 meters (12,388 ft.) tall. It is located about 100 kilometers (60 mi.) southwest of Tokyo on Honshu, Japan’s largest island, and roughly 46 kilometers (29 mi.) from the Pacific Ocean. Mount Fuji is the centerpiece of Fuji-Hakone-Izu (FOO-jee HAH-koh-neh EE-zoo) National Park, which was established in 1936. In addition to volcanic landforms, the park features hot springs, coastlines, and islands. In 2013, UNESCO, an agency of the United Nations, granted Mount Fuji the status of a World Heritage Site. That status ensures its protection and conservation. UNESCO honored Mount Fuji for its cultural importance to the people of Japan. Location of Mount Fuji.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji towers over Honshu, Japan’s largest island, about 100 kilometers southwest of Tokyo and roughly 46 kilometers from the Pacific Ocean. It is the centerpiece of Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park, established in 1936, which also features hot springs, coastlines, and islands. In 2013, UNESCO granted Mount Fuji World Heritage status for its cultural importance and to ensure its protection.

pages.text: The Formation of Mount Fuji The eruption of Old Fuji covered Komitake with lava. The eruption of New Fuji covered both of the older volcanoes. Geology Mount Fuji is a cone-shaped volcano. It is located where three huge plates in Earth’s crust meet. Its volcanic activity is caused by the Pacific Plate moving beneath the Philippine Plate and melting from the heat below. According to a Buddhist legend, an earthquake created Mount Fuji in 286 bce. In reality, it formed over a very long period of time. Its base is thought to have formed about sixty-five million years ago. The modern-day mountain mainly formed as a result of lava building up over hundreds of thousands of years.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji is a cone-shaped volcano where three huge plates in Earth’s crust meet. The Pacific Plate moves beneath the Philippine Plate and melts, causing volcanic activity. Old Fuji’s eruption covered Komitake with lava, and New Fuji’s covered older volcanoes. A Buddhist legend says an earthquake created Mount Fuji in 286 BCE, though lava built it over a long period.

pages.text: Mount Fuji has erupted more than seventy times in the last 2,200 years. The largest eruption in recorded history took place in 864 ce. The most recent large eruption occurred in 1707, less than two months after a massive earthquake. It caused enormous clouds of volcanic ash to fall on the city of Edo (modern-day Tokyo). It also destroyed villages and farmland nearby and caused a ten- year famine. Mount Fuji has been dormant since then. However, it is considered active, meaning that scientists expect it to erupt again.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji erupts, sending enormous clouds of volcanic ash over Edo, modern-day Tokyo. Ash falls on the city while villages and farmland nearby are destroyed, and a ten-year famine follows. The mountain has erupted more than seventy times in 2,200 years, with the largest recorded eruption in 864 CE and the most recent large one in 1707.

pages.text: After an enormous earthquake struck Japan in 2011, scientists became concerned that Mount Fuji might erupt. Large earthquakes near volcanoes often signal that an eruption is coming. An increase in volcanic activity was measured, but no eruption followed. However, since Mount Fuji is so close to Tokyo, one of the world’s largest cities, officials put new safety measures into effect. These include a new evacuation plan for more than a million people who might need to escape quickly. In addition, careful monitoring of Mount Fuji and a warning system are in place. Lava, airborne ash, and fast-moving masses of hot rocks and gases are all hazards if the mountain erupts.
pages.brief: Scientists monitor Mount Fuji closely after a huge 2011 earthquake, concerned that increased volcanic activity might signal an eruption. Officials prepare an evacuation plan for more than a million people near Tokyo and set up a warning system. Lava, airborne ash, and fast-moving masses of hot rocks and gases are shown as hazards if the mountain erupts.

pages.text: Mount Fuji’s Vegetation Zones Plants and Animals Many different kinds of plants grow on Mount Fuji’s slopes. The steady increase in elevation creates ever colder habitats going up the mountain. Temperature is an important factor in which kinds of plants can grow in each vegetation zone. The mountainous zone contains trees such as beech, oak, maple, cedar, and fir. A dense forest known as Aokigahara (ou-kee-gah-HAH-rah) (“Sea of Trees”) and the Asagiri (ah-SAH-gee-ree) highland—grasslands with cattle ranches—are both located here. Hemlock and fir trees grow at lower altitudes, and birch and larch grow higher up. No trees grow above roughly 2,200 meters (7,218 ft.) in elevation. The alpine zone usually has snow and subzero temperatures. Only mosses and lichens grow here.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji’s slopes show vegetation zones rising through colder habitats. In the mountainous zone grow beech, oak, maple, cedar, and fir trees, along with the dense Aokigahara forest and the Asagiri highland grasslands with cattle ranches. Hemlock and fir grow lower, birch and larch higher. Above roughly 2,200 meters, no trees grow; the alpine zone has snow, subzero temperatures, mosses, and lichens.

pages.text: Mount Fuji is home to thirty- seven types of mammals. These include the Japanese serow, a type of goat-antelope, as well as Japanese deer and occasional Asiatic black bears. More common are Japanese squirrels and foxes. They live in many habitats, from the base of the mountain to near the top of the subalpine zone. Japanese serows (suh-ROHS) live in forests in the mountainous zone. More than a hundred types of birds breed around Mount Fuji’s base because of the wide variety of habitats. A few kinds of birds live on the mountain year-round. Others migrate through the area or are summer or winter residents. The few amphibians and reptiles include one kind of tree frog. The mountainous zone contains the most insects, including many kinds of butterflies. Japanese paradise flycatchers live on the lower slopes of Mount Fuji. A male’s tail can be three times as long as its body.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji supports thirty-seven kinds of mammals, including Japanese serow, Japanese deer, occasional Asiatic black bears, Japanese squirrels, and foxes. More than a hundred types of birds breed around the base. A few amphibians and reptiles include one kind of tree frog. Insects including many butterflies are numerous in the mountainous zone and Japanese paradise flycatchers live on lower slopes.

pages.text: This Shinto shrine is devoted to the spirit of Mount Fuji. Sacred Symbol Mount Fuji is Japan’s sacred symbol. It has been seen as a sacred mountain for as long as people have lived in Japan. Early people built a shrine around 800 ce near Mount Fuji’s base. They hoped it would calm the god they believed was responsible for the volcano’s eruptions. Japan’s two main religions, Shinto and Buddhism, both consider Mount Fuji sacred. Shinto practitioners believe the mountain is the home of the goddess Konohana Sakuya Hime (koh-noh-HAH-nah SAH-koo-yah HEE-meh). Her name means “the Goddess of the Flowering Trees,” and her symbol is cherry blossoms. Many shrines built in her honor are located at the base and summit of Mount Fuji as well as at the bottom of the crater. Buddhists refer to Mount Fuji’s summit as zenjo, which means “a perfect state of meditation.” Both religions consider it important for worshippers to climb the mountain as a religious pilgrimage.
pages.brief: A Shinto shrine devoted to Mount Fuji’s spirit stands near it. Shinto practitioners believe the mountain is home to Konohana Sakuya Hime, Goddess of the Flowering Trees, whose symbol is cherry blossoms. Many shrines honor her at the base, summit, and crater bottom. Buddhists call the summit zenjo, a perfect state of meditation, and both religions value climbing as pilgrimage.

pages.text: Naming the Mountain No one knows for sure how Mount Fuji got its name. A Japanese folktale links the mountain with the concept of eternal life, or fu-shi (foo-SHEE) (“not death”). Another possibility is that it is named for Fuchi, the goddess of fire of the Ainu, Japan’s first people. Today, people in Japan call the mountain Fuji-san, Fujiyama, or Fuji no Yama (san and yama both mean “mountain”). Artist Katsushika Hokusai (kaht-SOOSH-kah HAWK-sie) (1760–1849) focused on Mount Fuji as a symbol of everlasting life. His woodcut prints titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826–1833) are Japan’s best-known artwork. Hokusai later added ten more prints to that collection and also created One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji in 1834. The Great Wave off Kanagawa by Katsushika Hokusai features Mount Fuji in the background and is one of the most famous pieces of art in the world.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji’s name has no certain origin. A folktale links it to fu-shi, meaning “not death,” while another possibility is Fuchi, the Ainu goddess of fire. People call it Fuji-san, Fujiyama, or Fuji no Yama. Artist Katsushika Hokusai made Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, and his famous print The Great Wave off Kanagawa shows Mount Fuji in the background.

pages.text: Many people report that Mount Fuji is much more beautiful when seen from a distance. Much of its surface is barren volcanic rock and dust. Visiting Mount Fuji Mount Fuji is one of Japan’s most popular tourist sites and may be the most climbed mountain in the world. As many as four hundred thousand people climb Mount Fuji each year. Close to two-thirds are Japanese. Climbing Mount Fuji is not difficult by mountain-climbing standards, and no special equipment is required. The hike up is more like backpacking than mountain climbing. It’s still challenging, though, as the trails are rocky and the weather changes often and is windy. Paved roads go halfway up the mountain, and public transportation is available to the 5th station, at 2,305 meters (7,562 ft.). Four main trails go up from there. Depending on the trail, it can take between four and ten hours to ascend and about half that time to descend.
pages.brief: Many visitors climb Mount Fuji, with as many as four hundred thousand people yearly and close to two-thirds Japanese. The hike is more like backpacking than mountain climbing and needs no special equipment, though trails are rocky and weather is windy and changeable. Paved roads and public transportation reach the 5th station, where four main trails begin.

pages.text: Lakes often create stunning views of Mount Fuji, as this reflected sunset shows. Mount Fuji’s official climbing season is early or mid-July to mid-September. During that time, trails and services are open, the weather is fairly mild, and the mountain is usually free of snow. The mountain is crowded during climbing season, and people often must line up and wait to get through certain areas. Winter climbing conditions are very difficult and are only recommended for the most experienced climbers. Reaching the summit isn’t the only reason to travel to Mount Fuji. Visitors also enjoy seeing the lakes and shrines along the way. Other popular activities include visiting Shiraito Falls, which is considered one of Japan’s most beautiful waterfalls. Nearby Mount Tenjo offers a great view for photographing Mount Fuji.
pages.brief: In the official climbing season from mid-July to mid-September, trails and services are open, weather is fairly mild, and the mountain is usually free of snow. It is crowded, and people often line up and wait. Visitors enjoy lakes, shrines, and Shiraito Falls, one of Japan’s most beautiful waterfalls. Nearby Mount Tenjo offers a great view for photographing Mount Fuji.

pages.text: So Much to Offer Mount Fuji is a symbol of peace and calm around the world. At the same time, it is an active volcano, which makes it a symbol of nature’s power and danger as well. For some, seeing Mount Fuji is a spiritual experience. Its ever- changing beauty inspires artists, photographers, and poets. Its natural habitats make it an ideal spot for many different plants and animals to live. Its habitats also make Mount Fuji a place of great interest to hikers and nature lovers. With so much to offer to so many different people, it’s no wonder that Mount Fuji is one of the most beloved places on Earth. Special Views of Mount Fuji A few times a year, Mount Fuji’s summit lines up with the rising or setting Sun, creating a dramatic star-shaped flash of light known as a Diamond Fuji. When viewed from the far side of a lake, the reflection creates a Double Diamond Fuji. And when the Moon lines up with the peak, that’s a Pearl Fuji. Pearl Fuji.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji symbolizes peace and calm, and as an active volcano it also stands for nature’s power and danger. Its ever-changing beauty inspires artists, photographers, and poets, while its habitats interest hikers and nature lovers. Special views include Diamond Fuji lining up with the Sun, Double Diamond Fuji reflected in a lake, and Pearl Fuji with the Moon at peak.

books.title: Rachel Carson
books.art_why: A biography of a named famous person.

pages.text: R achel Carson.
pages.brief: A portrait of Rachel Carson, the scientist and writer whose life story this book tells, shown alone with a calm, thoughtful expression. She is centered as the main subject, with a simple background that keeps attention on her.

pages.text: TABLE OF CONTENTS.
pages.brief: A quiet contents page with a clean layout, showing the book's sections arranged in order; no people or action are shown on this page. The page serves as an opening guide to the biography, with ample space and a calm, orderly feel.

pages.text: AN EARLY WARNING For months, Rachel Carson had been reading the research coming across her desk. The year was 1945, and she worked as a scientist and editor in chief for the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. It was her job to edit the department’s reports. Other wildlife biologists were raising concerns about a common pesticide known as DDT. DDT killed mosquitoes and other pests. However, researchers reported that wherever it was sprayed, birds and other wildlife were also dying. Tests raised concerns about its long-term effects on humans as well, but government officials ignored these reports. That July, Carson wrote to Reader’s Digest, a popular American magazine. She proposed writing an article about DDT and its negative effects. The publication was not interested, so Carson turned to other work. Twelve years later, DDT was being used more than ever, and it again came to Carson’s attention. By this time, however, she was a best-selling author. She would use her new fame to help protect the natural world she loved. How? By telling people the truth.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson sits at her desk in 1945, reading research reports and editing for the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. Nearby reports describe DDT and dying birds. She writes a letter proposing an article, but the magazine is not interested. Later, as a best-selling author, she resolves to tell people the truth.

pages.text: STARTING OUT Exploring nature was among Rachel Louise Carson’s earliest and happiest memories. Born in 1907, she grew up on a large homestead in western Pennsylvania. Rachel was the youngest of three children. As a young girl, she and her mother, Maria, spent many days wandering their land and watching wildlife. Rachel also loved to read and was soon writing and illustrating her own picture books about birds and other animals. She even published stories in a popular children’s magazine. By the age of ten, she already knew she wanted to be a writer. A young Rachel Carson Maria Carson was determined that her bright, hardworking daughter would have a chance to go to college. The family was always short on money, though. Robert Carson, Rachel’s father, struggled to keep a job. Maria taught piano, did odd jobs, and sold her china dishes to earn money for Rachel’s education.
pages.brief: Young Rachel Carson wanders a large Pennsylvania homestead with her mother, Maria, watching wildlife. Rachel also reads and makes her own picture books about birds and animals. The family struggles for money: her father looks for work while Maria teaches piano, does odd jobs, and sells china to pay for Rachel's education.

pages.text: In 1925, Rachel Carson enrolled at a nearby college. She arrived there planning to study English, but a biology course changed her life, and the professor became a mentor to Carson as well as a lifelong friend. Carson switched her degree to zoology—the study of animal life—and excelled. She graduated with high honors in June 1929. As a teenage girl, Carson had fallen in love with the sea through books. The summer after graduation, she visited the ocean for the first time. She was invited to do research at a marine biology lab on the coast of Massachusetts. Carson attended the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, which is dedicated to the study of marine science.
pages.brief: In 1925 Rachel enrolls at a nearby college, planning to study English. A biology course changes her direction, and she switches to zoology, graduating with high honors in 1929. That summer she visits the ocean for the first time and joins research at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts.

pages.text: Once there, she studied marine creatures up close and in their natural habitats. For Carson, it was a summer of bliss surrounded by aquatic scientists. She later credited her time there as inspiration for her work. Carson had already been accepted at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, for further studies in zoology. However, money problems continued to weigh on her family. Rachel’s parents moved to Baltimore to live with her. Working as a lab assistant, she became the family’s main financial support even as she continued her studies. In 1932, Carson completed her master’s degree. She had hoped to go on and get her doctorate—the highest degree possible—but two years later she was forced to quit the program for financial reasons. Carson’s love of writing soon came into play. Carson in 1932.
pages.brief: At Woods Hole, Rachel studies marine creatures up close in their natural habitats, surrounded by aquatic scientists. She then begins further zoology studies at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, while working as a lab assistant to support her family. In 1932 she completes her master's degree but later must quit doctoral study for financial reasons.

pages.text: HEROINES of ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE Rachel Carson and other female ecologists have often had to struggle for respect and recognition. Despite this, women have made great contributions to the environmental movement. Here are a few. Marjory Stoneman Douglas (1890–1998) Douglas was a determined defender of Florida’s wetlands. Her 1947 book The Everglades: River of Grass helped save that important ecosystem from development. Margaret Thomas Murie (1902–2003) For almost forty years, Murie studied the wilderness and wildlife of Alaska and Wyoming. She helped establish the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and campaigned for federal protections of other wilderness areas. Murie in 1974 Wangari Maathai (1940–2011) Maathai was a biologist from Kenya who founded the Green Belt Movement. The program trained Kenyan women to plant trees and restore deforested areas. For her work in conservation and women’s rights, she was awarded the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize. Jane Goodall (1934–2025) Goodall pioneered the study of wild chimpanzees in Tanzania. She was an international champion for the preservation of wildlife and animal habitats. Greta Thunberg (2003–) The young activist has inspired an international student movement demanding that governments address climate change. Thunberg in 2019.
pages.brief: This page presents five heroines of environmental science: Marjory Stoneman Douglas defending Florida's wetlands, Margaret Thomas Murie studying Alaska and Wyoming wildlife, Wangari Maathai planting trees in Kenya, Jane Goodall with wild chimpanzees in Tanzania, and Greta Thunberg leading students for climate action.

pages.text: THE WRITER AND THE SEA In 1936, Carson took a part-time position in Washington, D.C., in what would become the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (FWS). She was first tasked with writing short radio scripts about marine life. A year later, she was named an assistant aquatic biologist. The position allowed Carson to combine her scientific knowledge and writing talent. She explained complex environmental science in ways the average reader could not just understand but also enjoy. Carson excelled and soon rose to the position of editor in chief of all publications. On the side, she wrote science articles for magazines and newspapers to bring in extra cash. Her father had died in 1935, but Carson was still supporting her mother and other family members. In 1941, Carson published her first book, Under the Sea Wind. With poetic style, it described marine life in the sea and along the seashore. Book critics praised it for being beautifully written and scientifically accurate. However, Americans had turned their attention to fighting World War II (1939–1945), and it did not sell as well as Carson had hoped. Under the Sea Wind 9 Rachel Carson.
pages.brief: In 1936 Rachel Carson begins part-time work in Washington, D.C., writing radio scripts about marine life. She rises to assistant aquatic biologist and then editor in chief, explaining complex science clearly. She also writes magazine articles for extra money and publishes her first book, Under the Sea Wind, in 1941, though World War II keeps it from selling well.

pages.text: Carson did not realize it yet, but she was in an ideal place for her life’s work. Her projects sharpened her writing skills to a fine point. At the same time, she was studying the latest research by expert scientists. When vacations were possible, she and her mother escaped to the seashore. There, Carson would lose herself watching birds, exploring tidal pools, and tramping across mud flats in search of natural wonders. In 1951, Carson published The Sea Around Us. Like her previous title, it took readers on a voyage across and into the ocean using clear yet graceful language. Experts and nonexperts loved it, and critics praised it in glowing terms. This time, her book was a huge success. The Sea Around Us landed on the New York Times best-seller list, where it stayed for eighty-six weeks. Carson won the National Book Award for Nonfiction as well as other important prizes. Carson receives the National Book Award for Nonfiction in 1952.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson works among scientists and sharpens her writing, then escapes with her mother to the seashore to watch birds, explore tidal pools, and cross mud flats. In 1951 she publishes The Sea Around Us, which becomes a huge best-seller and wins the National Book Award for Nonfiction in 1952.

pages.text: Her earnings allowed her to leave the FWS in 1952 to write full-time. She also built a cottage on the rugged coast of Maine. There, the ocean was right outside her door. Carson had many other subjects she wished to write about. One in particular would turn out to be her most important work of all. Carson in 1952 RACHEL’S REFUGE The Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1966, not far from the cottage where Carson spent her summers. The refuge stretches along 50 miles (80 km) of coastline near Kennebunkport, Maine. It protects important wetlands and coastal habitat used by migratory birds and other wildlife. The refuge welcomes about three hundred thousand bird-watchers and other nature lovers each year.
pages.brief: With earnings from her book, Rachel Carson leaves the Fish & Wildlife Service in 1952 to write full-time and builds a cottage on Maine's rugged coast, with the ocean outside her door. Nearby, the Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge is later established along fifty miles of coastline near Kennebunkport, protecting wetlands and coastal habitat for migratory birds.

pages.text: A BOOK THAT STARTED A MOVEMENT The future of science and technology seemed bright after World War II. Scientists had released the power of atoms to create atomic bombs and nuclear energy. In medicine, antibiotics were saving countless lives by killing infections. There seemed to be no challenge that science couldn’t meet. Controlling destructive insects was one of those challenges. Pesticides such as DDT were the main weapon in this battle. Trucks would roll down neighborhood streets and spray the chemical over houses and gardens. Aircraft dropped it on forests and fields. Government officials said there was nothing to worry about. In July 1945, a young beachgoer is sprayed with DDT as a new machine is tested for the first time.
pages.brief: After World War II, science seems full of promise, with atomic energy and antibiotics. To control destructive insects, trucks spray DDT down neighborhood streets and aircraft drop it on forests and fields while officials say there is nothing to worry about. In July 1945, a young beachgoer is sprayed with DDT as a new machine is tested.

pages.text: Salmon and butterflies were among the many victims of DDT. By 1957, though, Carson’s doubts about pesticides had been renewed. She had read the reports about DDT during her time with the FWS. Now she was hearing reports from biologists and naturalists. They described dead and dying bird populations in places where DDT was used. Fish were being poisoned. Helpful insects like butterflies and bees were dying, too. Carson began collecting information for a new book. Her research revealed the likelihood that the chemicals in pesticides and herbicides could cause serious illness in humans, too, including cancer. Still, Carson knew her evidence had to be rock solid. She would be questioning whether huge chemical companies were poisoning people as well as wildlife. Her friends warned her that these giant businesses would do everything in their power to destroy her reputation. As she finished her drafts, she sent every chapter to experts for them to fact-check.
pages.brief: Salmon, butterflies, bees, birds, and fish are shown as victims of DDT. By 1957 Rachel Carson gathers reports from biologists and naturalists about poisoned wildlife. She begins collecting evidence for a new book, aware that chemical companies may attack her reputation, and sends each chapter to experts to fact-check.

pages.text: Even as she continued this work, Carson faced serious personal challenges. In 1957, one of her nieces died, leaving Carson to care for her young great-nephew. A year later, her beloved mother passed away. Then in 1960, Carson learned she had cancer. Progress on the book was slowed by surgery, treatments, and periods of intense pain. In September 1962, Silent Spring was released. The title described a world where birds and insects no longer sang or buzzed because chemicals had wiped them out. In the book, Carson carefully laid out the scientific evidence about the impact of pesticides and herbicides on the environment. It also raised questions about ways they might harm human health. Silent Spring stayed on the best-seller list for more than a year. It ignited a national debate about the safety of using chemicals to control nature. The chickadee is one of many birds discussed in Silent Spring. Carson’s third book has been translated into more than thirty languages.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson cares for her young great-nephew after her niece dies, grieves her mother's death, and faces cancer treatment while finishing her book. In September 1962, Silent Spring is released, describing a world where chemicals wipe out birds and insects. It lays out scientific evidence, becomes a best-seller, and ignites a national debate. A chickadee is among the birds discussed.

pages.text: Carson testifies before a Senate subcommittee in June 1963. Carson did not call for a total ban on these chemicals. However, she did urge the government to test them more carefully and regulate them more closely. She also urged readers to consider the long- term dangers of poisoning the environment. Again, she displayed her talent for explaining complex science in ways that nonscientists could grasp. As predicted, chemical manufacturers attacked. They criticized Carson’s research and qualifications—some simply because she was a woman. She was accused of being antibusiness and a nature fanatic. They said she would rather see people starve than use chemicals to make sure there was enough to eat.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson testifies before a Senate subcommittee in June 1963. She does not demand a total ban but urges careful testing and closer regulation of chemicals. Chemical manufacturers attack her research and qualifications, some simply because she is a woman, accusing her of being antibusiness and a nature fanatic.

pages.text: In the months that followed, Carson calmly explained her position in speeches and interviews. Other scientists defended her research and conclusions. Despite her failing health, Carson testified before members of the U.S. Senate. President John F. Kennedy and other political leaders pointed to Silent Spring as proof that the government needed to study environmental policies more carefully. In the summer of 1963, Carson and her great- nephew returned to the coast of Maine for a much- needed break. Her cottage there was her favorite place in the world. It would be her last visit. Carson looks down the coast in 1961.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson calmly explains her position in speeches and interviews while other scientists defend her research. Despite failing health, she testifies before the U.S. Senate, and President Kennedy points to Silent Spring as proof that environmental policies need study. In summer 1963 she returns with her great-nephew to her beloved Maine coast cottage for the last time.

pages.text: THE TROUBLE WITH DDT In 1939, the Swiss scientist Paul Müller developed what seemed like a miracle pesticide: dichloro-diphenyl- trichloroethane, or DDT for short. It killed insects but seemed to leave birds and other animals unharmed. It helped stop large outbreaks of insect-spread diseases such as malaria and typhus. Müller was awarded the Nobel Prize for his research. DDT was used widely to control insect pests in the 1940s and 1950s. However, biologists eventually found that its poisons built up in the tissues of animals, a process called biomagnification. What seemed harmless at first caused problems over time. For birds, it left their eggs brittle and prone to breaking. Some bird populations fell by more than 80 percent, including bald eagles, the U.S. national bird. Silent Spring put a spotlight on DDT and its effects. More research was done, and the U.S. government banned its use in 1972. Populations of bald eagles and other species rebounded. BIOMAGNIFICATION OF DDT eagle big fish plankton small fish When an animal eats other animals below it in a food chain, it ingests the DDT found in their tissues. The chemical builds up— biomagnifies—as it moves up the food chain. One example of how DDT moves through an ecosystem is shown here. The same process occurs on land, but with plants at the bottom of the food chain.
pages.brief: Scientist Paul Müller develops DDT in 1939; it kills insects and helps stop malaria and typhus, and he wins the Nobel Prize. Later, biologists find DDT builds up in animal tissues through biomagnification, making bird eggs brittle. A food chain shows plankton, small fish, big fish, and an eagle as the chemical builds up.

pages.text: A ROLE MODEL FOR TODAY “ Conservation is a cause that has no end,” Carson said in a 1963 speech. “There is no point at which we will say ‘our work is finished.’” She died the next year, but her vision of protecting the natural world lived on. In fact, it took on a life of its own. It is no exaggeration to say that Silent Spring helped inspire the environmental movement that followed. More Americans questioned the use of pesticides as well as uncontrolled pollution. Carson’s writing contributed to new laws to protect wilderness and wildlife as well as people. They included the Clean Air Act (1963), the Wilderness Act (1964), the Clean Water Act (1972), and the Endangered Species Act (1972). The pesticide DDT caused the number of bald eagles in the continental United States to plummet. By 1963, just 417 pairs were found nesting there. Today, thanks in part to Rachel Carson, that number is nearly 10,000.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson speaks about conservation, saying the work has no end. After her death, Silent Spring helps inspire the environmental movement and new laws protecting air, wilderness, water, and endangered species. The page also shows bald eagles recovering: only 417 nesting pairs by 1963, but nearly 10,000 today.

pages.text: Carson’s environmentalism grew out of her love of nature. She was fascinated by the beauty and science of ecosystems. Her life’s work was communicating that joy, believing that people would protect what they loved. She thought of humans as belonging to the natural world, not as its enemies. Carson and a cat keep company at her home in Maine in 1961. Today, wilderness areas and wildlife populations continue to shrink. Threats to the environment are greater than ever, including the global danger of climate change. At the same time, environmental awareness and activism have grown. With her determination, courage, and passion, Rachel Carson remains a hero and role model for the challenges we face.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson sits with a cat at her home in Maine in 1961, surrounded by the natural world she loved. Her life's work communicates that joy, believing people protect what they love. The page closes by noting that environmental threats, including climate change, continue, but awareness and activism have grown, and Carson remains a role model.

books.title: Money, Money, Money
books.art_why: Money, coins, banknotes and plastic cards all exist today and can be photographed directly.

pages.text: Money, Money, Money.
pages.brief: A wide spread of the many shapes money takes fills the page: stacked paper bills, a scatter of coins from different countries, and a plastic bank card, arranged on a plain surface. Warm light catches the metal edges of the coins.

pages.text: Bartering Thousands of years ago, people used to barter, or directly trade their goods with each other. People living near the ocean had fish and salt, which they traded with people living near the mountains who had fruits, wood, and furs. The barter system continues today. If you trade an apple from your lunch for someone else’s candy bar, you are bartering. However, there are a couple of problems with bartering. You might want some goods or valuable objects from someone, but they might not want the goods that you have. Additionally, many items are heavy, hard to carry, or don’t last long.
