pages.brief: Two groups meet to trade: coastal people holding baskets of fish and bags of salt, mountain people carrying fruit, firewood and furs. In a lunchroom a child swaps an apple for a candy bar. Nearby, a person struggles to carry a heavy, awkward load of goods.

pages.text: Currency In order to get around the problems of bartering, people invented currency, or objects that represented certain values. For example, a group of people might agree that a cow was worth twenty shells and a large fish was worth two shells. People could trade goods for currency and vice versa. Each culture around the world chose a different item to represent the value of its goods. The objects people used for currency were almost always light enough to carry, but rare enough that people couldn’t just pick them up off the ground. The rarer the currency was and the more work it took to find it, the more valuable it was.
pages.brief: People gather to agree on values: a cow stands beside twenty shells, a large fish beside two shells. Traders exchange goods for handfuls of small, light shells, and a few figures search a shoreline for rare, hard-to-find items worth far more than common ones.

pages.text: Some of the items used as currency in ancient times were bright or colorful stones, shells, leaves, feathers, lumps of silver and gold, salt, spices, and gems. In ancient Rome, soldiers got paid with bags of salt. From Africa to Asia, people traded with rare speckled shells that were only found on a few islands in the Indian Ocean. Some Native Americans used wampum, or beads made from clam shells, to trade and make treaties. Other Native Americans used eagle feathers. The Chinese used bundles of tea leaves, and European colonists in North America used tobacco leaves as their currency. The problem with currency of this type was that it was hard to decide how much a particular object was worth. If one shell was much larger than another shell, shouldn’t it be worth more? And what if you met somebody who didn’t think your shells were worth anything at all? Do You Know?
pages.brief: A table of early currencies: bright stones, shells, leaves, feathers, lumps of silver and gold, salt, spices and gems. Roman soldiers receive bags of salt; speckled shells from the Indian Ocean lie heaped; wampum beads and eagle feathers rest beside bundles of Chinese tea leaves and North American tobacco leaves.

pages.text: Coins One solution to the problems of using ordinary objects as currency was to make coins from precious metals. Precious metals are rare and valuable across cultures, and they are easily shaped and weighed. The first coins were minted, or produced, 2,600 years ago in Lydia, which is now a part of Turkey. From Lydia, coins quickly spread into the neighboring countries of Greece and Persia (now known as Iran). The earliest coins were hammered out of a natural combination of gold and silver called electrum. These coins were very rough and crude, with no patterns on the sides or standard sizes and weights. Later, coins were made from either pure gold or pure silver. They had standard weights, and the king’s seal was stamped on one side to confirm the coin’s quality.
pages.brief: In ancient Lydia, a craftsman hammers a rough lump of electrum into one of the first coins, its edges uneven and unmarked. Finished coins are stacked nearby. In the background, gold and silver coins of standard weight and stamped with a king's seal are carried toward Greece and Persia.

pages.text: Early European coins usually had a god’s head on one side and a seal from the maker on the other. Later coins pictured the heads of kings and rulers, with elaborate symbols on the other side. These pictures helped establish when, where, and by whom the coin was made. Even today, you can see the faces of presidents, kings, and queens on modern coins. These Greek coins had words, a picture of an owl, and a portrait of the goddess Athena. The Chinese melted copper and poured it into molds where it hardened into coins. Chinese coins had holes in their centers, so thousands could be easily carried on a ribbon or a stick. Instead of pictures, the Chinese coins, called cash, had words telling their worth, or denomination. Only the government could produce coins. Chinese cash could be held on a string or stick for easy carrying.
pages.brief: A Greek coin lies close up, showing an owl and the goddess Athena. Beside it, European coins carry a god's head and a maker's seal, and later kings' portraits. Chinese copper is melted and poured into molds; finished cash coins with square holes are threaded onto a ribbon and a stick.

pages.text: Minting Coins Coins are harder to make than you might think. Once the government decides to produce new coins, these are just some of the steps that must happen. 1 A designer draws a picture of the coin’s two sides on a large piece of paper. 2 Sculptors make a large, three-dimensional model of the coin. An engraving machine uses the model to make a die, or coin stamp. The die is sent to mints, or factories that produce coins. 3 Mints cut blank coins, called blanks, from a rolled-up sheet of the right kind of metal. The sheet can be as long as five football fields. 4 The blanks are heated, cooled, washed, and dried. 5 A machine called an upsetting mill creates the raised edge of the coin. 6 The coin press stamps the pattern from the die into the coin. 7 Inspectors make sure that there are no mistakes in the coin. Incorrectly made coins get melted down and recycled. 8 The coins are sent out to banks in armored trucks.
pages.brief: Inside a mint: a designer sketches both sides of a coin on large paper, a sculptor shapes a three-dimensional model, and an engraving machine cuts a die. A long rolled sheet of metal is punched into blanks, heated, washed and dried, then pressed and inspected. An armored truck carries coins away.

pages.text: Paper Money A Chinese man named Ts’ai Lun invented paper 1,900 years ago. But it wasn’t used for money until 700 years later when the Chinese government ran out of copper to produce coins. They switched to printing paper money. The earliest paper money was printed by hand by pressing wooden blocks covered with ink onto uniformly sized rectangles of paper. Although coins were still available, the lighter paper money quickly became more popular. In Europe, another invention changed the shape of money. Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable-type printing press in the mid-1400s. Gutenberg’s press allowed people to print paper money by machine, rather than by hand.
pages.brief: A Chinese printer presses inked wooden blocks onto identical rectangles of paper, making the first paper money after copper runs short. Lighter bills are counted and stacked. In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg works his movable-type printing press, sheets of printed money coming off by machine instead of by hand.

pages.text: The Value of Money Unlike gold or silver coins, paper money is worth very little by itself. It costs only four cents (U.S.) to print a bill, including the cost of the paper, ink, and the printer’s pay. So why is one piece of paper worth a hundred dollars? And why is another worth only one? Because the government says so. A hundred years ago, for each dollar in circulation, the government had one dollar’s worth of gold in a bank. This system was called the gold standard, because it ensured that every dollar represented its face value, or the number printed on it, in gold. Back then, you could trade your dollars for the same amount of gold at the bank.
pages.brief: A single paper bill is examined beside a small pile of coins, showing how little the paper itself is worth. Behind it, a bank vault holds stacked bars of gold under the gold standard, and a person hands dollars to a clerk in exchange for the same value in gold.

pages.text: Do You Know?
pages.brief: A quiet page of curiosity: one banknote and a handful of coins rest on a plain table, lit closely so their details stand out, inviting the reader to wonder why this paper is worth anything at all. Nothing else lies on the surface.

pages.text: Keeping Money Real Try This!
pages.brief: An activity page: a banknote is held up toward a bright lamp over a plain table, with a few coins set beside it, ready for close inspection. The scene is simple and hands-on, showing money being examined rather than spent.

pages.text: In order to defeat counterfeiters, most countries make their money using special, hard-to-copy tricks. Bills are printed on paper made with a secret formula. U.S. dollars are made of a mixture of about one-quarter linen and three-quarters cotton, with some red and blue fibers sprinkled throughout. However, the government keeps the exact formula a secret, the way Coca-Cola protects the secret recipe for their famous soda pop. A special thread below the portrait glows in ultraviolet, or “black,” light. Banks and some stores use special pens with ink that turns from black to yellow on real money, but stays black on fake money. The pictures and print on bills are designed to prevent easy copying. The portrait is large and detailed, placed slightly off-center, and made of very thin dashed lines. The patterns on the bill are small and complicated. Each bill has a serial number that shows when and where the bill was printed. In addition, many bills also have colored inks, magnetic inks, and inks that change color depending on the angle you look at them. Some bills have holograms or watermarks that produce an image only when you hold the bill up to the light.
pages.brief: Close-up of a bill under ultraviolet light: a thread beneath the portrait glows, red and blue fibers fleck the cotton-linen paper, and a watermark appears where light shines through. A pen marks the paper, and a hologram shifts color as the note tilts.

pages.text: Invisible Money: Checks and Credit Cards Most adults have checking accounts. Banks keep track of how much money a person has saved, and the person writes checks, or official notes, that stand for a certain amount. Checks can represent a large amount of money on one piece of paper. Many checking accounts also have debit cards that people can use to take cash from their accounts at ATMs or pay for things at shops and restaurants. Credit cards work like debit cards and checking accounts, except that instead of saving money in the bank, a person borrows the money from the bank. People use credit cards to buy items that cost more than they have in the bank. Then, they have to pay the money back, plus a fee called interest. If someone takes a long time to pay the money back, the interest gets bigger.
pages.brief: An adult writes a check at a bank counter while a clerk records the account. At an ATM, a debit card is used to take out cash. In a shop, a customer pays by credit card, and a later bill shows the borrowed money plus interest growing larger.

pages.text: Debit and credit cards Debit and credit cards are made of durable plastic. The person’s name and an individual number are stamped onto one side, along with the name of the bank where the account is. A magnetic strip on the top has special encoded information about the person’s bank account. When the card is swiped through a card-reading machine, the machine electronically calls the bank to make sure that the account has enough money in it. If the money is there, the price is taken from the person’s account and moved to the store’s, restaurant’s, or company’s account. It is easier to carry around one piece of plastic than it is to carry many bills. Plus, since cards have your name and information on them, the money is harder to steal than bills are.
pages.brief: A plastic debit card and a credit card lie face up, name and number stamped on one side and a magnetic strip along the top. A hand swipes a card through a card-reading machine at a till, and the machine contacts the bank to check the account.

pages.text: However, credit cards can be dangerous because people forget that they must pay back the money they borrowed. Many people who use credit cards irresponsibly owe so much money to the banks that the banks take back, or repossess, the things the person bought. Plastic cards are less visible than money, but they still buy the same goods. Our invisible money allows us to trade with people around the world. With the help of catalogs and the Internet, you can use a credit card to buy goods from a person or company in another country. Your money is automatically changed into a currency the other person can use. Shopping online with a credit card can instantly send money across oceans.
pages.brief: A person sits surrounded by things bought on credit, weighed down by a heavy bill, while a bank takes back a purchased item. In another scene, someone shops on a laptop with a credit card, buying goods from a company overseas as payment crosses oceans instantly.

pages.text: Conclusion Three thousand years ago, people bartered one good for another. Today, people trade with each other using bills, coins, and even invisible money. What sort of money do you think we’ll have in another three thousand years? At a stock market, people buy and sell stock. Stocks are pieces of companies. Stock costs more or less depending on the value of the company. But until the stock is sold, the money in it is not real.
pages.brief: A final spread brings three eras together: ancient traders swapping goods by hand, a modern hand holding bills and coins, and a card tapped at a screen. In the background, a stock market floor bustles with traders buying and selling shares in companies.

books.title: Special Effects
books.art_why: Real film sets, animatronic robots, green screens, models and CGI work all exist and can be photographed; this book is about a technology, not a named famous person.

pages.text: Introduction The gigantic ape stands high above New York City on the very top of the Empire State Building. He holds a woman in one of his massive hands. The ape gently puts the woman inside the building, thumps his chest, and roars menacingly at the squadron of planes circling just outside his reach. He strikes out at one of the planes, sending it spiraling to the ground in a ball of fire. The other planes attack, firing bullets at the huge creature. Some of the bullets hit and the ape is badly wounded. He lets out one last roar and lets go of the building, falling to the street.
pages.brief: A giant ape clings to the very top of the Empire State Building high above New York City, a woman held in one massive hand. Planes circle him; he thumps his chest, roars, strikes one plane so it spirals down in flames, then, badly wounded by bullets, lets go and falls.

pages.text: The scene we’ve described is from the movie King Kong and was made many decades ago! The movie would never have been possible if it hadn’t been for Willis O’Brien. A master of movie special effects in the 1920s and the 1930s, he helped create special-effects movies that audiences still love. A close-up of the gorilla model used in the 1933 film King Kong.
pages.brief: A close-up of the furry gorilla model built for the 1933 film King Kong, its ape face and shaggy body filling the frame. Willis O'Brien, a master of movie special effects in the 1920s and 1930s, made such special-effects movies possible.

pages.text: So, what are special effects? Special effects are the part of moviemaking that creates, or makes, pictures and sounds that can make movies seem real. Special effects allow a superhero to rescue anyone, anywhere, at any time. Special effects can create alien spacecraft soaring toward Earth at an alarming speed. Special effects can make buildings crumble, tornadoes twist, and dinosaurs, long extinct, come alive. Movies, or moving pictures, work by capturing a series of still images and replaying them quickly one after the other. Dinosaurs appear to come to life in this special-effects scene from Jurassic Park III (2001).
pages.brief: A dinosaur, long extinct, appears to come alive among ancient plants in a special-effects scene from Jurassic Park III, standing huge and real beside the places and creatures of its prehistoric world.

pages.text: Stop-Motion Animation So, how did O’Brien make King Kong possible? First, he constructed several gorilla models using a metal skeleton with joints like those found in human knees and shoulders. He padded the joints with cotton and foam rubber. He then covered them with rabbit skins to resemble the beast’s fur. Next, O’Brien studied the movements of gorillas in zoos. He also attended professional wrestling matches looking for ideas of how to make his creature battle the dinosaurs and other huge animals on Skull Island, King Kong’s home.
pages.brief: Willis O'Brien builds a gorilla model: a jointed metal skeleton like human knees and shoulders, padded with cotton and foam rubber and covered in rabbit skin for fur. He studies gorillas in a zoo and watches wrestling matches to plan how his creature will fight.

pages.text: O’Brien’s special-effects team then constructed detailed miniature sets, like a New York City street, to provide the backdrop for the animated models. Now it was time for O’Brien to use the process he invented: stop-motion animation. With stop-motion animation, the miniature models were photographed one frame at a time and put into different positions for each frame. When each frame of the developed film was projected in sequence, the models appeared to move with the illusion of being alive.
pages.brief: O'Brien's team builds a detailed miniature New York City street as a backdrop for the models. He photographs the small gorilla one frame at a time, moving it slightly into a new position for each frame, so that projected in sequence the models seem to move and live.

pages.text: Award-winning special effects The following films were either nominated for or won the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences award for Visual Effects. The year each film was released is listed. Have you seen any of these movies? 2012 Life of Pi (winner) 2014 Interstellar (winner) 2015 Star Wars: The Force Awakens 2016 The Jungle Book 2017 Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 2018 Avengers: Infinity War 2019 The Lion King Special effects have been used in movies for more than 100 years. Georges Méliès, a French magician, invented some of the earliest special effects. In 1899 he directed a movie called The Conjurer and used special effects to make himself disappear. Some members of his audience were so terrified by what they saw that they actually fainted! Since then, many types of special-effects tricks have been created.
pages.brief: The French magician Georges Méliès, director of the 1899 movie The Conjurer, makes himself disappear on a small stage before an audience, an early special effect. A few terrified people in the crowd faint away at what they see.

pages.text: Rear Projection Rear projection is a type of special effect that creates fake scenery behind an actor. For example: to make it look like a person is driving a car on a beach, the beach scene is filmed first. Then the beach scene is projected onto a screen. A car and a driver are placed in front of the screen and filmed.
pages.brief: A car and its driver sit in a studio in front of a large screen showing a filmed beach scene, so it looks as though the person is driving along the beach. Rear projection puts this fake scenery behind the actor while the car and driver are filmed.

pages.text: An actor flies through the air in front of a green screen. In the final shot, the background will be replaced with images of a busy market. Color-Replacement Photography With color-replacement photography, the movement of an actor or an animal, such as someone falling, is filmed in front of a chroma blue screen or a green screen. The background is shot at a different time. Then the action of an actor pretending to fall is layered on top of the colored screen. The color is then erased and the background becomes visible wherever the color was. This special effect is like cutting out the shape of an animal or an actor from a sheet of paper and pasting it onto different scenery, except the image is moving and so is the scenery!
pages.brief: An actor flies through the air in front of a bright green screen, filmed as if falling. In the final shot the green is erased and replaced with images of a busy market, the same falling action layered onto scenery shot at a different time.

pages.text: This technique is used every day on most weather portions of the news on TV. The weather anchor stands in front of a color screen while a technician puts the image of a map behind the anchor. The image brought into the picture shows up on any area that is the same color as the screen. You will never see a weather anchor on TV dressed in the screen’s color. That might cause a weather map to appear where their body should be! The cast of Emmerdale goes white water rafting in front of a green screen. The background will be replaced with wild rapids.
pages.brief: A television weather anchor stands in front of a plain color screen while a technician puts an image of a weather map behind her, the map showing up wherever the screen color is. In another studio the cast of Emmerdale raft white water in front of a green screen.

pages.text: Animatronics The huge shark crunching Quint’s boat in Jaws and the endearing creepiness of E.T. are unforgettable images. The process known as animatronics was used to create E.T. as well as the shark in Jaws. Animatronics is a type of special effect that creates characters using electronic robots. A special-effects crew controls the robots’ movements through remote control.
pages.brief: A special-effects crew works animatronic characters by remote control: the huge shark crunching Quint's boat in Jaws and the strange, endearing E.T. These characters are electronic robots, built and steered by a film crew rather than being living creatures.

pages.text: Animators study the movements of real animals and people and try to copy the movements electronically. Because animatronic creatures appear to move like living creatures, they can be filmed interacting with the actors and real animals. The dinosaurs in Jurassic Park were just as scary as E.T. was endearing, due to effective animatronics. Word Wise The word animatronics was coined in 1961 by Walt Disney and comes from the words animate and electronics.
pages.brief: Animators watch real animals and people move and copy those movements electronically, so animatronic dinosaurs in Jurassic Park seem alive as they interact with the actors beside them, moving through the scene like living animals.

pages.text: The actors riding the dragon highlight its size in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Part 2 (2010). Miniature Models Miniature models are often used in place of real buildings or other large objects. On film, the models look life-size. Sets and props can be made extra large or small to make people seem tiny or large. Sets include such things as houses, cities, or jungles—anywhere the acting takes place. Props are objects like chairs or swords that actors use.
pages.brief: Actors ride a huge dragon in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Part 2, a model that makes the creature look enormous beside them. Miniature models stand in for real buildings and large objects, and sets and props can be made extra large or tiny.

pages.text: Weather Special Effects Special effects are often used in movies to create weather conditions and natural disasters. For example, to film a violent storm at sea, actors do not need to go out in a real storm. That would be very dangerous. Instead, they can sit safely in a boat in a large pool or pond. A machine creates crashing waves in the water, huge fans produce powerful winds, and giant overhead sprinklers send down pouring rain. Filmmaker Ang Lee’s Life of Pi (2012) won an Academy Award for Visual Effects. One of the most challenging scenes to create was the storm scene. The tiger and the storm were created separately and then had to be meshed together. The scene is filmed in front of a blue screen, which can later be replaced with film of an actual storm. When snowstorms are needed in a movie, snowflakes can be made from bleached potato flakes, plastic flakes, or powdered laundry detergent.
pages.brief: Actors sit safely in a boat in a large pool while a machine churns crashing waves, huge fans blow powerful winds and giant overhead sprinklers pour rain for a violent storm at sea. Nearby, snowflakes made from bleached potato flakes fall for a snowstorm.

pages.text: Encanto (2021) features amazing CGI to create the mountain landscape of Colombia and the characters’ fantastical abilities. Computer-Generated Images (CGI) Computer-generated images can be used to create almost any imaginable effect in a movie— blazing fires, giant waves, or talking dinosaurs. Once the images are created on the computer, they can be changed, moved, copied, and combined with other images for the movie. Computers helped revolutionize the world of special effects in movies. With computers, special-effects artists can create movie scenes never thought possible. Now, computer-generated images can be used to create an entire movie like The Polar Express.
pages.brief: Computer-generated images build the mountain landscape of Colombia and the characters' fantastical abilities in Encanto. Artists create blazing fires, giant waves and talking dinosaurs on computers, then change, move, copy and combine the images into scenes once thought impossible.

pages.text: Conclusion Audiences in 1933 were awestruck by the special effects used in King Kong. And audiences of today are equally awestruck as they watch volcanoes erupt in cities, spaceships engage in battle, and huge ocean liners crack in half and sink to the bottom of the ocean. But today’s audiences know a little more about special effects than audiences of years ago. Does this mean that today’s audiences are bored with today’s movies? Not a chance! They still enjoy the “magic” they see on the screen. They love being frightened, amazed, and entertained. So, what’s left for movie special effects? Computer special- effects artists want to perfect a way to make a computer- generated human being look completely real. Will they achieve their goal? They probably will, because with special effects anything can happen, right? CGI-rendered human character.
pages.brief: Audiences watch volcanoes erupt in cities, spaceships do battle, and huge ocean liners crack in half and sink to the bottom of the ocean, all made by special effects. Beside these scenes a computer-rendered human character stands looking completely real.

books.title: Threats to Our Atmosphere
books.art_why: Real-world science and environment topic with satellites, factories, people, and Earth processes; photographs suit it.

pages.text: Threats to Our Atmosphere.
pages.brief: A wide view of Earth from space, with its thin blue atmosphere glowing along the curved horizon, clouds and oceans visible below. The scene is calm and majestic, introducing the air that surrounds the planet.

pages.text: Threats to Our Threats to Our Atmosphere Atmosphere.
pages.brief: A close view of Earth’s blue atmosphere from orbit, with sunlight striking the planet and clouds swirling over oceans and land. The atmosphere looks delicate and exposed in the darkness of space. No other objects appear.

pages.text: Layers of Earth’s atmosphere as seen from a satellite Introduction.
pages.brief: A satellite view of Earth from space shows the planet’s atmosphere as a thin band of layered blue haze along the curved horizon. Below, clouds and land are visible; above, the atmosphere fades into black space.

pages.text: Earth’s Atmosphere.
pages.brief: A broad view of Earth from space with the atmosphere surrounding the globe. Sunlight reaches the planet, clouds drift over oceans and continents, and the thin blue air wraps the world in a protective layer.

pages.text: The Ozone Layer.
pages.brief: A view from space of Earth’s upper atmosphere, showing a pale blue protective band high above the planet. Below it, clouds and oceans cover the surface; above it, the dark edge of space begins quietly.

pages.text: Ozone in the ozone layer is always being created and destroyed. Under normal conditions, the amount of ozone remains fairly constant, which means that the balance does not shift too greatly one way or the other. The part of sunlight known as ultraviolet (UV) light is responsible for both creating and destroying ozone. UV light creates ozone by splitting molecules of oxygen gas (O 2 ) into two individual oxygen atoms (O). If one of these oxygen atoms joins with a molecule of oxygen gas, a three-atom ozone molecule forms. UV light can also change an existing ozone molecule by removing one of its oxygen atoms. The freed oxygen atom then reacts with an ozone molecule (O 3 ), causing it to split into two oxygen molecules (O 2 + O 2 ).
pages.brief: A close, magnified view of oxygen molecules and ozone molecules high in the atmosphere, with invisible ultraviolet sunlight streaming through them. Some oxygen molecules split into single atoms, then join to form three-atom ozone; other ozone molecules break apart again.

pages.text: Do You Know? Sunlight is actually a mixture of visible and invisible light of various wavelengths. The visible light is made of different colors from red to violet. Long wavelengths, which are less powerful, produce red light. Shorter wavelengths, which are more powerful, produce blue and violet light. Light eventually becomes invisible as the wavelengths decrease. Powerful ultraviolet light is invisible. It can cause skin cancer and damage the eyes. It can hurt plants and kill ocean life. Some biologists think that an increase in ultraviolet light is bleaching the color out of corals around the world. Light Wavelengths.
pages.brief: Sunlight streams toward Earth, showing a range from long red wavelengths to shorter blue and violet ones, then invisible ultraviolet rays. Below, a person’s skin and eyes are exposed, plants stand in daylight, and colorful corals in the ocean look pale and bleached.

pages.text: Because ozone is always being created and destroyed, the amount of ozone in the ozone layer is fairly constant. The layer of ozone created keeps harmful UV light from reaching Earth’s surface. Ozone also forms near the ground. This ozone is harmful to plants and animals. It is called “bad ozone.” It forms when cars and factories release chemicals called pollutants into the air. On hot days, sunlight starts a reaction between the pollutants and oxygen, causing the formation of harmful ground-level ozone. If levels of ground-level ozone rise to dangerously high levels, a warning is sent out. People with breathing problems are told to stay inside.
pages.brief: A split scene: high above Earth, a protective ozone band blocks harmful ultraviolet light; near the ground, cars and factories release pollutants into hot, sunny air. A person with breathing trouble stays indoors while a warning is issued for dangerously high ground-level ozone.

pages.text: Discovery of the Ozone Hole In the 1970s, scientists in Antarctica measured an increase in the ultraviolet (UV) light reaching Earth. Later, satellites confirmed that UV light in some areas was not being absorbed by the ozone layer as much as in previous years. From the satellite data, scientists made maps that showed a hole in the ozone layer over the South Pole. By 1994, the ozone level had dropped to one-half of what it was in the 1970s. There were signs that the ozone hole above Antarctica was expanding past the polar region toward the equator, where more people lived. The ozone hole was becoming a threat to people and the environment. Math Minute A one-percent decrease in ozone in the stratosphere will cause a two-percent increase in UV-B light that reaches the ground. If ozone in the stratosphere decreases by ten percent, what is the increase in the percentage of UV-B light reaching the ground?
pages.brief: Scientists in Antarctica work in a cold, icy landscape, measuring ultraviolet light under a pale sky. Above them, a satellite orbits Earth, and a map-like view of the South Pole shows a large opening in the ozone layer spreading toward the equator, where more people live.

pages.text: Ozone destruction is greatest around the North and South Poles during winter, due to the winds and low temperatures common to polar regions. The ozone layer rebuilds during warmer months. (Winter in Antarctica, or the South Pole, occurs during summer in the Arctic, or North Pole.)
pages.brief: A polar winter scene at the South Pole with strong winds and bitter cold over ice and snow. High above, the ozone layer thins during the dark season. On the opposite pole, the Arctic is shown in its warmer summer months, where the ozone layer rebuilds.

pages.text: Chemical Causes of the Ozone Hole Scientists searched for causes of the changing ozone levels. They discovered that some factories release chemicals called CFCs, or chlorofluorocarbons, that could destroy ozone. The element chlorine in CFCs was the main problem. CFCs were used in air conditioners, insulating foams, and spray paint. As a result, large amounts of chlorine were regularly released into the atmosphere. Scientists also learned that another chemical, bromine, could destroy ozone. Bromine is found in substances that are known as ODCs, or Ozone Depleting Chemicals. Bromine can destroy forty-five times more ozone than an equal amount of chlorine found in CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons). ODCs are frequently found in chemicals used to control fires.
pages.brief: A factory releases chemicals into the air, while everyday objects such as an air conditioner, insulating foam, and a spray-paint can sit nearby. In a magnified view, chlorine and bromine atoms attack ozone molecules; bromine is shown as far more destructive, and fire-control chemicals appear too.

pages.text: CFCs and ODCs rise into the stratosphere, where sunlight breaks these molecules into chlorine and bromine atoms. The chlorine and bromine then break down ozone molecules. One chlorine atom can destroy one hundred thousand ozone molecules. The process stops when the chlorine and bromine drift into space. Natural sources of chemicals can also destroy ozone. One such source is erupting volcanoes. They spread hydrochloric acid high into the stratosphere, where it breaks down into chlorine gas, which destroys ozone. Volcanoes and other natural events destroy some ozone, but CFCs and ODCs from industry cause most of the damage.
pages.brief: Chemical molecules rise from industry into the stratosphere, where sunlight splits them into chlorine and bromine atoms. A magnified view shows one chlorine atom destroying many ozone molecules. Below, an erupting volcano sends a plume high into the sky, showing a natural source of ozone-destroying chlorine gas.

pages.text: The World Responds Even after ozone destruction was connected to CFCs and ODCs, many countries continued to produce them. These chemicals were so useful that nobody wanted to give them up. It took cooperation between the governments of many nations to address this global problem. Countries joined together in 1987 and signed the Montreal Protocol. This agreement called for reducing and later banning the production of CFCs and ODCs by 1996. This is a success story because it is the first time that many nations have tackled an environmental issue on a global scale. As a result, since the year 2000, CFCs and ODCs in the atmosphere have been decreasing. However, it may take years to tell whether or not the ozone layer will fully recover.
pages.brief: Representatives from many nations meet around a large table, signing an international agreement to reduce and ban harmful chemicals. Outside, factories and air conditioners still release CFCs, but the atmosphere above Earth begins to show signs of recovery as chlorine and bromine levels slowly decrease.

pages.text: Global Warming Engineers quickly developed alternative chemicals to CFCs and ODCs in hopes of restoring the ozone layer. However, some of these ozone-friendly alternative chemicals are also powerful greenhouse gases. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, when released into the atmosphere, trap heat near Earth’s surface in the same way that glass traps heat in a greenhouse. The result is a condition known as the greenhouse effect. Some scientists think an increase in gases that create the greenhouse effect has caused the temperature of the air around Earth to gradually rise.
pages.brief: A greenhouse stands under sunlight, with glass trapping warmth inside, while a view of Earth shows heat held near the surface by carbon dioxide and methane. Engineers work with alternative chemicals in a laboratory, hoping to restore the ozone layer without adding more powerful greenhouse gases.

pages.text: Earth has warmed by one degree over the last one hundred years. That may not seem like a lot, but scientists are concerned. Over time, a persistent warming trend might cause Earth’s temperature to rise higher and higher. A hotter Earth may lead to the melting of the polar ice caps and warming of the oceans. If ice on land melts, the world’s oceans would rise and flood land near the coast, destroying habitats of living things. A warmer Earth would also create changes in weather patterns that could lead to habitat destruction and the deaths of some plants and animals. Some living things that don’t move around, such as the oceans’ corals, would be trapped and doomed. The sea life that depends on the coral reefs for shelter and food would also die.
pages.brief: A warmer Earth is shown with melting polar ice caps and rising oceans flooding low coastal land. Corals sit trapped in warming seas, while shifting weather patterns affect habitats. Plants and animals face danger as the planet’s temperature rises higher over time.

pages.text: Greenhouse Gases Four different greenhouse gases contribute to global warming when they are released into the atmosphere. The four gases are carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorocarbons. Most scientists think that carbon dioxide causes about three-fourths, or 76 percent, of the increase in global warming. Machines using gas-powered motors, as well as power plants, produce carbon dioxide by burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas. The carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere by our cars, planes, trucks, and trains may contribute to greater global warming.
pages.brief: A busy road, airport, and power plant release exhaust into the sky, showing gas-powered cars, planes, trucks, and trains. Nearby, coal, oil, and natural gas are burned for energy. A magnified view shows carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorocarbons rising and trapping heat near Earth.

pages.text: Methane is responsible for about 13 percent of global warming. Methane is produced naturally in swamps and by livestock passing gas. It is also a product of rotting garbage. Nitrous oxide is the third-worst contributor to global warming. Nitrous oxide is found mostly in fertilizers. The nitrogen in fertilizers is an important plant food, but when it mixes with soil it produces nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide is also produced when animal waste decomposes. The final contributor to global warming is fluorocarbon gases. Fluorocarbons also contribute to the destruction of ozone. Fluorocarbons rarely occur in nature. They are almost totally human- made, so their production can be prevented.
pages.brief: A swamp releases methane bubbles while livestock graze and rotting garbage sits in a heap. Nearby, fertilizers are spread on fields and animal waste decomposes. In a magnified view, fluorocarbon gases rise from human-made sources, contributing both to global warming and to ozone destruction.

pages.text: Carpooling and taking public transportation would reduce the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere by gas-powered cars and trucks. World Debate Not everyone agrees on the seriousness of the global-warming problem. Some say that a one-percent rise is nothing to be concerned about. Others think that the problem will worsen and that people ought to take steps now to prevent future global warming. These people believe that we should find ways to reduce greenhouse gas production before it is too late. Reducing the amount of greenhouse gases may also slow down the destruction of the ozone layer. Global warming of the lower atmosphere actually cools the upper atmosphere. This cooling leads to conditions that can cause.
pages.brief: People carpool and board a bus, reducing exhaust from gas-powered cars and trucks. Around a world debate, some people look unconcerned while others urge action to cut greenhouse gases. Above Earth, a split view shows the lower atmosphere warming while the upper atmosphere cools, creating conditions that may harm the ozone layer.

pages.text: So, if we can learn how to decrease the production of greenhouse gases, we might prevent further destruction of the ozone layer. There are no definite answers to the problem of global warming, but many scientists around the world are looking into effective solutions. They say it is in everyone’s best interests to understand as much as possible about decreasing the release of greenhouse gases.
pages.brief: Scientists around the world study Earth’s atmosphere and the ozone layer, looking for effective solutions to global warming. They discuss ways to decrease the release of greenhouse gases, believing it is in everyone’s best interests to understand as much as possible about the problem.

pages.text: What You Can Do to Help.
pages.brief: A person stands on Earth’s surface, looking up at the atmosphere and thinking about ways to help. The scene is open and hopeful, with no specific actions shown, only a sense of personal responsibility for protecting the air.

books.title: M Is for Mexico
books.art_why: Modern Mexico and real places, people, and landmarks can be photographed.

pages.text: M Is for Mexico Great tales from Mexico MEXICO MEXICO Come on in, the water’s fine MEXICO.
pages.brief: A bright, welcoming view of Mexico fills the page, with land and calm water inviting visitors in. The scene feels like the cover of a travel collection about Mexico, with a warm, open mood and no people needed to suggest the country’s many stories.

pages.text: A mariachi band My Travel Brochure By Juan Rodriguez Ms. Brown’s Fifth-Grade Class Welcome to Mexico! I love my beautiful country and am so happy we can explore it together. Mexico has a lot of rich history and culture. The people who live here are very kind, and their hospitality is out of this world! There is so much here to see and do. The question is not what you want to do, but whether you will have the time to do it all. You might want to relax on the shores of Mexico’s many beaches or visit some of our wonderful museums, historic sites, or ancient ruins. You could even go for a horseback ride in the mountains, a boat ride through the wetlands, or listen to local mariachi music. Whatever you want to do or see, Mexico has something for you!
pages.brief: Juan Rodriguez stands beside his travel brochure display, welcoming readers to Mexico. Around him are hints of mariachi music, beaches, museums, historic sites, ancient ruins, mountains, wetlands, and horseback riding, all shown as choices for a visit. His friendly expression shows pride in his beautiful country and its kind people.

pages.text: The Land Let’s begin our tour by learning a little bit about Mexico’s geography. Mexico is located at the southern part of North America. The United States is its neighbor to the north. Guatemala and Belize are its neighbors to the south. The country is divided into North and South, just like the Americas. In southern Mexico, most states have large rural areas with a large farming population. The northern states are wealthier than the southern states and are mostly urban and industrialized. More than half of the country’s population lives in the central part of the country. This area is what is called the Valley of Mexico. Mexico City, Mexico’s capital, is in the valley. It is one of the twenty largest cities in the world! About 22 million people live in the Mexico City area while about 130 million people live in the entire country of Mexico. Mexico City.
pages.brief: A map-like view of Mexico in North America shows the United States to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the south. The country is divided into northern, central, and southern areas. Mexico City sits in the Valley of Mexico, with a crowded urban area suggesting about 22 million people in the capital region.

pages.text: Mexico’s States The land in Mexico covers 756,066 square miles (1,972,550 sq km). How big is that? Well, you could fit about five countries the size of Mexico into the United States. I bet you didn’t know that Mexico has states, too. It has 31 states and a federal district. All of these areas have cool places to visit! Mexico’s blue water and landforms are as diverse as its people and culture.
pages.brief: A wide view of Mexico’s land shows 31 states and a federal district, with blue water and varied landforms across the country. The scene stretches from coast to interior, suggesting the land covers 756,066 square miles. Diverse landscapes hint at the many cool places to visit within Mexico.

pages.text: Mexico’s many unique landform regions include the Mexican plateau, the central plateau, Gulf Coastal Plain, Pacific Coastal Lowlands, southern highlands, Chiapas Highlands, Tabasco Plain, the Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) Peninsula, Sierra Madre Occidental and Sierra Madre Oriental, and the Sonoran Desert. If you review that list, you’ll notice that very few sound alike. Chihuahuan Desert Sonoran Desert.
pages.brief: A varied landform scene shows the Mexican plateau, central plateau, Gulf Coastal Plain, Pacific Coastal Lowlands, southern highlands, Chiapas Highlands, Tabasco Plain, Yucatán Peninsula, Sierra Madre Occidental, Sierra Madre Oriental, and the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts. The regions look different from one another, with deserts, highlands, plains, and peninsula landscapes.

pages.text: Ring of Fire Do You Know? Volcán Pico de Orizaba has not erupted since 1687. No one climbed it until 1848. The volcano is the third highest in North America. Do you know what the first two highest points are? Since Mexico is a diverse land, it ranks third in the world for the most varied plant and animal species. Did you know that Mexico is also in the “Ring of Fire”? That means that it is located in an area where volcanoes in the Pacific Ocean are very active. I hope you will take the time to visit Mexico’s Volcán Pico de Orizaba. This is a fascinating dormant volcano and the country’s highest point. It rises to 18,406 feet (5,610 m). From cities to rural areas, from deserts to rainforests, from wetlands to canyons, Mexico has every kind of environment you’re looking for! Let’s explore more about my country.
pages.brief: Volcán Pico de Orizaba rises as a dormant volcano and Mexico’s highest point at 18,406 feet. Around it are diverse plants and animals, suggesting Mexico’s varied species. The scene also hints at the Pacific Ring of Fire, with active volcanoes in the distance. Deserts, rainforests, wetlands, and canyons appear as part of Mexico’s environments.

pages.text: When to Visit One thing to keep in mind is that Mexico’s climate along the coast is hot and humid. If you don’t like hot and humid weather, you should plan your trip from October through May. Of course, the temperatures are almost always milder inland and in the mountains. If you love dry weather, try visiting Baja (BAH-hah) California or the Sonoran or Chihuahuan Deserts. It is dry in these places year-round. Cacti in the Sonoran Desert in Baja California.
pages.brief: Cacti stand in the Sonoran Desert in Baja California under dry, sunny weather. The open desert contrasts with hot and humid coastal areas and shows a place that stays dry year-round. Mild, comfortable conditions suggest why visitors might plan a trip from October through May, while inland and mountain areas look milder.

pages.text: My Country’s History Before the Spanish conquered the Aztecs in 1521, Mexico was part of what is called Mesoamerica. The Olmecs, Maya, Teotihuacán (tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN), Toltec, and the Aztec peoples lived in Mesoamerica for a long time before the Spanish arrived. You can visit some of the buildings they left behind such as temples, pyramids, and even ball courts! The Aztecs were the most powerful of the Mesoamerican civilizations. The Spanish invasion of the Aztecs changed the people and the land. Spain sent some of its people to live here. Spanish colonizers forced many Indigenous peoples to abandon their own religions to become Catholic. Colonizers also forced Indigenous peoples to learn Spanish. Although many Indigenous languages are no longer spoken, about 1.5 million people speak Náhuatl, the language of the Aztec Empire. Today Spanish is the official language of Mexico. Mexico was a colony of Spain until 1810. Many Mexicans revolted against Spain, and in 1821, Mexico officially won its independence. It is now a republic.
pages.brief: A historical scene of Mesoamerica before the Spanish conquest shows Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacán, Toltec, and Aztec peoples and the temples, pyramids, and ball courts they left behind. Spanish colonizers arrive, changing religion and language. The Aztec Empire is shown as powerful, and Mexico’s later revolt leads to independence in 1821 and a republic.

pages.text: Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlán, capital of the Aztec Empire Mexico City Now, let’s begin our tour of some of the great cities to visit. We’ll begin in the heart of Mexico— Mexico City. When the Aztecs ruled, it was called Tenochtitlán (tay-nohch-teet-LAHN). Many of the ancient ruins in and around Mexico City were built by the Aztecs. The Templo Mayor (Great Temple) was actually the site of the capital of the Aztec Empire. It was built during the 1300s and 1400s. The Spanish tried to bury it, but in 1978 the amazing temple’s ruins were uncovered. It is now a museum.
pages.brief: The Templo Mayor ruins in Tenochtitlán, capital of the Aztec Empire, stand in Mexico City. The Great Temple was built in the 1300s and 1400s, then buried by the Spanish; its ruins were uncovered in 1978. The site is now a museum, with ancient stone remains in the heart of the modern city.

pages.text: In Mexico City, there are many cathedrals and other examples of Spanish architecture. The largest cathedral in Latin America is Catedral Metropolitana. Would you believe it took nearly 300 years to build? Throughout the city you can see painted or sculpted art by famous Mexican artists. One of the most well known is muralist Diego Rivera. From 1929 to 1935, he painted murals showing Mexican history in the courtyard of the Palacio Nacional (pah-LAH-see-oh nah-see-oh-NAHL). The site of the palace has been home to many rulers. Moctezuma, who was an Aztec emperor, lived on the same site before the Spanish conquest. After the Spanish conquest, it was home to Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés (air-NAHN kor-TESS). Today, the offices of Mexico’s president are inside. The palace faces the Plaza de la Constitución (often called the Zócalo). This is one of the world’s largest public squares. Mexico City’s largest park is another major attraction. This was where the Aztecs used to spend their summer vacations! You can spend a part of your vacation at Bosque de Chapultepec (BOHSS-keh DEH chah-pool-teh-PEK), too. You can visit a zoo or botanical garden, buy a balloon or a snack, and then visit museums or art galleries and not even leave the park!
pages.brief: Mexico City shows the Catedral Metropolitana, the largest cathedral in Latin America, taking nearly 300 years to build. Nearby, Diego Rivera’s murals in the Palacio Nacional show Mexican history, and the palace faces the huge Zócalo. Bosque de Chapultepec offers a zoo, botanical garden, balloons, snacks, museums, and art galleries in one large park.

pages.text: There are other art museums and centers throughout the city, including the Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Dolores Olmedo Patiño, Museo Mural Diego Rivera, Museo Frida Kahlo, and many, many more. Frida Kahlo was a self-taught painter known for her bold self-portraits. My favorite painting of hers has a monkey in it! Self-portrait with Monkey by Frida Kahlo However, if shopping is what you want to do while in Mexico City, you won’t be disappointed at the Bazar del Sábado (Saturday Market) in the Plaza San Jacinto in the San Ángel neighborhood. You can buy Mexican fruits, vegetables, or even candy, at the Mercado de la Merced. Candy at the Saturday Market.
pages.brief: Frida Kahlo’s bold self-portrait with a monkey appears beside a view of Mexico City art museums and centers, including the Palacio de Bellas Artes and Museo Frida Kahlo. The Bazar del Sábado in Plaza San Jacinto shows Mexican fruits, vegetables, and candy at the Saturday Market and Mercado de la Merced.

pages.text: Central and Southern Mexico Just northwest of Mexico City, you can find more examples of Spanish colonial architecture. Sometimes this area is called the Colonial Heartland. It is also the heart of Mexico’s rich agriculture. The Spanish built many cities and towns here to take advantage of the silver deposits. If you visit the city of Taxco, southwest of Mexico City, you can find many beautiful silver shops. Farther west there are many beaches. One place known for its beaches is Acapulco (ah-kah-POOL-koh). Decades ago, Puerto Vallarta became a popular beach resort for Hollywood stars. Spanish colonial architecture If you get tired of the beach, you can visit the city of Colima. Colima has been rebuilt over and over again because frequent earthquakes continually damage it.
pages.brief: Spanish colonial architecture stands in the Colonial Heartland northwest of Mexico City, an area rich in agriculture and silver. Taxco shows beautiful silver shops, while Acapulco and Puerto Vallarta offer beaches. Colima appears as a city rebuilt after frequent earthquakes. The scene includes towns, silver deposits, beaches, and earthquake damage.

pages.text: Guadalajara is the country’s second largest city after Mexico City. There are many great places to visit in Guadalajara (gwah- dah-lah-HAH-rah). There is the city’s famous Cathedral, which took more than two centuries to build. You can take a short walk from the Cathedral and see a lot of Spanish colonial architecture. But like many regions in Mexico, you can also just enjoy being outside! The country’s largest lake, Lago de Chapala, is a great place to go boating. You may want to check out the waterfalls, tropics, and mountains at Huasteca Potosina (wahss-TEH-kah poh-toh-SEE-nah) located in the state of San Luis Potosí. I also recommend that you take a boat ride to see Tamul waterfall. It drops 344 feet into a canyon! The Cathedral at Guadalajara Fishermen at Lago de Chapala, Mexico.
pages.brief: Guadalajara, Mexico’s second largest city, shows its famous Cathedral and Spanish colonial architecture. Nearby, fishermen work at Lago de Chapala, the country’s largest lake, with boats on the water. Huasteca Potosina in San Luis Potosí shows waterfalls, tropics, and mountains, including Tamul waterfall dropping 344 feet into a canyon.

pages.text: Central and southern Mexico have many ancient ruins of Mesoamerican civilizations. Teotihuacán is probably one of the greatest examples of all Mesoamerican cities. It has two great ancient temples: the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, which people visit more than any other Mesoamerican site. Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacán So what was Teotihuacán? It was once a place where about 125,000 people lived in about ce 400. The word Teotihuacán means “the place where gods were created.” People who lived there were called Teotihuacanos, but many different Indigenous peoples inhabited Teotihuacán. At that time, it was one of the world’s largest cities. Monte Albán (MOHN-teh ahl-BAHN) in the state of Oaxaca (wah-HAH-kah) was a city of the Zapotec people. You can visit what was their ceremonial site on top of a mountain! At one time, this was also a cultural center for the Olmec and the Teotihuacanos. Pyramid of the Moon at Teotihuac á n.
pages.brief: Teotihuacán shows the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, great ancient temples visited by many people. The city once held about 125,000 people around ce 400 and was one of the world’s largest cities. Monte Albán in Oaxaca appears as a Zapotec ceremonial site on a mountain, also a cultural center for Olmec and Teotihuacanos.

pages.text: El Tajin in Veracruz The Gulf Coast and Yucatán Peninsula Moving out to the tropical plains and jungle of the Gulf Coast, we find land that was once home to several Mesoamerican cultures, including the Maya, Olmec, and Totonac. Olmec artifacts are all over this region, especially in the Parque-Museo de La Venta. Mayan hieroglyphics You can visit ancient pyramids at El Tajin. This was a major religious center for the Totonac who lived here between ce 900 and 1150. Or you can check out Quiahuiztlán (kee-uh-weet-ZLAN), a hilltop city where some 15,000 Totonac people once lived.
pages.brief: El Tajin in Veracruz appears as an ancient pyramid and major religious center for the Totonac people between ce 900 and 1150. Mayan hieroglyphics are shown, and Olmec artifacts fill the Parque-Museo de La Venta. Quiahuiztlán is a hilltop city where about 15,000 Totonac people once lived on the Gulf Coast.

pages.text: Mayan ancient ball court The Mayan ruins at Chichén Itzá are the best preserved of anything the Maya left behind. There are temples, Mexico’s largest ancient ball court, and an observatory. The Maya were fascinated with looking at the stars, just like me! They even had their own writing system. Uxmal is another Mayan site that you should visit. Most of the Spanish cities and towns in the Yucatán were actually built on top of Mayan ruins. What other cool things are there to see and do on the Gulf Coast? Just about everything! There are many museums, cathedrals, and churches. Don’t forget to stop in the city of Veracruz! The waterfront promenade and arcades are a lot of fun. Like the Colonial Heartland, this region is also a center for agriculture. Sugarcane, cacao (yum!), and coffee are grown here. Coffee beans.
pages.brief: Chichén Itzá shows Mayan temples, Mexico’s largest ancient ball court, and an observatory, with the Maya studying the stars and using their own writing system. Uxmal is another Mayan site. On the Gulf Coast, Veracruz has a waterfront promenade and arcades, while sugarcane, cacao, and coffee grow in the agricultural region.

pages.text: The Yucatán Peninsula is also well known for its white sand beaches, and has plenty of them considering it’s surrounded by water on three sides, like Baja California. The world’s second longest barrier reef (after Australia’s) is located near the islands of Cozumel and Isla Mujeres (EESS- lah moo-HEH-ress). It is a popular place to snorkel and scuba dive. Cancún is probably the most popular spot to get a suntan. This region is well known for its breathtaking natural wells called cenotes. Probably the most visited one is the Cenote de Dzitnup (si- NOH-tee day ZEET-nup) near Valladolid (bah-yah- doh-LEED). Can you believe that it was discovered only a half century ago? Scuba lessons Great Mesoamerican Reef near Cozumel and Isla Mujeres.
pages.brief: The Yucatán Peninsula shows white sand beaches surrounded by water on three sides. Near Cozumel and Isla Mujeres lies the world’s second longest barrier reef, a popular place for snorkeling and scuba diving. Cancún is a sunny spot for a suntan, and the Cenote de Dzitnup near Valladolid appears as a breathtaking natural well.

pages.text: Copper Canyon in Northern Mexico Northern Mexico Many of Mexico’s deserts, mountains, and canyons are located here. You might have heard of the Grand Canyon in the United States, but did you know that Copper Canyon is even bigger? It is more than one mile deep and part of the Sierra Madre Occidental range. You can take a train to get a close-up view of this deep canyon, its waterfalls, and lakes. The Rarámuri (rah-RAH-moo-ree) people who live there are famous for the drums and violins they make. If you are looking for great beaches and resorts, like Cabo San Lucas, then Baja California is the place for you. It is a peninsula, so water is around three of its sides. In the winter, you can even spot whales swimming along the shore as they migrate south! Cabo San Lucas in Baja California.
pages.brief: Copper Canyon in northern Mexico is deeper than the Grand Canyon, more than one mile deep in the Sierra Madre Occidental range. A train gives a close-up view of the canyon, waterfalls, and lakes. The Rarámuri people make drums and violins. Baja California shows Cabo San Lucas beaches and resorts, with whales migrating south offshore in winter.

pages.text: You won’t find any Aztec ruins in Baja. Why? Because the Aztecs didn’t live here! But you can find some ancient cave paintings. Many believe the ancestors of the Cochimi painted the cave pictures. They show people and animals in black and red. Cave paintings at Baja California Probably the most amazing ancient ruins in this region are the adobe buildings at Paquimé (pah-kee-MEH). Adobe is a brick made with mud and grass. Often many bricks were used to create buildings that look like today’s apartment buildings. Between the 900s and 1300s, more than 3,000 people lived in adobe buildings near the Casas Grandes river. No one really knows what happened to the people who lived there. Ancient ruins at Paquim é.
pages.brief: Baja California shows ancient cave paintings with people and animals in black and red, attributed to ancestors of the Cochimi. No Aztec ruins appear here. In northern Mexico, Paquimé shows adobe buildings like apartment houses, where more than 3,000 people lived between the 900s and 1300s near the Casas Grandes river.

pages.text: If you’re not interested in ruins or the beach, you may enjoy whale watching in a boat. In Guerrero Negro, blue whales are often spotted along the Sea of Cortés. If you get seasick, you can visit them and many other sea mammals on land at the nearby Laguna San Ignacio, Bahia de Magdalena. Cultural center in San Miguel de Allende A whale dives, showing its tail in the Sea of Cortés. Mexico has vibrant culture, breathtaking land, beautiful waters, abundant history, and delicious food. You have to agree: Mexico has much to offer—so come visit!
pages.brief: A blue whale dives in the Sea of Cortés near Guerrero Negro, showing its tail during whale watching. On land at Laguna San Ignacio and Bahia de Magdalena, other sea mammals can be seen. A cultural center in San Miguel de Allende appears, along with Mexico’s vibrant culture, land, waters, history, and food.

books.title: Energy Sources: The Pros and Cons
books.art_why: The book covers real modern energy technology, places, and equipment that can all be photographed.

pages.text: The Endless Need for Energy The United States is a modern society. Like all modern societies, it uses a lot of energy. Scientists define energy as the ability to do work. Many kinds of things can be called work. Getting an automobile to move down a road or an airplane to fly is work, and so is producing electricity or running the machinery in a factory. The energy used by the United States and other modern societies comes from many sources. Much of it comes from the burning of fuels, such as coal and gasoline. Other energy comes from the power of flowing water, from the light of the Sun, the wind, or from the splitting of atoms. Machines in this car factory need energy to build cars.
pages.brief: Inside a large car factory, industrial machines assemble automobiles along a production line. The factory represents a modern society that uses energy for work such as moving vehicles, producing electricity, and running machinery. Energy comes from burning coal and gasoline, flowing water, sunlight, wind, and splitting atoms.

pages.text: All energy sources have their pros and cons— their good points and bad points. Modern societies have to make many decisions about how best to produce energy. The needs of the society have to be balanced against the need to protect the environment. These choices are not always easy to make. Energy Use in the United States, 1949–2005 The United States uses more energy than it produces. What does this tell you about the energy future of the United States?
